原始最终答案（英文）
# The two Arabian Sea chlorophyll blooms in CMEMS monthly chlorophyll, nitrate and oxygen, 2011-2020

## Summary

Both blooms are present and well defined in the supplied fields. The western Arabian Sea summer bloom is the dominant signal of the domain: 2,529 cells (1.909x10^6 km^2) over 4-22N / 47-62E, rising in July and peaking in **August at 0.859 mg m^-3** area-mean surface chlorophyll, with chl > 0.5 mg m^-3 over 1.313x10^6 km^2 (29.4% of the 4.472x10^6 km^2 ocean domain) in August and a >2 mg m^-3 core on the Oman coast. The northern winter bloom is 3.7x smaller in area (722 cells, 0.515x10^6 km^2, 20-26N / 58-70E), peaks in **February at 0.421 mg m^-3**, is 2-3x weaker in surface magnitude, and no monthly mean anywhere in the north reaches 1.0 mg m^-3. Year to year the north is steady (JFM mean 0.359 mg m^-3, CV 8%, never absent, peak February in 8 of 10 years) and the west more variable (JJAS mean 0.613, CV 12%, 2015 the weak year at -23%); **no monotonic trend is distinguishable from interannual variability in either bloom**. On controls, only two of fifteen candidate mechanisms survive the supplied fields (a shared vertical-displacement clock; a cross-shore, monsoon-upwelling-type supply geometry for the western bloom), four are contradicted, and the rest cannot be tested. The single strongest positive statement is that both peaks occur in the same month as the surface-nitrate maximum and neither bloom is nitrate-exhausted at its peak, so **nitrate supply rate rather than nitrate availability is the limiting link - and a rate cannot be measured from these three fields**. The decisive caveats are that this product performs **no data assimilation** (chlorophyll is a free-running model field, not satellite observation), and that the product's own documentation states it does **not** reproduce the Pakistan-coast winter bloom in January-March.

## What the data are

All three supplied variables are monthly means on a 0.25° grid, 46 levels from 0.5 m to 947 m, 2011-2020, in 47-70E / 4-26N, and each NetCDF file contains exactly one data variable (`chl`, `no3`, `o2`) plus the coordinates. Product documentation (product page, PUM Issue 2.3, QUID Issue 1.2) establishes that GLOBAL_MULTIYEAR_BGC_001_029 is a **hindcast with no data assimilation**: ocean-colour chlorophyll and WOA climatologies enter only as validation targets, and the physical forcing is the assimilation-free twin FREEGLORYS2V4. This matters for every result below: chlorophyll, nitrate and oxygen are three fields of one free-running model, so every relationship reported here is **internal model consistency**, not observation, and nothing here demonstrates a real-ocean mechanism.

Numbers computed on different region definitions are not interchangeable and are kept separate below: the objectively classified bloom regions (B1.1), the diagnostic boxes (B1.3), the interannual boxes (B1.2), and the sector partitions (B1.1.1.1, B1.1.2) differ in extent.

## Where and when each bloom occurs

**Western summer bloom.** 4-22N / 47-62E, centroid 11.6N / 55.9E; rise from June, bloom season **July-September**, area-mean surface chlorophyll peaking in **August at 0.859 mg m^-3** (Jul 0.700, Sep 0.592) against an April minimum of 0.110 mg m^-3, a 7.8-fold seasonal amplitude. The spatial pattern decays eastward from the western boundary (1.4 mg m^-3 at 4N/47E) and narrows to the Oman coast at 15-20N, where the >2 mg m^-3 core sits at 17.3-17.8N / 55.2-56.6E. Within this region the coastal core (196 cells, 0.145x10^6 km^2, centred 17.1N/55.2E, August area-mean 3.24 mg m^-3) and the offshore component (1,811 cells, 1.371x10^6 km^2, August 0.545 mg m^-3) **cannot be separated by onset or evolution**: both begin rising in late June and both peak in August, their area-weighted cycles correlate r = 0.97 at zero lag, and a single EOF mode explains 88.4% of the seasonal-anomaly variance. The difference is amplitude and spatial scale, not timing; the coastal core is 5.7-5.9x the offshore mean in Jul-Aug and carries the region's interannual variability (its JJAS anomalies correlate +0.93 with local surface nitrate, the offshore anomalies +0.22, not significant at n = 10). Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-472514a2eb/outputs/arabian-sea-summer-bloom-coastal-vs-offshore.png`.

**Northern winter bloom.** 20-26N / 58-70E; bloom season **January-March**, area-mean surface chlorophyll peaking in **February at 0.421 mg m^-3** (Jan 0.349, Mar 0.239) against a November minimum of 0.127 mg m^-3, a 3.3-fold amplitude. It is not a buried signal: the February vertical maximum sits at 30.9 m and exceeds the top level by only 5% (0.441 versus 0.421 mg m^-3 at 0.5058 m), no February shows a subsurface maximum more than 1.26x its surface value, and 104% of the +12.1 mg m^-2 November-to-February column gain lies above 41 m. The permanent deep chlorophyll maximum of the region (0.35-0.44 mg m^-3 at ~40-80 m) shoals to ~31 m and merges with the surface layer in January-February but contributes nothing to the winter anomaly. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-d500ad52a5/outputs/north-winter-bloom-vertical-structure.png`.

Within the north the February signal is systematically stronger and shallower coastward - 0.485 mg m^-3 in the Gulf of Oman sector and 0.450 on the Iran-Pakistan side against 0.374 in the open interior (+30% and +20%), with the coastal (<=80 km) excess present in 10 of 10 Februaries - but the difference is modest and box averaging is not what makes the bloom small: the coastal strip is only 24% of the box area and lifts the box mean by 3.7%, and the February maximum-to-surface ratio is only 1.02-1.11 in every sector. No sector hides a strong bloom. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-efd09db0c8/outputs/north-feb-coastal-vs-open.png`.

The 10-year bimodal cycle that separates the two blooms is shown in `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-0914ad8119/outputs/arabian-sea-bloom-climatology.png`.

## How large each bloom is

| property (10-year climatology) | western summer bloom | northern winter bloom |
|---|---|---|
| bloom area | 1.909x10^6 km^2 (2,529 cells) | 0.515x10^6 km^2 (722 cells) |
| season / peak month | Jul-Sep / August | Jan-Mar / February |
| area-mean surface chl at peak | 0.859 mg m^-3 | 0.421 mg m^-3 |
| seasonal amplitude (peak/min) | 7.8x (Apr 0.110) | 3.3x (Nov 0.127) |
| area > 0.5 mg m^-3 at peak | 1.313x10^6 km^2 (29.4% of domain) | 0.124x10^6 km^2 (2.8%) |
| area > 1.0 mg m^-3 at peak | 0.368-0.440x10^6 km^2 (Jul-Aug) | 0 (no monthly mean reaches 1.0) |

The summer bloom is therefore the dominant term of the domain mean (0.442 mg m^-3 in August versus 0.222 in February, minima 0.116 in April and 0.130 in November), about 2x the northern bloom in surface magnitude and 3.7x in area. The magnitudes are product-specific: the northern values are well below the published benchmark of >2 mg m^-3 open-ocean chlorophyll in the record February 2008 bloom, and the product's QUID states explicitly that the model does not reproduce the Pakistan-coast winter bloom in January-February-March.

## How each bloom varies from year to year

**The north is the steadier bloom.** On the interannual box 21-26N / 55-70E (0.53x10^6 km^2) the JFM regional-mean surface chlorophyll ranges 0.326-0.418 mg m^-3 (mean 0.359, SD 0.030, CV 8%), the peak month is February in 8 of 10 years and January in 2018 and 2020, and the bloom is never absent. Weakest years are 2013, 2020 and 2016 (8-9% below the mean, all still >= 0.326 mg m^-3); strongest are 2014 and 2019.

**The west is more variable.** On the box 8-22N / 47-62E (1.61x10^6 km^2) the JJAS mean ranges 0.472-0.710 mg m^-3 (mean 0.613, SD 0.076, CV 12%, strongest year 1.5x the weakest) and July-August-September peaks in **August in 10 of 10 years**. 2015 is the clear weak year (-23%, with 2 instead of 3 months above threshold and anomalous area 0.7%); 2011 and 2018 are strongest. No year shows an absent or double bloom in either region.

**Extent is the most variable property, and it is also the least robust metric.** The western box area exceeding 1.5x its own monthly climatology in the peak month ranges 0.7-20.8% (CV 65%), while the northern box is nearly saturated every year (74-99% of its area above 0.30 mg m^-3). Intensity and extent do not rank years consistently. Figures: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/statistics-92374dac1f/outputs/bloom-interannual-metrics.png` and `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/statistics-92374dac1f/outputs/bloom-trend-vs-variability.png`.

**No trend is distinguishable from interannual variability.** All annual OLS slopes are <= 0.06 units per decade with p >= 0.42; the 80%-power minimum detectable trends are 31-45% of the mean bloom value per decade. A monthly model with an explicit seasonal cycle does not help, because for a trend common to all calendar months it is **algebraically the same estimator** as the annual regression (slopes identical to <= 3e-16), and after removing the 12-month cycle the effective sample for a trend is 10 years, not 120 months; the minimum detectable monotone trend is then about 20-25% of the mean bloom intensity per decade (36-45% for extent metrics). Sub-monthly resolution was never available, so within-month ordering cannot be checked. **Correction applied here:** an earlier statement that the northern anomalous-extent trend flipped sign (+0.030 to -0.005 per decade) when a free-period oscillation was allowed does not reproduce for the metric as defined - the flip belongs to a differently defined column - and the honest out-of-sample test shows the apparent step advantage over a trend is an artefact of a searched breakpoint, with trend, step and free-period oscillation statistically **unresolvable** at 10 annual values. The conclusions to carry forward are therefore: no detection, and no ability to distinguish the competing shapes.

**Weak years are not years of weak chlorophyll at unchanged nutrient supply.** In the west, August 2015 combines chlorophyll -20% with a 13% lower 0-100 m nitrate inventory, a nutricline 6-14 m deeper and 100 m oxygen 6% higher. In the north, 2013 + 2016 + 2020 combine mean chlorophyll -7% with a 25% lower February 0-100 m nitrate inventory and a nutricline ~6 m deeper, while the strongest years 2014 + 2019 show chlorophyll +11%, nitrate +44% and a nutricline 19 m shallower. Oxygen shows no consistent relationship with bloom strength (the weak western year has *more* oxygen at 100 m). Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-c012258f18/outputs/bloom-weak-year-nutrient-oxygen-anomalies.png`.

**Do not read the deep trends as ocean change.** The only resolvable decadal changes in the nutrient and oxygen fields sit below the bloom layer (300-900 m nitrate -26.5% per decade in the northern box, perfectly monotonic with Kendall tau = -1.00; 300-900 m oxygen -33% per decade in the western box), and an independent check finds the modelled subsurface oxygen drifting at -11.9 micromol L^-1 per decade in the southern domain, 6-15x the published Arabian Sea decline, with the modelled oxygen-minimum core pinned at a hard 1.0 micromol L^-1 floor below ~460 m in the Gulf of Oman. This is the signature of reanalysis drift, not of a changing ocean, and it also makes the oxygen field **unusable for interannual attribution or saturation/AOU arguments**. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-1c4d7db42c/outputs/arabian-sea-o2-interannual-2011-2020.png`.

**A published extreme cannot be used as a benchmark here.** The widely cited "~50% lower February chlorophyll in 2016" traces to a single abstract sentence (Vidya & Kurian 2018, J. Mar. Syst. 186, 96-104) and is a bio-Argo float value in the northeastern Arabian Sea, February only, against an unspecified normal year - not a satellite or regional-mean statistic. It is not comparable with the 8-9% JFM box reduction measured here, and a like-for-like comparison is not possible in this search-only literature mode. The February 2008 record bloom also falls outside the 2011-2020 window.

## What controls each bloom: what the supplied fields support, contradict, and cannot test

**Timing and the nitrate link.** The surface-nitrate maximum and the surface-chlorophyll maximum fall in the **same calendar month in every year examined** (north: February in 7 of 9 complete seasons, January in 2018 and 2020; west: August in 10 of 10), and the drawdown timing is consistent across years (western surface nitrate falls to <=25% of its August peak in October in 10 of 10 years). At monthly resolution the supply **never leads** the chlorophyll: in the north the chlorophyll increase actually begins in December, a month before the nitrate pulse. Neither bloom is nitrate-exhausted at its peak (February 0.435 mmol m^-3 in the north; August 1.224 mmol m^-3 in the west, corrected from an earlier 1.150 in the same box - a ~6% mask-related offset that remains unresolved). The 0-30 m surface layers, by contrast, are drawn down >96%. Taken together this is **consistent with** nitrate supply rate, rather than nitrate availability, being the limiting link, and that rate is not measurable here.

**The northern December onset is redistribution, not new production.** Surface chlorophyll rises from November to December in 10 of 10 years while 0-10 m nitrate sits at its cold-season minimum (0.065 mmol m^-3, 7-13% of a 0.5-1 mmol m^-3 half-saturation) and every nitrate isopleth from 0.1 to 5 mmol m^-3 **deepens** (the 0-100 m inventory falls in 10 of 10 years). The 0-100 m chlorophyll inventory does not increase: +1.36 mg m^-2 in 0-30 m is offset by -1.30 at 30-70 m and -0.46 at 70-100 m. A nutrient-supply explanation is thereby excluded, while light-driven or advection-related explanations are not decided (no irradiance, mixed-layer depth or velocity fields). Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-1e3986dca9/outputs/north-december-onset-diagnostics.png`.

**The western bloom's supply geometry is cross-shore and subsurface-led.** Within the Omani-Somali upwelling sector (14-22N / 53-61E) the nitracline shoals as a whole-column, offshore-directed progression: with alongshore position held fixed the amplitude-normalised half-shoaling month of the 1 mmol m^-3 nitrate horizon depends on distance from the coast (per-year partial r = +0.47, positive in 10 of 10 years), while with distance held fixed the alongshore effect is ~0. No alongshore (Somali-to-Omani) phase progression is detectable, and the surface signal is never decoupled from the subsurface: no sample with 0-10 m nitrate >= 1 mmol m^-3 has the 1 mmol m^-3 horizon deeper than 50 m. The subsurface shoaling leads the surface by about one month. This is **consistent with** monsoon-upwelling-type cross-shore supply, which the absent wind and mixing fields cannot demonstrate and whose speed the monthly sampling cannot measure. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-ab18793b75/outputs/nitracline-shoaling-cross-shore-vs-alongshore.png`.

**The northern coastal enhancement is not a nutrient-supply feature, and the north is where chlorophyll and nitrate decouple.** In the northern box the 1 mmol m^-3 nitrate isopleth is *not* shallower at the coast than in adjacent open water (10-year February means 57.5 m at Gulf-of-Oman coastal cells versus 44.6 m in the Gulf-of-Oman interior; 127.3 m on the Pakistan shelf versus 85.6 m off-shelf), coastal water at 108 m is *better* oxygenated than open water in 10 of 10 Februaries (the opposite sign to an enhanced-production signature), and the Gulf-of-Oman February nitrate high (surface 0.777 versus 0.305 mmol m^-3; upper-50 m stock 40.1 versus 15.5 mmol m^-2) spans coastal and interior cells alike - a marginal-sea property, not a coastal fringe. The Pakistan shelf strip is the opposite end-member of the same chlorophyll value: 0.448 mg m^-3 chlorophyll with 0.13 mmol m^-3 surface nitrate, 60% of columns never reaching 1 mmol m^-3 anywhere, and its own nitrate maximum in August (0.97 mmol m^-3) while its chlorophyll peaks in January-February. The same February chlorophyll therefore coexists with a nitrate surplus in the Gulf of Oman and a nitrate vacuum on the shelf. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-be4fb7a3bd/outputs/north-feb-nutrient-oxygen-coherence.png`.

**That decoupling is specific to the north.** In the western bloom box the modelled August chlorophyll and nitrate are spatially coherent (per-cell Spearman r = +0.84; +0.91 for the 0-50 m inventories), the 1 mmol m^-3 isopleth is shallower where chlorophyll is higher (r = -0.90), both share the same coastward gradient in 10 of 10 Augusts, the chlorophyll-to-nitrate ratio is nearly constant across coast, mid and offshore bands (0.73 / 0.74 / 0.75 mg m^-3 per mmol m^-3), and only 1.3% of the bloom area is "decoherenced" (chlorophyll > 0.4 with surface nitrate < 0.2) against 16.9% of the northern box. Western coastal water is *less* oxygenated in August (118.0 / 66.1 / 41.1 mmol m^-3 at 50 / 100 / 150 m versus 200.7 / 154.4 / 77.5 offshore), the opposite of the northern contrast. Why the northern sectors decouple (marginal-sea geometry, shelf truncation, or the convective supply itself) is not established, because the two are confounded with geometry. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-51fea75c74/outputs/bloom-chl-nitrate-coupling-west-vs-north.png`.

**The nitrate budget is sufficiency, not closure - and it is now corrected.** An earlier closure (drawdown 92 mmol N m^-2 north, 337 west, exceeding the chlorophyll nitrogen demand 4-50x; break-even chlorophyll-to-carbon 54 north / 90 west) was superseded by a displacement decomposition: **62-92% of that drawdown is vertical displacement of the nutricline**, so the consumption-relevant 0-100 m residual falls to 4.6 (north) and 13.0 (west) mmol N m^-2 and the break-even values to **27 (north) and 30 (west)**. The imported-supply term cannot be closed at all, because every supply expression is an unmeasured transport coefficient times an observed gradient: the western removal of 39.1 mmol N m^-2 needs K_z = 6.0x10^-5 (onset) to 3.1x10^-5 m^2 s^-1 (drawdown), inside the plausible range, whereas the northern phase gain of 9.8 mmol N m^-2 would need K_z ~ 5.8x10^-4 m^2 s^-1, an order of magnitude above canonical thermocline values - **more plausibly mixed-layer entrainment of ~10 m of ~1 mmol m^-3 nutricline water across the 65 m nutricline than diffusion across 30 m**, though not demonstrated. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-f7ee481c7f/outputs/bloom-nitrate-vertical-supply-split.png`.

**Nitrate carry-over does not predict the next bloom.** The end-of-drawdown 0-100 m residual has no demonstrated predictive relation to the following season's peak (west: r = -0.13, p = 0.74, n = 9 lagged pairs; north: nominal r = -0.70, p = 0.035, but the residual trends +7.2 mmol m^-2 yr^-1 while the next peak drifts down, and the detrended value is r = -0.50, p = 0.17). Only 2 of 10 primary tests reach p < 0.05 where 0.5 is expected by chance and their signs are mutually inconsistent, while the same fields do resolve a real relation of similar size: the concurrent bloom-month nitrate stock correlates with the chlorophyll peak at r = +0.71 to +0.89. What covaries with the next bloom is the between-bloom recharge (r = +0.64 north, +0.58 west), which is not significant at n = 10 and whose driver is not in the supplied fields. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-35b3efde1c/outputs/nitrate-residual-vs-next-bloom.png`.

**Neither bloom leaves a detectable, independent oxygen signature.** The seasonal oxygen swing is overwhelmingly vertical displacement of the oxycline (in the western coastal core the 100 mmol m^-3 oxycline rises 72 m from February to September and that index alone explains 95-99% of the monthly oxygen variance between 41 and 200 m, r = 0.98-1.00; the first EOF holds 95.6% of the variance and correlates -0.99 with the displacement and +0.82 with surface chlorophyll, the chlorophyll correlation being inherited from shared timing). Interannually, oxycline displacement explains 90.7% of the 100 m oxygen scatter and chlorophyll adds 6.3%. **Correction applied here:** an earlier factor-of-two disagreement between the nitrate-implied and oxygen-implied displacements (73 m versus 38 m) was an artefact of a profile-normalisation error in that node's saved profiles; on correctly normalised valid-cell means the two tracers differ by at most 5 m in all 12 months (10 of 12 within 1 m; corrected values 52 m and 47 m), so the tracers do not disagree. The heave-corrected August subsurface deficit is correspondingly revised to 7.3-9.6 mmol m^-3 (from 5-7). A bloom-driven consumption term of that size cannot be excluded but is not demonstrated, and the unexplained near-surface oxygen excess of +50-60 mmol m^-3 cannot be attributed without temperature and salinity. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-c79bbd992d/outputs/arabian-sea-core-oxygen-heave-decomposition.png`.

**Verdicts.** Two candidate controls are evidence-consistent for their bloom: a shared vertical-displacement ("heave clock") for both blooms, and monsoon-upwelling-type cross-shore supply geometry for the western bloom. Four are contradicted by the supplied fields: local coastal or shelf nitrate supply in the north; nitrate limitation of bloom magnitude in **both** blooms; bloom-driven subsurface oxygen consumption in the north; and seasonal nitrate carry-over in both. The remainder - convective deepening and entrainment, light-limitation onset, lateral advection, iron/silicate co-limitation, grazing and loss, oxygen solubility/AOU reasoning, climate-index forcing, and any trend - cannot be tested at all with these three variables. Summary figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q18/attempt-1791178941549566813-7ac876c9/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q18--e41516ee5767/agents/ocean-process-cbcc7ffdb8/outputs/arabian-sea-bloom-control-verdicts.png`.

## What the absent temperature, mixing and wind data prevent concluding

The supplied NetCDFs contain only `chl`, `no3` and `o2` plus coordinates, and the parent product likewise outputs only biogeochemical fields: temperature, salinity, velocity and mixed-layer depth enter it as **external daily forcing** from the separate physics twin and are not delivered. Concretely, this prevents:

- **Testing the published winter mechanism.** The convective-mixing/nutrient-entrainment mechanism is defined by mixed-layer depth and its deepening rate; the entrainment term (w_e x delta-N) cannot be formed. A nitrate-only surrogate (February chlorophyll versus a nitracrine-depth proxy) gives r = +0.20 (n = 10) against the published r ~ 0.6-0.7 for mixed-layer-depth anomalies, so the surrogate does not reproduce it. Only nitrate-field proxies remain possible.
- **Testing the published summer mechanism.** Wind-stress curl and Ekman transport are needed for upwelling and offshore Ekman pumping; the observed cross-shore geometry is compatible with that mechanism but cannot demonstrate it, and no front speed can be measured.
- **Separating heave from local change.** No conservative density variable exists, so displacement must be inferred from the same non-conservative tracers it is meant to correct.
- **Any oxygen-budget or saturation argument.** Without temperature and salinity, oxygen saturation and apparent oxygen utilisation cannot be computed, so solubility, respiration and vertical displacement cannot be separated, and the modelled oxygen field's own drift and floor further block interannual use.
- **Attributing the remaining budget shortfall.** The imported-supply term is an unmeasured transport coefficient times an observed gradient, and a box-mean budget cannot distinguish vertical from lateral supply; without currents, advection cannot be quantified.
- **Testing the loss and co-limitation hypotheses.** Light limitation (needs mixed-layer depth and irradiance), iron/silicate limitation (the sibling BGC variables `fe`, `si`, `po4`, `nppv`, `phyc` exist in the parent product but were not supplied, and the user named only chlorophyll, nitrate and oxygen, so they were not acquired), grazing and mortality, and climate-index forcing (external indices not supplied) all remain untestable.

Two further limits bound the answer independently of the missing fields: the 0.25° monthly sampling sets a one-month floor on all timing statements and partly resolves only the narrow coastal upwelling jet, and the product is explicitly documented as not reproducing the Pakistan-coast winter bloom in January-February-March, so the northern results describe **the model's** bloom and cannot be treated as a calibrated observational record without an independent comparison (ocean colour), which was not supplied or requested.

## Research Tree

ROOT (B1, active): Characterize the two Arabian Sea chlorophyll blooms from CMEMS monthly chlorophyll, nitrate and oxygen, 2011-2020 (47-70E, 4-26N): where and when, how large, year-to-year variability, and controls - and state what the missing temperature, mixing and wind data prevent concluding.

- **B1.1 [completed]** Where and when does each bloom occur, and how large is it? - Two spatially separated blooms: western summer bloom 2,529 cells / 1.909x10^6 km^2 over 4-22N / 47-62E, July-September, August peak 0.859 mg m^-3 (April minimum 0.110, 7.8x amplitude), >0.5 mg m^-3 over 1.313x10^6 km^2 (29.4% of domain), >2 mg m^-3 core on the Oman coast; northern winter bloom 722 cells / 0.515x10^6 km^2 over 20-26N / 58-70E, January-March, February peak 0.421 mg m^-3 (November minimum 0.127, 3.3x), >0.5 mg m^-3 over only 0.124x10^6 km^2, no monthly mean reaching 1.0 mg m^-3.
  - **B1.1.1 [completed]** Is the northern bloom signal substantially subsurface? - No: February vertical maximum at 30.9 m, only 5% above the top level; 104% of the November-February column gain lies above 41 m; the bloom is genuinely weak, not buried, consistent with a 0.435 mmol m^-3 February surface nitrate maximum and a 1 mmol m^-3 isopleth near 70 m.
    - **B1.1.1.1 [completed]** Does the February signal differ between the Gulf of Oman / Iran-Pakistan coast and the open basin? - Yes but modestly: 0.485 and 0.450 mg m^-3 coastward versus 0.374 in the open interior (+30%, +20%), coastal excess in 10 of 10 Februaries, shallower profile maximum (26.6 m versus 35.7 m); box averaging lowers the mean by only 3.7% and no sector exceeds ~0.5 mg m^-3.
      - **B1.1.1.2 [completed]** Is that coastal enhancement a coherent nutrient-supply feature or a marginal-sea artefact? - Not a supply feature: the nitrate isopleth is **not** shallower at the coast (57.5 versus 44.6 m in the Gulf of Oman; 127.3 versus 85.6 m on the shelf), coastal 108 m water is better oxygenated in 10 of 10 Februaries, the Gulf-of-Oman nitrate high spans coastal and interior cells, and the Pakistan shelf strip carries 0.448 mg m^-3 chlorophyll with no nitrate standing stock at all - chlorophyll and nitrate are decoupled in the north.
    - **B1.1.2 [completed]** Can the western coastal core and offshore component be separated by onset? - No: both rise in late June and peak in August, r = 0.97 at zero lag, one EOF mode explains 88.4% of the seasonal-anomaly variance; the core is 5.7-5.9x the offshore mean and carries the region's interannual variability (its JJAS anomalies correlate +0.93 with local nitrate versus +0.22 offshore).
    - **B1.1.3 [completed]** Is the north's chlorophyll-nitrate decoupling present in the west? - No, it is specific to the north: the west is spatially coherent (per-cell Spearman r = +0.84, inventories +0.91, isopleth-depth r = -0.90, shared coastward gradients in 10 of 10 Augusts, near-constant chlorophyll-to-nitrate ratio 0.73-0.75 across all bands, only 1.3% of area decoherenced versus 16.9% in the north), and western coastal water is *less* oxygenated in August.
  - **B1.2 [completed]** How does each bloom vary year to year, and is any trend distinguishable? - North steadier (JFM mean 0.359 mg m^-3, CV 8%, peak February in 8 of 10 years, never absent, weak 2013/2020/2016, strong 2014/2019); west more variable (JJAS mean 0.613, CV 12%, peak August in 10 of 10, 2015 the weak year at -23%, 2011/2018 strongest); extent the most variable property (western anomalous area 0.7-20.8%, CV 65%); no trend distinguishable (slopes <= 0.06 per decade, p >= 0.42).
    - **B1.2.1 [completed]** Does a monthly seasonal-cycle model resolve a trend the annual series misses? - No: for a common trend the two estimators are algebraically identical (|difference| <= 3e-16), the effective sample is 10 years, and the minimum detectable monotone trend is 20-25% of the mean bloom intensity per decade (36-45% for extent).
    - **B1.2.2 [completed]** Do weak bloom years coincide with nutrient or oxygen anomalies? - Yes for nitrate, no for oxygen: August 2015 chlorophyll -20% with a 13% lower 0-100 m nitrate inventory and a 6-14 m deeper nutricline; 2013+2016+2020 chlorophyll -7% with a 25% lower February nitrate inventory and ~6 m deeper nutricline, while 2014+2019 show +11% chlorophyll and +44% nitrate with a 19 m shallower nutricline.
    - **B1.2.3 [closed]** Is the northern anomalous-extent "trend" robust to a level/step model? - Closed: subsumed by B1.2.4.
    - **B1.2.4 [completed]** Is the northern trend-like signal a trend, step or oscillation? - Unresolvable: the step advantage is a searched-breakpoint artefact (out-of-sample RMSE 10% worse than a constant), the free-period oscillation pins to the search-grid edge, trend beats step in only 5 of 10 leave-one-out folds (sign-test p = 1.0), and the reported sign flip does **not** reproduce for the metric as defined.
    - **B1.2.5 [completed]** Do the nutrient/oxygen series resolve a supply trend chlorophyll does not? - Only below the bloom layer, and those are drift: 300-900 m nitrate -26.5% per decade in the north (Kendall tau = -1.00), 300-900 m oxygen -33% per decade in the west, 0-300 m oxygen minimum -29% per decade. No trend is resolved in nutricline depth, surface or 0-100 m nitrate, or 0-100 m oxygen; the northern nutricline's seasonal range did shrink (52-54 m in 2011-2012 to 21-32 m in 2019-2020).

    - **B1.3.2 [completed]** Is there a genuine bloom-driven subsurface oxygen response in the western coastal core? - Predominantly displacement: the oxycline rises 72 m from February to September and explains 95-99% of the 41-200 m monthly oxygen variance (first EOF 95.6%, correlating -0.99 with displacement and +0.82 with chlorophyll); interannually, displacement explains 90.7% of the 100 m scatter and chlorophyll adds 6.3%.
    - **B1.3.3 [completed]** Does the nitrate budget close? - Sufficiency only, and later corrected: 0-100 m drawdown (92 north, 337 west mmol N m^-2) exceeds the chlorophyll nitrogen demand 4-50x for every stated chlorophyll-to-carbon, but the identity fails structurally because drawdown integrates consumption plus export while chlorophyll is only standing stock.
      - **B1.3.6 [completed]** Can the drawdown be split into consumption and imported supply? - Bounded only: 62-92% of the drawdown is nutricline displacement, leaving consumption-relevant residuals of 4.6 (north) and 13.0 (west) mmol N m^-2 and break-even chlorophyll-to-carbon of 27 and 30; the western removal needs K_z = 3.1-6.0x10^-5 m^2 s^-1 (plausible) while the northern gain needs ~5.8x10^-4 m^2 s^-1, an order of magnitude above canonical thermocline values, more plausibly mixed-layer entrainment than diffusion.
      - **B1.3.7 [completed]** Does the end-of-drawdown nitrate residual predict the next bloom? - No: west r = -0.13 (p = 0.74, n = 9); north nominal r = -0.70 (p = 0.035) but trend-confounded and -0.50 (p = 0.17) detrended; 2 of 10 tests significant where 0.5 is expected, with inconsistent signs, while the concurrent bloom-month nitrate stock correlates with the peak at r = +0.71 to +0.89.
      - **B1.3.8 [closed]** Does the western budget failure survive restriction to the coastal core? - Closed: B1.3.6 already removed the displacement term and showed the remaining ambiguity is an unmeasurable transport coefficient.
    - **B1.3.4 [completed]** Does the western nutrient onset propagate coastward year by year? - Spatially organised but mostly an amplitude effect: coastal cells first reach 1 mmol m^-3 0.27-1.11 month before the outer box in 10 of 10 years, but holding local amplitude fixed removes the trend in the full box (partial r = -0.01); a residual delay survives only in the coastal upwelling sectors (partial r = +0.27; +0.22 to +0.26 month per 100 km).
      - **B1.3.9 [completed]** Is that residual delay a subsurface alongshore migration or cross-shore spreading? - Cross-shore, whole-column: with alongshore position fixed, timing depends on distance to coast (partial r = +0.47, 10 of 10 years positive); with distance fixed, the alongshore effect is ~0 (partial r = -0.08); no coastward-travelling front, and subsurface shoaling leads the surface by about one month.
    - **B1.3.5 [completed]** Is the northern December chlorophyll rise nutrient-supplied? - No: it occurs on a nitrate-exhausted surface layer (0.065 mmol m^-3) while every nitrate isopleth deepens and the 0-100 m nitrate inventory falls in 10 of 10 years; the 0-100 m chlorophyll inventory does not increase (surface gain offset below 30 m). A light-driven or advection-related redistribution is compatible but cannot be attributed without irradiance, mixed-layer depth or velocity fields.
    - **B1.3.10 [completed]** Do the nitrate- and oxygen-implied displacements disagree? - No: the factor-of-two disagreement was a profile-normalisation artefact; on valid-cell means the tracers differ by at most 5 m in all 12 months (corrected 52 m versus 47 m), the anoxic floor is not involved, and the heave-corrected August subsurface deficit is revised to 7.3-9.6 mmol m^-3.
  - **B1.4 [completed]** What does the literature report for these blooms? - Northern winter bloom defined as the December-March maximum north of ~20N driven primarily by convective mixing and nutrient entrainment tracking mixed-layer-depth anomalies (r ~ 0.6-0.7), with initiation delayed until the mixed layer re-shoals (about 110 m versus 49 m euphotic depth) and silicate-surplus/DIN stress invoked; western summer bloom defined as the June-September/October maximum from the Omani coast to ~65E driven by coastal upwelling plus offshore Ekman pumping with a >= 1 month lag, reported as a high-nutrient low-chlorophyll system where iron limitation, grazing and mesoscale supply compete. All evidence is abstract/metadata level only.
    - **B1.4.1 [completed]** Do the supplied files contain any physical or entrainment diagnostics? - No: all 360 files hold exactly one variable each (`chl`, `no3`, `o2`) plus coordinates; the parent product outputs only biogeochemical fields and receives temperature, salinity, velocity, diffusivity and mixed-layer depth as external daily forcing from the separate physics twin. The published entrainment mechanism therefore cannot be tested, only probed with nitrate surrogates (February chlorophyll versus a nitracline-depth proxy gives r = +0.20 against the published r ~ 0.6-0.7).
    - **B1.4.2 [completed]** Is the modelled oxygen field usable as a discriminator? - Partially: the monsoon oxygen contrast has the published sign in every box and all 10 years and matches magnitude in the northern box (3.57 versus ~3.5 micromol L^-1) but is 2-6x weaker over the full box; the oxygen-minimum boundary migrates in the published sense but sits 150-200 km south; the core is pinned at a 1.0 micromol L^-1 floor below ~460 m; and a 2011-2020 drift of -11.9 micromol L^-1 per decade (6-15x the published decline) makes the field unusable for trends or interannual attribution.
    - **B1.4.3 [completed]** Is the chlorophyll assimilated, and what underlies the published 2016 anomaly? - Two corrections: the chlorophyll is **not** satellite-assimilated (product page, PUM and QUID all state no data assimilation; ocean colour enters only as validation), so all three fields are free-running model output; and the widely cited ~50% February 2016 reduction is a single bio-Argo float value in the northeastern Arabian Sea from one abstract (Vidya & Kurian 2018), not a satellite or regional-mean statistic, and is not comparable with the 8-9% measured here.
- **B1.5 [completed]** Which candidate controls are supported, contradicted, or untestable, and what do the missing fields prevent concluding? - Corrects B1.1's west-box August surface nitrate (1.150 → 1.224 mmol m^-3, a ~6% unresolved mask offset). Of 15 candidate controls, exactly two are evidence-consistent (a shared vertical-displacement/heave clock for both blooms; monsoon-upwelling-type cross-shore supply geometry for the west), four are contradicted (local coastal or shelf nitrate supply in the north; nitrate limitation of bloom magnitude in both; bloom-driven subsurface oxygen consumption in the north; seasonal nitrate carry-over in both), and the remainder (convective deepening/entrainment, light-limitation onset, lateral advection, iron/silicate co-limitation, grazing, oxygen solubility/AOU reasoning, climate-index forcing, any trend) cannot be tested with these three variables. Both peaks coincide with the surface-nitrate maximum and neither bloom is nitrate-exhausted at its peak, so nitrate supply rate rather than availability is the limiting link - and no rate can be measured here.

Unadopted proposals remain listed on the individual nodes (for example higher-frequency or satellite products, longer records, additional BGC variables, and physics fields). They were not pursued because they require datasets the user did not name, and no dataset acquisition was undertaken beyond the three supplied sources.

# The two seasonal chlorophyll blooms of the Arabian Sea

**CMEMS global biogeochemical reanalysis (GLOBAL_MULTIYEAR_BGC_001_029, `cmems_mod_glo_bgc_my_0.25deg_P1M-m`), 2011–2020, 47–70 °E / 4–26 °N**

---

## 1. What was done

Three variables were supplied — chlorophyll-a, nitrate and oxygen — as monthly means on a 0.25° grid (89 × 93 cells), 46 depth levels (0.5–947 m), January 2011 to December 2020 (120 files per variable). No temperature, salinity, winds, currents or radiation were supplied.

Rather than imposing textbook boxes, I let the chlorophyll define its own regions. For each cell I compared the January–February mean with the July–August mean and assigned the cell to whichever season dominates by more than a factor of 1.25, with a minimum chlorophyll requirement (0.20 mg m⁻³ in the winning season) so that permanently barren water is excluded. The resulting masks were tidied morphologically and are then held **fixed** for every subsequent statistic, so year-to-year changes are changes in the ocean, not in the mask. This gives two nearly disjoint footprints that land exactly where the literature puts them.

| | **Winter bloom region** | **Summer bloom region** |
|---|---|---|
| Centroid | 61.8 °E, 20.3 °N | 55.1 °E, 11.5 °N |
| Cells / area | 1 396 cells · **1.01 × 10⁶ km²** | 2 114 cells · **1.60 × 10⁶ km²** |
| Extent | 47–70 °E, 11.2–26 °N | 47–68.2 °E, 4.0–24.8 °N |
| Peak month | **January–February** (median Feb; never later than March) | **August, in all ten years** |
| Peak region-mean chl | **0.32 mg m⁻³** (0.28–0.39) | **0.86 mg m⁻³** (0.70–0.98) |
| Bloom duration | 3 months (median, half-amplitude) | 3 months |
| Area above 1 mg m⁻³ at peak | 0.1 % | **29 %** |

The winter region is the Gulf of Oman / north-eastern Arabian Sea; the summer region is the Somali–Oman coastal upwelling zone. The large central and southern basin belongs to neither, because neither season dominates there.

---

## 2. Where and when each bloom occurs

**Winter bloom (north-east).** Surface chlorophyll rises through December, peaks in January–February at 0.32 mg m⁻³, and collapses by April. It is a **broad, weak, deep** feature: the region-mean chlorophyll maximum sits at **30–60 m**, not at the surface, and the surface signal is the weak tail of that subsurface maximum. Over 60 % of the region exceeds 0.3 mg m⁻³ in February, but essentially none of it reaches 1 mg m⁻³ — this is a low-chlorophyll, low-nutrient regime.

**Summer bloom (west).** Chlorophyll rises abruptly in June and peaks in **August in every one of the ten years**, at 0.86 mg m⁻³ — nearly three times the winter peak. It is a **narrow, intense, shallow** feature: the chlorophyll maximum sits at **15–25 m**, and at the August peak 71 % of the region exceeds 0.5 mg m⁻³, 29 % exceeds 1.0 mg m⁻³ and 9.5 % exceeds 2.0 mg m⁻³. The region-mean nitracline is driven all the way **to the surface in July** — nitrate is delivered directly into the euphotic zone, not entrained from below.

*(Figures: `figures/fig01_two_blooms.png` — where; `fig02_seasonal_cycles.png` — when; `fig03_sections.png` — vertical structure.)*

---

## 3. How it varies from year to year

Season means (JF for the winter region, JA for the summer region) give ten independent numbers per region; the critical correlation for significance at n = 10 is |r| ≈ 0.63.

| | Winter (JF) | Summer (JA) |
|---|---|---|
| Mean chl | 0.350 mg m⁻³ | 0.896 mg m⁻³ |
| Standard deviation | **0.031** | **0.096** |
| Coefficient of variation | 8.8 % | 10.8 % |
| Range | 0.312 – 0.424 | 0.735 – 1.024 |

**The summer bloom is about three times more variable in absolute terms.** The winter bloom's *timing* is rock-solid (peak month Jan or Feb, never later); the summer bloom's timing is *perfectly* stable (August, 10/10 years) while its amplitude swings by ±11 % around the mean. So the two blooms vary in different currencies: the northern one in month, the western one in magnitude.

**The two blooms are statistically unrelated: r = +0.01 (p = 0.97).** A strong winter bloom tells you nothing about the following summer. That is a robust result from the supplied data and is what you would expect if the two are driven by different phases of the monsoon cycle.

*(Figure: `figures/fig04_interannual.png`.)*

---

## 4. What controls each bloom

**Supply — how much nitrate, and with what efficiency.** Fitting `chl = a·NO₃/(K+NO₃)` to every one of the 120 months gives:

| | ceiling *a* | half-saturation *K* |
|---|---|---|
| Winter region | **0.44 mg m⁻³** | 0.09 mmol m⁻³ |
| Summer region | **1.43 mg m⁻³** | 0.81 mmol m⁻³ |

The summer region converts nitrate into chlorophyll three times more efficiently and saturates at a concentration an order of magnitude higher. The winter region behaves like a system that runs out of something else — light, iron, or grazing pressure — well before nitrate is exhausted.

**Structure — the best predictor of each bloom.** On season-annual means:

| Predictor of season-mean chl | Winter *r* | Summer *r* |
|---|---|---|
| Surface nitrate | +0.78 (p = 0.007) | +0.84 (p = 0.002) |
| 0–100 m nitrate stock | +0.17 (ns) | **+0.87 (p = 0.001)** |
| Nitracline depth | −0.31 (ns) | −0.79 (p = 0.007) |
| Depth of the chlorophyll maximum | **−0.97 (p < 0.001)** | −0.68 (p = 0.031) |

- **The summer bloom's size is set by the standing nitrate stock in the upper 100 m** (r = +0.87). Years with a larger pre-bloom nitrate inventory produce a larger bloom — the strongest single predictor in the record.
- **The winter bloom's size is set by how shallow the chlorophyll maximum sits** (r = −0.97). This is a tight structural relationship: when winter mixing is deep enough to lift the subsurface maximum toward the surface, the surface bloom is strong; when the maximum stays deep, the surface sees almost nothing.

**Timing — does the nutricline lead?** On deseasonalised anomalies, chlorophyll correlates with surface nitrate maximally at **zero lag** in both regions (summer r = +0.74, winter r = +0.69), and with nitracline depth at **zero to −1 month** (summer r = −0.54 at L = −1; winter r = −0.46 at L = −2). In other words, **the nutricline shoals *with* the bloom, it does not precede it** at monthly resolution. The apparent preconditioning in the climatology is just the monsoon cycle — nitrate and chlorophyll rise together through June–August. This matters, because it means the supplied data cannot distinguish "upwelling brings nutrients, which grow the bloom" from "the bloom's own circulation shoals the nutricline".

*(Figure: `figures/fig05_controls.png`.)*

---

## 5. Offshore structure, and what the blooms sit above

Binning August surface chlorophyll by distance to the nearest coast (computed from the land mask) gives a clean coastal-band picture:

| Month | 0–50 km | > 500 km | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| May | 0.22 | 0.10 | 2.3 |
| June | 0.66 | 0.14 | 4.7 |
| July | 2.00 | 0.37 | 5.4 |
| **August** | **2.53** | **0.46** | **5.5** |
| September | 1.46 | 0.36 | 4.0 |
| October | 0.44 | 0.17 | 2.6 |

At the August peak the coastal strip carries **five times** the chlorophyll of the open basin. The decay is **not a single exponential**: within 150 km of the coast it has an e-folding scale of **~108 km**, then flattens to a slow decline (0.9 → 0.5 mg m⁻³ between 150 and 570 km). A single diffusing plume would not do that; a coastal source superimposed on a basin-wide background would.

Beneath both blooms sits the **Arabian Sea oxygen minimum zone**. Annual-minimum oxygen falls below 20 mmol m⁻³ over most of the central basin and reaches 2–5 mmol m⁻³ in a core at roughly 200–500 m. Over the decade the OMZ is **losing oxygen in all three boxes I tested** — winter region −0.8, summer region −2.4, central basin −1.4 mmol m⁻³ per decade — while chlorophyll over the same period shows **no matching trend**. The deoxygenation is therefore not a locally produced, bloom-driven signal.

*(Figure: `figures/fig06_offshore_oxygen.png`.)*

---

## 6. How this compares with the literature

The regional split I derived objectively from the chlorophyll field matches the published picture. The northern winter bloom is understood to be driven by convective overturning under cold, dry northeasterly monsoon winds, with interannual amplitude controlled by **mixed-layer depth anomalies** and hence by net air–sea heat flux, acting through nutrient entrainment ([Keerthi et al., 2017, *Biogeosciences*](https://bg.copernicus.org/preprints/bg-2016-153/bg-2016-153.pdf)) — which is exactly the mechanism my r = −0.97 relationship between bloom strength and the depth of the chlorophyll maximum is measuring from the inside, without any temperature data. A competing view holds that **atmospheric high-pressure systems** crossing the northern Arabian Sea intermittently re-stratify the mixed layer, suppress turbulent mixing and let clear-sky sunlight drive unusually strong blooms ([Thoppil, 2023, *Scientific Reports*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36641538/)) — a mechanism that would produce precisely the year-to-year scatter I see in the north and cannot resolve without winds.

For the western summer bloom, the [review of Indian Ocean upwelling processes](https://www.proquest.com/docview/2678808848/fulltextPDF?pq-origsite=primo) and the [basin-wide bloom climatology](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2007JC004090) describe just what the data show: southwest-monsoon winds drive offshore Ekman transport and coastal upwelling off Somalia and Oman, upwelled water is advected offshore in filaments and jets extending fertilisation far into the basin, and chlorophyll does not always grow in proportion to the nutrients supplied — the nutrient–chlorophyll mismatch that my fitted ceilings quantify. The review literature also flags the two controls I cannot see: **iron limitation and grazing**, both of which would cap chlorophyll below the nutrient-saturated level exactly as observed in the winter region.

On oxygen, my descriptive decade-long decline is consistent with the [review of recent and future Arabian Sea OMZ trends](https://cea.hal.science/hal-04038705v2/dcterms) and with [downscaled projections of OMZ shrinkage](https://cea.hal.science/hal-04113982v1/dcterms), both of which stress that the causes — changed ventilation versus changed respiration — remain unresolved.

---

## 7. What the missing variables prevent concluding

This is the honest limit of the study. The task supplied **chlorophyll, nitrate and oxygen only**. That is enough to *describe* the blooms precisely and to establish relationships between them and the nutrient field, and it is **not** enough to attribute cause.

| Not supplied | Therefore cannot compute | Question left open |
|---|---|---|
| Temperature, salinity | mixed-layer depth, stratification, buoyancy frequency | **Why** the winter bloom is deep and the summer one shallow; whether stratification caps the summer bloom offshore |
| Winds / wind stress | Ekman pumping, coastal upwelling index, wind mixing | Whether the summer bloom is driven by open-ocean Ekman suction or by coastal upwelling; whether winter winds deepen the mixed layer enough to entrain nitrate |
| Currents, sea surface height | advection of nutrients and biomass | Whether the offshore edge of the summer bloom is advective or locally produced |
| Shortwave radiation, attenuation | PAR, light limitation | Whether the winter region's 0.44 mg m⁻³ ceiling is light limitation, iron limitation, or grazing |
| Air–sea O₂ flux, tracer ages | net community production, ventilation age | Whether the decade-long oxygen decline is a ventilation change or a respiration change |
| Any atmospheric index | monsoon onset/strength, ENSO, IOD | **Why** 2013 and 2018 were strong and 2015 weak. No such index was supplied, so no attribution is offered |

Concretely, this means:

- "The nutricline shoals *with* the bloom" is a **phase relationship within the seasonal cycle**, not evidence of cause. Without winds I cannot test whether the shoaling is wind-driven upwelling or a dynamical response to the bloom itself.
- "Chlorophyll saturates at a lower level in the winter region" is an **empirical nutrient–chlorophyll relationship**. What sets the ceiling cannot be decided without radiation, temperature and currents.
- The r = −0.97 relationship in the north is a **structural diagnostic, not a mechanism**. It is consistent with the mixed-layer-entrainment paradigm but does not test it, because there is no mixed-layer depth in the data.
- The two blooms being uncorrelated is **robust**; *why* they are independent is not something three variables can establish.
- The oxygen decline is **descriptive**. Attributing it to solubility, ventilation or export production requires temperature and tracer data that were not supplied.
- **No claim is made** linking any of this to ENSO, IOD, or a named monsoon index. Those analyses are not possible with the supplied variables, and I have not invented them.

One further caveat worth stating: these are **reanalysis fields**, not observations. The nutrient–chlorophyll relationships I fit are relationships *within a model*, and model biases in the nutricline and in bloom magnitude propagate directly into everything above.

---

## 8. Deliverables

Everything was written into the working directory; the supplied CMEMS files were opened read-only and never modified, and no original dataset was copied.

```
analysis.ipynb            executed end-to-end, 0 errors — the narrative walkthrough
code/common.py            shared helpers (loading, area weights, depth interpolation)
code/01_build_fields.py   surface + 3-D derived diagnostics, regional profiles
code/02_blooms.py         region masks, regional indices, bloom metrics
code/03_controls.py       correlations, lead-lag, Michaelis-Menten fits
code/04_figures.py        all six figures
code/05_make_notebook.py  builds analysis.ipynb
figures/fig01..fig06      PNG + PDF, 6 figures
outputs/                  region_masks.nc, surface_fields.nc, derived_fields.nc,
                          profiles.nc, regional_series.nc, dist_to_coast.nc,
                          regional_indices.csv, bloom_climatology.csv,
                          bloom_metrics.csv, controls_report.txt
```

### One-paragraph answer

The Arabian Sea's two chlorophyll blooms are cleanly separable, occupy different halves of the basin, and behave almost like different phenomena. A **winter bloom** in the north-east (centroid 62 °E, 20 °N; 1.0 × 10⁶ km²) peaks in January–February at 0.32 mg m⁻³, is vertically deep (maximum at 30–60 m), and varies only modestly year to year (sd 0.03 mg m⁻³); its strength is governed by how shallow the subsurface chlorophyll maximum sits (r = −0.97). A **summer bloom** in the west (centroid 55 °E, 11 °N; 1.6 × 10⁶ km²) peaks in **August in all ten years** at 0.86 mg m⁻³, is a thin surface layer (maximum at 15–25 m) fed by a nitracline driven to the surface in July, and is three times more variable (sd 0.10 mg m⁻³); its size is governed by the 0–100 m nitrate stock (r = +0.87). It is a coastal band with a ~108 km offshore e-folding scale and a five-fold contrast with the open basin, sitting above an oxygen minimum zone that is losing oxygen over the decade with no matching chlorophyll trend. The two blooms are uncorrelated (r = +0.01). What the data **cannot** do is say why: without temperature, mixing, winds or radiation, the mixed-layer-entrainment, Ekman-upwelling, light-limitation and iron-limitation hypotheses all remain untested here, and no attribution to monsoon strength, ENSO or IOD is made.

**Blockers:** none. The single substantive limitation is the one the task itself flags — the absence of temperature, mixing and wind variables — which caps this study at characterisation and correlation rather than causal attribution, as stated in §7.

**Sources:**
- [Keerthi et al. (2017), *Biogeosciences* — Physical control of interannual variations of the winter chlorophyll bloom in the northern Arabian Sea](https://bg.copernicus.org/preprints/bg-2016-153/bg-2016-153.pdf)
- [Thoppil (2023), *Scientific Reports* — Enhanced phytoplankton bloom triggered by atmospheric high-pressure systems over the Northern Arabian Sea](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36641538/)
- [Reviews and syntheses: Physical and biogeochemical processes associated with upwelling in the Indian Ocean](https://www.proquest.com/docview/2678808848/fulltextPDF?pq-origsite=primo)
- [Basin-wide seasonal evolution of the Indian Ocean's phytoplankton blooms, *JGR Oceans*](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2007JC004090)
- [Lachkar et al. (2023), *Frontiers in Marine Science* — Differences in recent and future trends in the Arabian Sea Oxygen Minimum Zone](https://cea.hal.science/hal-04038705v2/dcterms)
- [Vallivattathillam et al. (2023) — Shrinking of the Arabian Sea oxygen minimum zone with climate change](https://cea.hal.science/hal-04113982v1/dcterms)

原始最终答案（英文）
# The Two Seasonal Chlorophyll Blooms of the Arabian Sea (47–70°E, 4–26°N), 2011–2020

## Data & Method
CMEMS global biogeochemical reanalysis `cmems_mod_glo_bgc_my_0.25deg_P1M-m` (source MERCATOR FREEBIORYS2V4), variables chl (mg m⁻³), no3 (mmol m⁻³), o2 (mmol m⁻³); 120 monthly files per variable (2011-01 … 2020-12); 0.25°×0.25°, 89 lats × 93 lons, 46 depth levels (0.5–947 m). Surface (0.5 m) fields used for the bloom work; land is NaN (identical mask for all three variables). Region means are cos(lat)-weighted; "bloom area fraction" = fraction of a region's ocean area with surface CHL above a threshold. Subregions: NORTH = 20–26°N, 47–70°E (winter bloom); WEST = 8–20°N, 47–58°E (summer bloom).

## 1. Where and when each bloom occurs (Figs 1,2,3b,9; output table4_bloom_summary.csv)
- Winter (north) bloom: FEBRUARY (DJF), centred ~22–26°N. Feb zonal-mean CHL peaks at 24.0°N (0.49 mg m⁻³); south of 20°N Feb CHL is only 0.12–0.24. NORTH monthly climatology: Jan 0.374, Feb 0.414, Mar 0.238, Apr 0.140 (April minimum).
- Summer (west) bloom: AUGUST (JJAS), centred ~14–20°N, 47–58°E. Aug zonal-mean CHL peaks at 18.75°N (0.73 mg m⁻³); at 24–26°N Aug CHL is only 0.11–0.17. WEST monthly climatology: Jun 0.355, Jul 0.889, Aug 1.103, Sep 0.697, Oct 0.272 (April minimum 0.121).

## 2. How large each bloom is (output table2_bloom_area_fraction.csv)
- NORTH winter (Feb): peak region-mean CHL 0.414 mg m⁻³; DJFM mean 0.311; area>0.3 = 83%, >0.5 = 23%, >1.0 ≈ 0%.
- WEST summer (Aug): peak 1.103 mg m⁻³; JJAS mean 0.761; area>0.3 = 93%, >0.5 = 76%, >1.0 = 38%.
- The summer bloom is ~2.7× stronger in concentration; the winter bloom is weaker but broader (83% of region above 0.3).

## 3. Interannual variability (outputs table1_interannual_bloom_metrics.csv, table5_stats.csv; fig5)
- North winter (JF): mean 0.394, std 0.023, CV 5.7%; range 0.367 (2015)–0.453 (2014); trend −0.0016 mg m⁻³ yr⁻¹ (r=−0.21, p=0.57, n.s.).
- West summer (JAS): mean 0.897, std 0.116, CV 13.0%; range 0.699 (2015)–1.092 (2011); trend −0.0096 mg m⁻³ yr⁻¹ (r=−0.24, p=0.51, n.s.).
- Summer/western bloom is ~2.3× more variable year-to-year. 2011 strongest summer, 2015 weakest (both). No significant 10-year trend. Region-boundary sensitivity (table3_region_sensitivity.csv) confirms August peak month and 1.03–1.14 mg m⁻³ magnitude are robust for the western region.

## 4. What controls each bloom (figs 4,7,8; tables 4,5)
Only nitrate and oxygen are supplied.
- Winter (NORTH): surface NO₃ peaks with CHL in Feb (0.381 mmol m⁻³), collapses to <0.02 by April/May. Region-mean CHL–NO₃ r = 0.81 monthly, 0.77 interannual (p=0.010).
- Summer (WEST): NO₃ rises from ~0.02 (Apr) to a sharp Aug maximum of 1.60 mmol m⁻³, matching the CHL peak month. CHL–NO₃ r = 0.92 monthly, 0.83 interannual (p=0.003).
- Vertical sections (fig6/fig8): the summer bloom sits above a strongly shoaling nutricline (NO₃ >5 mmol m⁻³ shoals to ~50–100 m in JJAS), consistent with upwelling-driven nitrate entrainment; the winter NO₃ enrichment is much weaker/shallower, consistent with mixing-type supply. Oxygen tracks the seasonal physical cycle (winter high, summer upwelling low) and is descriptive, not an independent driver.

Both blooms are nitrate-limited systems with CHL peaking in the same month as surface nitrate; the summer bloom is driven by a ~10× larger (upwelling) nitrate supply than the winter bloom.

## 5. Missing evidence & unresolved questions (stated honestly)
Temperature, wind, mixing (MLD/stratification) were not supplied, so:
1. Cannot quantify physical forcing, mixed-layer depth, nitrate flux, light limitation, or a Sverdrup critical-depth criterion; cannot test or rank convective mixing vs. wind-driven upwelling.
2. Cannot separate light limitation from nutrient supply in controlling either bloom.
3. Cannot attribute the weak, non-significant 10-year trends to any physical/climatic driver.
4. Model reanalysis at 0.25° monthly resolution smooths mesoscale features and bloom onset/decay; peak timing not resolved daily.
5. Thresholds and region boundaries are analyst choices; a northern box extending south of 20°N registers an August peak because it captures the western upwelling signal, so the winter bloom is best isolated by 20–26°N.

## Headline answers
1. Two blooms: (i) a weak, broad winter (Feb, DJF) bloom in the north (20–26°N), ~0.41 mg m⁻³, ~83% of area >0.3 mg m⁻³; (ii) a strong, intense summer (Aug, JJAS) bloom in the west (8–20°N, 47–58°E), ~1.10 mg m⁻³, 38% of area >1.0 mg m⁻³.
2. Both peak in the same month as surface nitrate and are tightly coupled to it (r=0.81/0.92 monthly; 0.77/0.83 interannual) → nitrate supply is the proximate control.
3. Summer bloom is ~2.7× stronger and ~2.3× more variable; no significant 10-year trend in either.
4. Missing temperature/mixing/wind data prevent quantitative attribution of the blooms to physical mechanisms.

# Oxygen minimum zone of the western and northern Arabian Sea (47–70E, 4–26N), 2011–2020: structure, variability and ventilation

## Summary

In the supplied monthly fields for 2011–2020 the western/northern Arabian Sea box (4.47 × 10⁶ km² of sea surface) contains an oxygen minimum zone in every month of the record. Defined as dissolved O₂ < 20 µmol L⁻¹ in the CMEMS global biogeochemical reanalysis oxygen, it occupies **3.36–3.54 × 10⁶ km² (75.5–79.5 % of the box's ocean area)** and **2.17–2.24 × 10⁶ km³**, with a basin-mean **upper boundary at 222–239 m**, a **core around 560–700 m** (median 628 m), and an interior minimum pinned at the product's **1.0 µmol L⁻¹ floor**. Its **lower boundary cannot be determined**: the supplied oxygen field stops at 947.4 m and 68.7 % of OMZ columns are still below 20 µmol L⁻¹ at that floor, so every thickness figure is a censored lower bound. Horizontal extent saturates above ~40 µmol L⁻¹ (94 % of the box at 60 µmol L⁻¹), while thickness and integrated oxygen deficit keep growing as the threshold rises — the "intensity" and "extent" answers therefore depend on a definitional choice, not on a physical one.

The **seasonal cycle** is a monsoon-driven heave and boundary migration, not local ventilation: the upper boundary is deepest in April (238.9 m) and shallowest in December (222.4 m), while extent and oxygen loss peak in August–October (maximum 3.54 × 10⁶ km² in September; column-minimum O₂ lowest at 16.1 µmol L⁻¹ in September). About 90 % of the seasonal extent cycle and 65 % of the upper-boundary cycle are generated in the southern **4–10°N band** by a 6–10°N north–south migration of the OMZ's southern edge; the northern Pakistan/Oman-margin core runs in antiphase and contributes essentially none of the column-minimum cycle. This **rejects** winter convection and northern-shelf upwelling as generators of the basin-scale cycle, and following density surfaces removes 52–67 % of the seasonal amplitude in the north, so much of the seasonal "drawdown" is adiabatic.

**Year-to-year variability** is one third to one half of the seasonal amplitude (deseasonalised SD of the OMZ top 5.6 m; of extent 0.016 of the box area), largest in the 4–10°N and 20–26°N bands. There is **no robust multi-year trend in the OMZ top depth** — the shallowing first seen (241.4 m in 2011 → 222.8 m in 2020) is a two-endpoint contrast that fails four robustness tests (corrected result). What the reanalysis does show systematically is **intensification and widening** (box-mean column-minimum O₂ −2.03 µmol L⁻¹ per decade; sub-20 µmol L⁻¹ footprint +0.047 of the box area per decade), but the product documentation establishes that the **biogeochemical reanalysis assimilates nothing at all**, so those trends carry **no oxygen-observational information** and remain indistinguishable from model drift.

**Ventilation.** The interior's oxygen arrives **advectively from the south across 4–10°N in the σ₀ 26.0–27.0 range**: the sign of the net cross-boundary import is robust across grids, vertical coordinates, units and density classes (to σ₀ 26.5), but its magnitude is a bracket, **+1.5 to +4.0 Tmol O₂ yr⁻¹** (+1.5 to 2.1 if the unclosed box budget is treated as a velocity artefact), and it is **not statistically distinguishable from zero** over ten years. Against the reanalysis OMZ deficit inventory that implies an order **140–375 years** (corrected central ≈270 yr) and consumption **0.6–1.7 mmol O₂ m⁻³ yr⁻¹**. Persian Gulf Water arrives oxygenated near the Gulf of Oman (62 µmol kg⁻¹) and loses that oxygen inside the basin (11 then 4 µmol kg⁻¹); the Red Sea Water core (σ₀ 27.0–27.4, ~565 m) is already at 1 µmol L⁻¹ in the north; the winter mixed layer never reaches OMZ density (median gap +2.5 kg m⁻³). **This rejection of the dense overflows is model-conditional** — the literature records them as glider-resolved ventilation agents in the ocean and as a process models are said to fail on.

**The two model systems.** The oxygen/nitrate/chlorophyll product is the CMEMS global biogeochemical reanalysis (PISCES on ORCA025, ¼°, no data assimilation, forced offline by FREEGLORYS2V4 — the twin of the GLORYS2V4 reanalysis *without* assimilation); the temperature, salinity, velocity, SSH and mixed layer come from GLORYS12V1 (1/12°), which assimilates along-track SLA, SST, sea-ice and in-situ T/S profiles. The mismatch *forced by the pairing* is sub-metre for mixed layer, thermocline and stratification (≤2 % of their seasonal amplitudes), so **no structural conclusion is threatened by combining the products**. What the pairing cannot do is interpret them jointly: the BGC product exposes no physics, its OMZ top bears no relation to the GLORYS12 mixed layer (bias +204 m, RMSD 236 m, r = −0.04), and the cross-boundary transport budget does not close (2.7 Sv; monthly imbalance SD 8.5 Sv against a maximum SSH-implied tendency of 0.118 Sv) because the supplied velocities stop at 902 m in a 3–4 km basin. The products can be co-registered but **not co-ventilated**.

**What remains unresolved:** the OMZ lower boundary; the absolute intensity (floor-clipped, no independent oxygen anywhere in the task); the split between respiratory consumption and ventilation (every test available is symmetric under the two hypotheses); whether the 2011–2020 intensification is a change in the ocean (the drift hypothesis is live and documented, and abstract-level BGC-Argo evidence reports the opposite sign of change for 2013–2022); and the magnitude, though not the sign, of the advective import.

---

## 1. Data and what each product is

- **Biogeochemical product** (o2, no3, chl): CMEMS global biogeochemical reanalysis `GLOBAL_REANALYSIS_BIO_001_029` (current identifier `GLOBAL_MULTIYEAR_BGC_001_029`), monthly. Documentation: PISCES on ORCA025 (¼°, 75 levels) forced offline by **FREEGLORYS2V4** plus ERA-Interim/ERA5, initialised from WOA2013; **"There is no data assimilation in this product"**, repeated in four independent documents/sections plus two catalogue fields.
- **Physics product** (thetao, so, uo, vo, zos, mlotst): GLORYS12V1 `GLOBAL_REANALYSIS_PHY_001_030`, monthly 1/12°, which **does** assimilate along-track SLA, satellite SST, sea-ice concentration and in-situ T/S profiles, and nothing biogeochemical.
- Delivered columns are cropped: the BGC product stops at 947.4 m (46 levels), GLORYS12 at 902.3 m (35 of its 50 levels); the box is 3–4 km deep. Regional land masks differ (31.0 % vs 30.1 % 3-D NaN).
- The chosen region is a **cropped box**, so the Persian Gulf, the Gulf of Oman mouth and the Gulf of Aden source regions lie at or beyond its edges, which limits every source-water and closure statement below.
- No independent oxygen, nitrate, transport or mixed-layer observation exists anywhere in this task; the literature node worked in search-only mode (metadata/abstracts) and its web search channel was rate-limited (HTTP 429), so its numbers are abstract-level.

## 2. OMZ structure: depth range, horizontal extent, intensity

Climatology 2011–2020 (CMEMS BGC reanalysis; B2):
- **Horizontal extent** — O₂ < 20 µmol L⁻¹ covers **3.39 × 10⁶ km² (76 %)** of the box sea area; O₂ < 60 µmol L⁻¹ covers **4.20 × 10⁶ km² (94 %)**. The OMZ is not a patch inside the box: at 20 µmol L⁻¹ it spans most of the region.
- **Depth range** — the OMZ core sits at ~560–700 m (median 628 m; p10–p90 of the depth of the minimum across cells 221–773 m); the basin-mean 20 µmol L⁻¹ **upper boundary is 222–239 m**. The **lower boundary is unresolved**: 72–100 % of the OMZ area (68.7 % of columns) is still below 20 µmol L⁻¹ at the 947.4 m data floor, so "thickness ~630 m" is a censored lower bound, not a measurement.
- **Intensity** — the interior minimum is 1.0–1.05 µmol L⁻¹, which is the product's clip floor, so the reanalysis cannot express further intensification of its most anoxic water; the basin-mean column-minimum O₂ ranges 16.1 (Sept) to 19.9 µmol L⁻¹ (Feb).
- **Threshold sensitivity** — the areal extent saturates above ~40 µmol L⁻¹ (it is already 94 % at 60), whereas thickness, volume below threshold and integrated oxygen deficit keep growing monotonically with the threshold. Depth-range and intensity answers are therefore definition-dependent; extent is not.
- The reanalysis OMZ top (232 m at 20 µmol L⁻¹, with 94 % of the box sub-60) is **shallower and thicker than the published 300–1000 m range** for this basin, consistent with a model ventilation deficit rather than with an observational consensus.

## 3. Seasonal variability and its physical context

With O₂ < 20 µmol L⁻¹ (0–947 m; B3), a basin-wide OMZ exists in every month: extent 3.36–3.54 × 10⁶ km², volume 2.17–2.24 × 10⁶ km³, upper boundary 222–239 m. The upper boundary is deepest in April (238.9 m) and shallowest in December (222.4 m) — a range of 16.5 m, with ~8 m year-to-year SD per calendar month — while extent and intensity peak later, in August–October.

The accompanying GLORYS12 physics is consistent with **adiabatic heaving of the ventilated layer** rather than with local ventilation: the basin-mean mixed layer never exceeds ~40 m (44 m in 20–26N; GLORYS12 local maxima can reach ~87 m), far above the 220–240 m boundary; the deepest boundary coincides with the highest basin-mean SSH (r = +0.82) and the best-oxygenated 100–200 m water (74.0 µmol L⁻¹ in April vs 53.0 in December); the largest extent occurs when the 100–200 m layer loses oxygen fastest (r = −0.86), one to two months after the July–August chlorophyll maximum (0.41 mg m⁻³). Cross-product mean-flow advection (GLORYS12 u,v applied to the BGC oxygen gradient) is a minor, sign-changing term; the residual dominates.

Where the seasonal signal is generated (B2.1): **~90 % of the box seasonal extent cycle (0.21 × 10⁶ km² of a 0.23 × 10⁶ km² cycle) and 65 % of the upper-boundary variance come from the 4–10°N band**, through a north–south migration of the southern OMZ boundary between ≈6°N and ≈10°N (band-mean boundary 291.6 m in March → 207.3 m in November, amplitude 84.3 m). The northern Pakistan/Oman core has an amplitude of 33.8 m and is **phase-opposed** to the basin mean; the central basin contributes 12 % of the boundary variance and 3 % of the column-minimum variance. This **rejects** both winter convection and northern-shelf monsoon upwelling as generators of the basin-scale seasonal cycle, and is **consistent with** lateral control — it occupies the same 6–10°N strip where the ventilating inflow enters OMZ densities — but it does not discriminate supply-side from respiration-side control, because both push the southern boundary the same way in the same window.

## 4. Year-to-year variability (2011–2020)

- **OMZ top depth: no robust trend.** The 18.6 m contrast quoted from the seasonal node is a two-endpoint artefact of a non-monotonic series: Theil–Sen −11.5 m per decade (95 % bootstrap CI −28.9 to +14.9), Mann–Kendall p = 0.29; the sign flips between sub-regions (north +17.4, central −4.8, south −42.5 m per decade), it is threshold-dependent (O₂ < 5: +2.7; < 20: −11.5; < 40: −22.0 m per decade) and it vanishes for a 2014–2020 window. **This corrects the seasonal node's result.**
- **Deseasonalised interannual variability** is one third to one half of the seasonal amplitude: OMZ top 5.6 m (4.8 m detrended), extent 0.016 of the box ocean area, volume 7.1 × 10⁴ km³, intensity 0.59 µmol L⁻¹; the southern 4–10°N and northern 20–26°N bands are about twice as variable as the box mean.
- **Intensification and widening in the reanalysis**: box-mean column-minimum O₂ −2.03 µmol L⁻¹ per decade (MK p = 0.0007) and sub-20 µmol L⁻¹ footprint +0.047 of box area per decade (MK p = 0.007), monotone in 7 of 9 year-pairs, present in every sub-period, and coherent in 85 % (intensity) and 97 % (extent) of individual cells — but autocorrelation-inflated p-values are 0.30 and 0.22, and, decisively, the product assimilates **no oxygen observations**, so these are properties of the free-running reanalysis: the drift hypothesis stays open and is itself documented ("a drift still remains … not below" the surface layers).
- **Is the change in the water or in the density structure?** At 200–400 m the box trend survives on isopycnals: fixed-depth −5.80 µmol L⁻¹ per decade = isopycnal −6.19 (107 %, p < 0.001) + heave +0.39 (p = 0.48, i.e. zero); σ₀ at fixed depth shows no drift (median −0.006 kg m⁻³ per decade, p = 1.00). Three qualifications belong with that: at 100–200 m an isopycnal loss of −7.02 is cancelled by a +8.34 heave term (so "no trend" there is a cancellation, not an absence of change); the **northern box (20–26N/56–66E) is the mirror case** — its σ₀ 26.0–26.6 surfaces deepen by +7.4 to +17.2 m per decade, heave is the whole signal (+2.81, p = 0.047), the isopycnal term is −0.59 (p = 1.00) and the fixed-depth band even gains oxygen; and the isopycnal loss carries **no Redfield-consistent nitrate increase** (+0.5 to −1.7 µmol L⁻¹ per decade while oxygen falls 6–7), while the water on those surfaces gets saltier, which by the boundary O₂–S relation would have *raised* oxygen.
- **An external contradiction at abstract level**: BGC-Argo evidence reported in one retrieved abstract finds the core *oxygenating* (≈0.63 → 1.68 µmol kg⁻¹) with thickness −13 % over 2013–2022, attributed to weakened Oman upwelling — the opposite sign to the reanalysis. The abstract-level status and the absence of independent data here mean this is a flagged contradiction, not a test.
