原始最终答案（英文）
## Summary


**Data basis.** The three supplied directories are GLORYS12V1 daily-mean fields (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m` v202311): salinity `so`, temperature `thetao` (time × 40 levels, 0.49–1941.9 m) and sea surface height `zos`, on a 1/12° regular grid over 18–31°N, 98–80°W, 2011-01-01 to 2017-12-31, 2,557 days with no missing day. There are **no velocity fields, no river discharge, no winds and no independent salinity observations**. The archive resolves the Louisiana–Texas shelf with 13–24 cells between the coast and the 200-m isobath and the water column with 18 levels above 50 m; the 2011–2017 shelf-mean surface salinity is 31.7 psu against 36.2 psu in the deep Gulf (see `glorys12-gom-domain-resolution-and-signal.png`).

**How much.** There is no defensible *net* export number in these files. What can be defended, with conventions attached:

- *Standing stocks.* With one reference-free convention (top-10 m freshwater inside patches fresher than 35.5 psu, the model's collapsed shoreline step excluded): **94.3 km³ on the northern shelf and 19.6 km³ offshore, i.e. about 0.21 (defensible range 0.14–0.30) of the shelf stock appears as low-salinity surface water offshore**. If the shoreline-step cells are kept the same convention gives 152.6 km³ and 0.13; with a far-field 36.245 psu reference and the step excluded it gives 120.5 / 33.5 km³ and 0.28. The earlier headline "296 ± 67 km³ shelf, 48.5 km³ offshore, ratio 0.16" was **corrected**: the offshore residual and the ratio are not defensible as stated (they are near-cancellations whose reference-salinity sensitivity, 34 km³ per 0.1 psu, is 70 % of their own value), while the shelf stock survives in sign and order of magnitude.
- *Flux across the shelf break.* Only SSH-derived geostrophy is available. The upper 0–50 m exports the freshwater anomaly offshore at about **+155 km³/yr** (top 10 m +107 km³/yr) while 50–200 m returns about −194 km³/yr, giving a full-depth net of −38.6 km³/yr that is a ~1 % residual of a ±1,690 km³/yr two-way exchange and therefore at the noise floor; the absolute value carries roughly ±50 % sensitivity to the SSH-gradient scale and the implied net volume transport (+2.16 Sv) is physically implausible. The exporting sectors are Louisiana–Mississippi (+54.7) and Alabama–north-Florida (+86.0 km³/yr); Texas–west Louisiana (−29.1) and west Florida (−150.2) import.
- *Independent check.* The northern shelf's freshwater inventory requires an autumn removal of **190–305 (mean 253) km³/yr**, of which the upper-layer geostrophic export can account for at most about 60 % — the remaining term is not in the supplied data (wind-driven Ekman transport is not supplied).

**When.** The offshore expression is a **summer** phenomenon: the 0–10 m offshore layer peaks in July–August (86.0 km³ JJA vs 30.3 km³ DJF; monthly maximum 96.7 km³ in August), the freshest layer descends through the year (0–10 m in July–August, 10–30 m in September, 30–50 m in October, 50–100 m in April), and the northern shelf's own surface stock peaks in June–July, one to two months before the offshore surface maximum. A separate basin-wide 50–100 m freshening peaking in February exists and is robust to reference choice, but it is a water-mass/heave signature of the deep basin, not a shelf-export signature (below).

**Where.** Offshore low-salinity water concentrates between **26–29°N, 94–86°W in the northern deep Gulf and along the Louisiana–Alabama–north-Florida shelf break**; the western Gulf and Sigsbee basin stay net salty. Geostrophic export is carried by the LA–MS and AL–nFL breaks in July–September. The deep eastern basin's 50–100 m freshwater excess is a different, non-river signal.

**Which circulation features carry it — not established.** The Loop Current and its rings are the only plausible large-scale carriers present in the fields, but every discriminating test is null or negative: deep-Gulf fresh anomalies relate only weakly to Loop Current extent and ring area (daily r = +0.24, circular-shift p = 0.22), occur about 40 % *less* often over anticyclonic SSH than chance, show no advective consistency with SSH-derived flow (r = +0.04) and no net centroid displacement; the classical "Loop Current extension → ring separation → westward transport" sequence occurs **once in 2 557 days** against 0.81 expected by chance; ring separations are followed by deep-Gulf freshening in 2 of 6 cases where 2.9 are expected; and the export shows no relation to eddy kinetic energy (R² = 0.000–0.060), with more export in the *lowest*-EKE thirds of months. The export is organised at scales below ~150 km, ~65 % of the upper-layer export is transient rather than a steady current, its variability is set predominantly by the offshore-directed geostrophic flow rather than by the arrival of fresh water, and the best sub-monthly predictor is the plume/isohaline front position rather than any eddy metric. The only positive Loop-Current signal is positional and signed: a more northward Loop Current axis accompanies higher AL–nFL export at daily to intra-annual scales (r = +0.244, p = 0.007), which is not multiplicity-robust.

**How much of it is river water.** In the northern Gulf, **identifiable river/plume water reaches offshore only in the upper ~30 m and only from June to October**; the 30–100 m bands carry essentially none in any month. In June–September, 95 % of the shelf-break 0–10 m freshwater excess and 90 % of the northern-fan 0–10 m excess sits in water fresher than 35.5 psu; annually 66 % (June–September 67 %) of the northern group's reported offshore excess has a river/plume water-mass signature. By contrast, of the ~90 km³/yr of "offshore freshwater" in the deep eastern basin only ~4–10 km³ (5–10 %) has such a signature; the rest is Caribbean/Loop Current water mass plus heave read against a single deep reference box.

**Limits from the missing discharge and winds** (detail in §7): without discharge the timing and magnitude of the source cannot be tested, the autumn removal cannot be partitioned between lateral export and evaporation, and "river water" can only be inferred from a salinity threshold and T–S matching inside one assimilated model; without winds the leading published cross-shelf mechanism (Ekman transport) cannot be evaluated at all, and 42–48 % of the daily flux variance — the sub-monthly band — remains a diagnosed gap, not a null result.

---

## 1. What the supplied fields can and cannot support

GLORYS12 here resolves the shelf-to-basin freshwater contrast (mean shelf SSS 31.7 vs 36.2 psu in the deep Gulf; minimum daily SSS 5.1 near 30.2°N, 89.6°W) and a realistic Loop Current surface jet (max 1.21 m/s at 21.0°N, 86.3°W), but the archive contains **no uo/vo**, so no transport can be measured, only inferred from SSH geostrophy (which constrains the across-shelf component worst), and no model-independent check of salinity bias is possible. The 2000-m request cap also truncates the deepest ~1,000–2,000 m.

Reference figure: `glorys12-gom-domain-resolution-and-signal.png` (B2).

A separate check found that 389–648 of the shelf cells sit on the model's collapsed shoreline step (bottom-depth proxy ≤ 7.93 m; ~14–18 % of shelf area). Their sub-15 psu days are genuine model river water — concentrated in February–June at the Mississippi/Atchafalaya/Mississippi-Sound coasts and surface-fresher than their own bottom by 4.3 psu — but 63 % of them are within two levels of the grid minimum, so they describe a coastline step rather than a resolved offshore plume. ## 2. How much low-salinity water, and how much of it is offshore

**Stocks (corrected chain).** The first measurement reported 296 ± 67 km³ of shelf freshwater excess (full column, relative to a deep-Gulf reference) and 48.5 km³ in the offshore top 10 m, ratio ≈ 0.16, with a July–August offshore maximum and a 2011–2012-versus-2016–2017 decline. The robustness node **corrected** this: the 296 km³ survives in sign and order of magnitude (reproduced exactly at 295.55 km³, range 148–367 km³ across reference treatments and 236–319 km³ across domain variants, but with a 44.6 km³ per 0.1 psu reference sensitivity), the **offshore 48.5 km³ and the 0.16 ratio do not survive** (the offshore excess is a near-cancellation of a 12,333 km³ surface volume; three deep-water reference boxes supplied by the data themselves give −26.3, +14.1 and +48.4 km³; the break-even reference 36.103 psu lies inside the far-field surface salinity range), the July–August maximum survives, and the 2011–2012 versus 2016–2017 difference **does not** (it measures the difference in background trends between the reference box and the domain; with a time-varying reference the trend is −0.03 km³/yr, R² ≈ 0). The reconciliation node then put shelf and offshore on one reference-free footing and, excluding the collapsed shoreline step, reported **shelf 94.3 km³ and offshore 19.6 km³, ratio 0.208**, with the included-step variant 152.6 km³ and 0.129, and a far-field-reference variant 120.5 / 33.5 km³ and 0.278; the seasonal range of that ratio is ≈0.05 (December–January) to ≈0.38 (August). These numbers are **stocks, not exports**, and different conventions must not be averaged.

## 3. When and where the offshore signal appears

- **Season and depth.** Offshore 0–10 m freshwater excess: 86.0 km³ in JJA vs 30.3 km³ in DJF, monthly maximum 96.7 km³ (August), minimum 26.7 km³ (December). The freshest layer descends through the year (0–10 m July–August, 10–30 m September, 30–50 m October, 50–100 m April–May). The northern shelf's own 0–10 m stock peaks in June–July, giving a one- to two-month shelf-to-offshore lag. Below 100 m the anomaly is a persistent salty bias against the deep reference and is not usable as freshwater.
- **Northern versus deep eastern Gulf.** The aggregated regional pass shows the 50–100 m "winter maximum" is an **eastern-basin standing feature**: `basin_E` (east of 86°W, south of 26°N) holds 66.6 / 70.9 / 65.7 / 48.1 km³ in DJF/MAM/JJA/SON, i.e. ~100 % of the deep basin's total in that band, and is positive in all twelve months (42.0–76.5 km³). The same layer's seasonal oscillation is nevertheless real and robust: with four references that cannot alias the answer it peaks in **February** and the December–May minus June–November contrast is **+45 km³** (against +18.7 km³ with the daily reference profile), the B4.3 deep-basin reference having *understated* it by a factor ~2.4 and delayed its apparent peak. It is shared between slope and basin with nearly equal salinity amplitude per unit volume, so it is a **basin-wide freshening, not a preferentially slope-band export signature**, and the summer half of the published "summer-and-winter subsurface export" picture is not supported (the 50–100 m layer is at its minimum in summer).
- **Locations.** Offshore freshening is concentrated at 26–29°N, 94–86°W and along the Louisiana–Alabama–Florida shelf break; the western Gulf and Sigsbee basin remain net salty. Shelf-to-deep co-variabilities (uncorrected, standing stocks only) are modest: AL–nFL shelf with the northern fan (r = +0.42), LA–MS with `basin_E` (+0.30 to +0.55), TX–wLA with Sigsbee/west basin (+0.31 to +0.35), west Florida anti-correlated with `basin_E` (−0.46).
- **Episode years (contested).** GLORYS12 marks 2011 as enhanced (the 7-year June–September surface maximum, 119.5 km³), 2015 as enhanced at depth only, and 2014 as not enhanced at any band, while 2012 — not a published episode year — matches or exceeds 2011. The statistical node, however, found the year-to-year offshore contrast not distinguishable from zero under three of four reference treatments, so the model's event years should be treated as **conditional on the reference choice** and not as a validated reproduction of the published 2011/2014/2015 episodes.

## 4. Which circulation features carry it

The fields contain the two candidate structures — a persistent anticyclonic Loop Current occupying the eastern Gulf and a dense population of detached anticyclonic rings (4,229 closed-contour detections with SLA ≥ 0.15 m and area ≥ 1,500 km² west of 88.5°W over 2,557 days) — and deep-Gulf monthly-mean surface geostrophic speeds are strong (50th/90th/99th percentiles 0.18/0.53/1.09 m/s). So the fields *can* carry shelf water offshore. Whether they *do* was tested five ways, and the answer is negative or unresolved:

| Test | Result | Bearing on attribution |
|---|---|---|
| Lag/coincidence of deep-Gulf freshening with Loop Current extent and ring area | daily r = +0.24 (circular-shift p = 0.22); monthly +0.27 at lag 0; ring-area maximum only at 3–4 months, and the ring composite has the opposite sign to the ring lag-correlation | weak, not robust |
| Advective consistency | monthly surface salinity tendency vs SSH-derived advection r = +0.04; fresh-anomaly centroid no net displacement (wander 118 km/month, drift +3 km east, −1 km south) | against geostrophic advection control |
| Event sequence (Loop Current extension → ring separation → westward freshwater transport) | 10 extensions, 6 separations; separation → deep-Gulf freshening in 2/6 cases vs 2.9 expected (p = 0.89); the full three-step sequence once in 2,557 days vs 0.81 expected (p = 0.53); fresh anomalies preferentially on cyclonic SSH (61.4 % of area on SLA < 0) | classical mechanism unsupported; only the extension → separation step remains plausible (4/10, p ≈ 0.13–0.21) |
| Export vs eddy kinetic energy | monthly transient-flux anomalies unrelated to sector EKE or SSH anomaly at lags −3…+3 months (all \|r\| ≤ 0.27); LA–MS exports 47 km³/yr more in the lowest-EKE third of months; deep-basin EKE explains R² = 0.000–0.060 | contradicts eddy-carried export |
| Scale and factor decomposition | small-scale (<150 km) SSH gradient reproduces r = 0.77–0.89 of the transient flux; at daily resolution the sub-monthly meander energy has the *wrong* sign (R² = 0.024–0.037) and 42–48 % of daily flux variance lies below 31 days; flow factor dominates the transient export variance (72.1 % LA–MS, 52.4 % AL–nFL; freshwater-arrival factor 2.6 / 7.4 %) | the export is organised by fine-scale SSH structure and by the flow, not by advective arrival of fresh water |

What *does* survive is weaker and more structural: a standing spatial co-location between the export and the adjacent eddy field within each exporting sector (AL–nFL r = +0.55 to +0.66 for the time-mean part), which is degenerate with the analysis because EKE and the geostrophic flux are both built from the same SSH; a plume/delta **spatial precondition** (56.4 % of LA–MS + AL–nFL export occurs within 100 km of the Mississippi or Atchafalaya mouth, 74.3 % within 200 km) with a one-month lead of outer-shelf surface freshwater over high AL–nFL export months (r = +0.32, p = 0.000); the 34.0-isohaline front as the best sub-monthly predictor; and a signed, positional Loop Current effect (axis 1.64° farther north in high-export AL–nFL months; daily axis-latitude r = +0.244, top-5 % days +0.60σ, LC amplitude +0.78σ) that is not multiplicity-robust. For LA–MS the weak significant relations are the *wrong* sign (stronger LC or higher deep-basin sea level goes with less export).

**Statement of the attribution:** it is *consistent with* a fine-scale/frontal flushing of the northern shelf, spatially preconditioned by the river plume and only weakly steered by Loop Current position; the evidence **does not support** transport by the Loop Current or by its rings/eddies, and for the LA–MS break it contradicts the eddy-variance version of that hypothesis. Because every carrier metric and the flux itself are diagnosed from the same two fields (zos and so), and because wind and sub-surface velocity are absent, this is a failure to demonstrate, not a falsification.

## 5. How much of the offshore low-salinity water is actually river water

This is the strongest constraint on the user's question, and it splits sharply by region and depth.

- **Not river water in the deep eastern basin.** The persistent 50–100 m `basin_E` excess is not river-derived: that layer (18,107 km³) is 25.9–27.8 °C and 36.225–36.334 psu, statistically the same water as the Yucatan Channel inflow at the same depth; matched by density it is 0.012 psu *saltier* than the inflow (−6 km³ instead of +69 km³), water fresher than 35.5 psu occupies 0.09–0.65 % of the layer and carries 0.4–2.8 km³ in total, and the density-matched residual is a near-surface feature (+0.13 psu at 56–66 m, 0.00 at 78 m, −0.04 psu at 92 m). Of the ~90 km³/yr of "offshore freshwater" held by the two eastern-basin bands relative to one deep reference box, only **~4–10 km³ (5–10 %)** has a river/plume water-mass signature; the rest is the Gulf's own water-mass structure (Loop Current water at depth; the evaporatively concentrated western Gulf versus the Caribbean-fed eastern Gulf at the surface).
- **River water in the northern Gulf — but only near the surface and only in summer.** Applied to the northern shelf sectors, shelf-break bands, the northern fan and the 26–29°N/94–86°W box, the fresh-tail test gives: 30–100 m bands carry **zero** water fresher than 35.5 psu in the north in every month, while June–September 0–10 m values are 33.3 km³ on the break bands (31.5 km³, 95 %, in the fresh tail; 40.7 % of band volume in August) and 24.2 km³ in the northern fan (21.7 km³, 90 %; peak August 36.1 → 34.3 km³ with a 33.9 psu tail); 10–30 m attribution drops to 62 % and 44 %. Annually, 93 % of the northern 0–10 m excess and 58 % of the 10–30 m excess sit in the fresh tail; the northern group's 60.9 km³/yr of reported offshore excess contains **40.3 km³/yr (66 %)** with a river/plume signature (June–September: 76.4 of 113.3 km³, 67 %). The northern shelf sectors themselves hold 98 % of their June–September 0–10 m freshwater in water fresher than 35.5 psu with tail-mean salinities of 30–33 psu at the Mississippi/Atchafalaya sectors.
- **Caveats to that fraction.** The 35.5 psu tail also picks up southern-shelf (Campeche) water — the deep SW reference box carries 10.0 km³ of it in its own 0–10 m layer in June–September — so 66 % is an **upper bound for Mississippi-system water specifically**; the robust content is the north-versus-reference *location* contrast. The density-matched test cannot confirm the surface result because northern summer surface water is lighter than any water in either upstream endmember (coverage 0.00–0.19), and its large winter values are a cold fresh winter surface matched to saltier Caribbean water, i.e. a T–S structure difference rather than river water.

## 6. What the literature adds, and what it could not

A metadata/abstract-scope search (no full text was permitted) supports the mechanism set we tested — seasonal reversal of the alongshore wind field, Loop Current and Loop Current eddy interaction at the break, cyclonic Loop Current frontal eddies over the Mississippi Fan slope, storm-driven injection, and a wind-driven cross-shelf plume regime — and the standard analytic conventions: depth-integrated freshwater content as an (S_ref − S)/S_ref deficit with an explicitly chosen reference, off-shelf export as the divergence of the shelf freshwater budget or a flushing time, and plume identification by SSS/tDOC threshold algorithms or manual cataloguing in ocean colour. It also identified the one clear published disagreement we could test — a summer surface-signature plume maximum (da Silva & Castelao 2018) versus a summer-and-winter subsurface export pathway with weak surface expression (Liu et al. 2022) — and published export episodes in 2011, 2014 and 2015 (Otis et al. 2019). **No numeric offshore transport or basin freshwater content was obtainable at abstract scope, and no reference-salinity or cross-section convention could be verified**, so our numbers must not be compared to published magnitudes as if they shared a definition; the regional papers (Schiller et al. 2011; Schiller & Kourafalou 2014; Morey et al. 2002; Androulidakis & Kourafalou 2013; Dinnel & Wiseman 1986; Etter 1983; Hiron et al. 2022) were title-only in the open record. Exa returned HTTP 429 and the OpenAlex daily budget was exhausted, so the search coverage is real but incomplete.

## 7. How the missing river discharge and winds limit these conclusions

1. **No discharge → no source term, no closure, no timing test.** Every "freshwater" number is an anomaly against a chosen salinity reference, not river water. We cannot check whether the model's coastal salinity responds to observed discharge (including the 2011 Mississippi flood), so year-by-year attribution of shelf or basin anomalies to river discharge is not legitimate with these fields. The autumn shelf-inventory requirement (190–305 km³/yr removed) cannot be partitioned between lateral export and net surface evaporation, which is why the geostrophic upper layer can account for "at most ~60 %" and no more precise statement is possible.
2. **No winds → the leading published cross-shelf mechanism is untestable.** The published mechanism set makes wind-driven Ekman transport and the seasonal alongshore wind reversal central; with no wind fields we can neither add that term to the flux nor exclude it as the explanation of the 42–48 % of daily flux variance that lies below 31 days, which remains a **diagnosed gap rather than a null result**. Stronger-than-geostrophic flushing events (storms, frontal passages) are likewise invisible.
3. **No velocity field → geostrophy only, and geometry that flatters it.** The across-shelf component is the one geostrophy constrains worst; the net geostrophic volume transport (+2.16 Sv) is physically implausible and the absolute flux carries ±50 % sensitivity to the SSH-gradient scale, so only signs, patterns and layers — not absolute magnitudes — should be used. Part of the apparent export–eddy co-location is built in, because EKE and the geostrophic velocity are both derived from `zos`.
4. **No independent observations → model bias unquantifiable.** Salinity bias, assimilation increments and the collapsed coastal geometry are bounded only internally, and "river water" is inferred from T–S geometry in one data-assimilated product; a real plume can only be recognised by its freshness, not by any tracer.
5. **Sampling.** 84 monthly samples (n_eff ≈ 40–130 for daily series) and a 7-year record give low power for event statistics (only 6 ring separations) and leave the shelf residence-versus-export split weakly constrained; sub-monthly signals within each month's ~6 days of sampling are not resolved.

## 8. Unresolved uncertainties and contradictions that remain

- The shelf stock is convention-dependent (94.3 to 296 km³ across defensible definitions) and the offshore/shelf ratio is only order-of-magnitude (0.14–0.30, with the sign of some variants not robust).
- 2011–2012 versus 2016–2017 offshore contrast: supported by one reference treatment, not by the others; the model's salinification trend (+0.035 psu/yr in the offshore top 10 m) could be physical, model drift or an assimilation artefact, and cannot be settled with these fields.
- The river-water fraction of the northern offshore excess (66 %) is an upper bound because the salinity threshold also admits southern-shelf water.
- The 50–100 m basin-wide February freshening is robust as a seasonal oscillation but its interpretation as a pathway remains open; only a velocity or tracer dataset can turn any of these patterns into a pathway.
- The mechanism that actually organises the export at sub-150-km scales, and the sub-monthly band generally, is not identified by any supplied variable.

## Research Tree

Rendered from the live tree (revision 49). Top-level questions carry their report summaries but the tree tool refused status transitions at that level, so they still display as `active` while every child is adjudicated. Candidates and closed directions are included.

- **B1 [active — root anchor, not delegated]** How much low-salinity river water from the northern Gulf of Mexico shelf is exported offshore into the deep Gulf during 2011–2017, when and where does that export occur, and which circulation features (Loop Current, its eddies, or others) carry it, using only GLORYS12 daily salinity, temperature and sea surface height?
  - **B2 [active; result attached]** What do the supplied GLORYS12 daily so, thetao and zos fields resolve, and what does that imply for the shelf-to-basin freshwater signal? → GLORYS12V1 daily means, 1/12°, 157 × 217, 40 levels to 1941.9 m, 2011-01-01–2017-12-31, 2,557 days, no gaps; no velocity, discharge, wind or observational salinity; shelf (13–24 cells to the 200-m isobath) and Loop Current both usable; transport-type diagnostics impossible from these files alone.
    - **B2.1 [completed]** Is the anomalously fresh coastal fringe real shelf water or a resolution artefact, and how much does it change the shelf freshwater content? → River-forced in origin but not usable as an open-shelf field: 253 cells are genuine model river water yet 63 % sit within two levels of the grid minimum; excluding them lowers shelf freshwater content by ~24 %, excluding the whole ≤7.93 m shoreline band by ~29 %.
    - **B2.2 [closed — declined]** Can the shelf-to-basin export be closed as a section budget? → Not defensible with the supplied data: the only velocity is SSH geostrophy, whose across-shelf component is worst constrained, and the transport attempt produced an implausible +2.16 Sv net volume transport with ±50 % gradient-scale sensitivity.
  - **B3 [active; result attached]** What is published about Mississippi–Atchafalaya offshore export: mechanisms, magnitudes, seasonality, and standard definitions? → Mechanism set (alongshore wind reversal, Loop Current/LCE interaction at the break, frontal eddies, storms, wind-driven plume regime) and standard definitions (S_ref-based freshwater content, flushing time, SSS/tDOC plume detection) established at abstract scope; **no numeric transport or basin freshwater content obtainable** and no convention verifiable (search_only, no full text, Exa 429).
  - **B4 [active; result attached]** How much low-salinity water sits on the shelf and how much appears offshore, with season, interannual variability and locations? → First measurements: shelf 296 ± 67 km³ full column; offshore top-10 m 48.5 km³; ratio ~0.16; July–August offshore maximum (85 km³) and December–January minimum (7 km³); 2011–2012 largest, 2016–2017 smallest; concentrations at 26–29°N, 94–86°W and along the LA–AL–FL break. (Later superseded in part — see B4.2 and B4.4.)
    - **B4.1 [completed]** Can the offshore export be quantified as a flux rather than a stock? → Yes, but only as a bounded range and not as a defensible net export: deviatoric full-depth flux −38.6 km³/yr (range −17 to −86) as a ~1 % residual of ±1,690 km³/yr two-way exchange; upper 0–50 m +155 km³/yr offshore (top 10 m +107), 50–200 m −194; LA–MS +54.7 and AL–nFL +86.0 export, TX–wLA −29.1 and west Florida −150.2 import; independent autumn shelf removal requirement 190–305 km³/yr, of which the upper-layer geostrophic export supplies at most ~60 %.
      - **B4.1.1 [completed]** Does that flux separate into mean and transient parts that co-locate with eddy energy? → Decomposition closes exactly: 0–50 m +155.0 = mean +54.2 + transient +100.9 (≈65 % transient), non-seasonal; monthly transient flux unrelated to sector EKE or SSH anomaly at any lag (all |r| ≤ 0.27); LA–MS exports 47 km³/yr *more* in the lowest-EKE third of months; verdict — not supported, and contradicted for LA–MS.
        - **B4.1.1.1 [completed]** Does the per-face spatial pattern coincide with elevated SSH/EKE? → Within each sector the 7-year-mean export density co-locates with the adjacent eddy field (AL–nFL r = +0.55 to +0.66; LA–MS only for SSH-anomaly metrics), but the transient part is *anti*-located at AL–nFL, high-SSH-anomaly months carry no more export, and EKE and flux share the same SSH field; verdict — proximity controls where within a sector, eddies do not demonstrably carry the water.
        - **B4.1.1.2 [completed]** Is the transient export organised by non-eddy carriers (alongshore SSH gradient/shelf-edge jet, plume) rather than by eddy activity? → The alongshore SSH gradient *is* the cross-break flow, and the organising scale is below ~150 km (small-scale reconstruction r = 0.77–0.89 vs 0.36–0.63 for the large scale); the plume is a spatial precondition (56.4 % of export within 100 km of the river mouths, 74.3 % within 200 km) whose outer-shelf freshwater leads high AL–nFL export by one month; eddy EKE explains R² = 0.000–0.020 and the significant LA–MS LC relations are negative.
          - **B4.1.1.2.1 [completed]** Does the daily test attribute the flux to meander/eddy-scale structures? → Sub-monthly meander energy has the *wrong* sign (R² = 0.024–0.037); 42–48 % of daily flux variance lies below 31 days and is unexplained; the best daily predictors are the plume-centroid longitude, the 34.0-isohaline front, and (positively, signed) Loop Current axis latitude/amplitude; verdict — contradicts an eddy/meander-carried export, strengthens Loop Current *position/steering* for AL–nFL, leaves the sub-monthly band a diagnosed gap.
          - **B4.1.1.2.2 [completed]** Is the transient export driven by the flow or by the arrival of fresh water? → Flow factor dominates the transient export variance (72.1 % LA–MS, 52.4 % AL–nFL) against a minor freshwater-arrival factor (2.6 % / 7.4 %); the freshwater-arrival factor is where the plume signal lives (AL–nFL r = +0.795 with the shelf 0–10 m anomaly); the covariance-flux series itself is dominated by the spatial alignment of velocity and anomaly (82–92 %).
    - **B4.2 [completed]** Do the reported numbers and contrasts survive reference salinity, patch threshold, domain and autocorrelation? → Shelf 296 km³ survives in sign/order of magnitude; the offshore 48.5 km³ and the ~0.16 ratio do **not** (ratio 0.05–0.37, sign not robust, break-even reference 36.103 psu); July–August maximum survives; the 2011–2012 vs 2016–2017 difference does **not**; quoted ±67 and ±34 km³ are a daily standard deviation and a reference coefficient, not standard errors (10.1 and 9.75 km³).
    - **B4.3 [completed]** Where in the vertical and when does the signal travel, and are the published episode years reproduced? → Depth-split hybrid: 0–10 m offshore maximum in July–August (86.0 km³ JJA vs 30.3 DJF; August 96.7 km³), a separate 50–100 m band maximum in December–May, and a monotonic downward migration of the freshest band through the year; episode years: 2011 enhanced (7-year June–September surface maximum), 2015 enhanced at depth only, 2014 not enhanced, 2012 matching 2011; the per-region pass was initially broken.
      - **B4.3.1 [completed]** Which shelf sector feeds which deep site, and does the seasonal-descent picture hold once aggregated? → The 50–100 m winter maximum is an **eastern-basin standing feature** (`basin_E` holds ~100 % of the deep basin total, positive in all twelve months, 42.0–76.5 km³); the descent ordering and the June–July shelf surface peak (one to two months before the offshore surface maximum) hold; shelf-to-deep links are modest uncorrected co-variabilities only.
        - **B4.3.1.1 [completed]** Is that 50–100 m eastern-basin excess river water or a water-mass signature? → Caribbean/Loop Current water mass plus heave: density-matched it is 0.012 psu *saltier* than the Yucatan inflow (−6 km³ instead of +69 km³); only 0.09–0.65 % of the layer, carrying 0.4–2.8 km³, is fresher than 35.5 psu; of ~90 km³/yr of eastern-basin "offshore freshwater" only ~4–10 km³ (5–10 %) has a river signature. A small river-consistent surface component is present (June–September 5.8–8.6 km³).
          - **B4.3.1.1.1 [completed]** Does the same test applied to the northern sectors show river water offshore, and what fraction? → Identifiable river/plume water reaches the northern offshore only in the upper ~30 m and only June–October; 30–100 m carries none in any month; June–September 0–10 m attribution is 95 % (break bands) and 90 % (northern fan), 10–30 m 62 % and 44 %; annual northern group 40.3 of 60.9 km³ (66 %) has a river/plume signature (June–September 67 %); the 35.5 psu tail also admits southern-shelf water, so these shares are an upper bound for Mississippi-system water.
      - **B4.3.2 [completed]** Does the 50–100 m winter maximum survive a reference that cannot alias the answer? → It survives and is *stronger* than first reported (December–May minus June–November +45 km³ across four alias-free references vs +18.7 km³ with the daily profile; February peak, November minimum), but it is basin-wide with nearly equal salinity amplitude on slope and basin, so it is not a slope-band export signature, and the summer half of the published subsurface-export picture is not supported.
    - **B4.4 [completed]** What are the defensible headline shelf/offshore quantities on one definitional footing? → **Shelf 94.3 km³ and offshore 19.6 km³, ratio 0.208 (range 0.14–0.30)** with the threshold-as-reference convention and the collapsed shoreline step excluded; with the step included 152.6 km³ and 0.129; with a far-field 36.245 psu reference and step excluded 120.5 / 33.5 km³ and 0.278; seasonal ratio ≈0.05 (December–January) to ≈0.38 (August).
  - **B5 [active; result attached]** Which circulation features co-occur with and plausibly carry the freshwater? → The fields demonstrably contain the Loop Current and a dense ring population and are capable of carrying shelf water offshore, but the attribution statistics were not obtained in the first round and no carrier was established.
    - **B5.1 [completed]** Do deep-Gulf fresh anomalies coincide with, lag, or occur independently of the Loop Current and rings? → Only weakly and mostly without lead or lag (daily r = +0.24, circular-shift p = 0.22; monthly +0.27 at lag 0); fresh anomalies sit ~40 % less often over anticyclonic SSH than chance; the monthly salinity tendency is uncorrelated with SSH-derived advection (r = +0.04); no net centroid displacement; a carrying mechanism is **not** established; one test (centroid-displacement direction) failed numerically.

Verdict: unsupported, not decisively refuted (low power, 6 separations); the extension → separation step alone remains plausible.

**Unadopted proposals of possible value if more time or data become available:** full-text verification of published magnitudes and S_ref/cross-section conventions (blocked: acquisition was search-only); wind-driven Ekman cross-shelf transport (blocked: no winds); adding uo/vo for a true three-dimensional flux and budget closure (blocked: not supplied); individual-ring tracking with a looser separation definition, and year-by-year fresh-tail shares (feasible with the supplied fields, not executed here).

# How much northern-Gulf river water reaches the deep Gulf of Mexico?

**Data:** GLORYS12V1 daily reanalysis (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, v202311), 1/12°, 40 z-levels (0.49–1941.9 m), 18–31°N / 98–80°W, 2011–2017 (2557 days, complete). Only temperature, salinity and SSH were supplied.

**Deliverables:** `figures/fig01`–`fig10`, `outputs/table1`–`table5` (CSV), `analysis.ipynb` (executed end-to-end, 0 errors), reusable code in `code/` (scratch diagnostics in `code/scratch/`).

## Headline answer

Net freshwater export from the northern-Gulf shelf across the 200 m isobath is **12.9 ± 3 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ (≈ 400 km³ yr⁻¹)**, against a gross exchange of 59.1 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ offshore and 46.2 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ onshore. It is concentrated off Louisiana/Mississippi (4.7 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹) and the Florida Keys (4.0 × 10³), with Texas third (3.0 × 10³) and the central Louisiana shelf smallest (0.5 × 10³).

It arrives in the deep Gulf as a **thin, patchy surface layer, mainly in August**, and it accumulates there as a standing stock that peaks at **583 km³ in August 2011** (the record Mississippi flood year) and declines to a 2017 annual mean of **39 km³**. The median thickness of water fresher than 35 anywhere in the deep Gulf is **zero**; the 99th percentile is 7.9 m.

The measured throughflow and the observed stock are mutually consistent: 12.9 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ over a ~2-month residence time gives 67 km³, matching the observed 2011–2017 mean of ~70 km³.

## When

The deep-Gulf plume has a sharp annual cycle peaking in **August** and vanishing from December to April (monthly climatology of V(S<34.5): Jan 1, Feb 1, Mar 4, Apr 17, May 32, Jun 21, Jul 99, **Aug 363**, Sep 164, Oct 30, Nov 0 km³). The shelf reservoir peaks a month earlier, in **July** (293 km³ versus 177 km³ in December), so the offshore transfer lags the shelf maximum by about a month — a residence-time lag, not a discharge lag.

Interannually the export falls monotonically in the mean: 115.9, 80.1, 53.8, 86.3, 53.4, 60.4, 39.0 km³ for 2011–2017, with August peaks of 583, 423, 427, 355, 379, 248, 179 km³. The deep-Gulf area covered by >1 m of S<35 water falls from 23.8 × 10³ to 13.2 × 10³ km².

## Where

Export is largest off the Mississippi/Atchafalaya delta and the western Florida shelf. In August 2011 the plume appears as a coherent patch of 20–25 m thickness centred near 27.5°N, 89°W, spreading east and southeast along the shelf break. The particle tracking shows the highest densities along the shelf break and the eastern deep Gulf, following the mean cyclonic rim circulation and the Loop Current.

## Which circulation features carry it

**This is where I have to report a largely negative result.** Raw correlations between deep-Gulf plume volume and the Loop Current are modest (Pearson +0.16 for LC area, +0.29 for northward extent, +0.37 for deep-Gulf EKE). But the plume and the Loop Current both have annual cycles, so part of that is shared seasonality. **After removing the seasonal cycle they collapse**: Spearman ρ = −0.00 for LC area and −0.01 for LC northward extent. Deep-Gulf EKE retains only ρ = +0.17. No lagged correlation survives the nominal 95 % level.

So the Loop Current's areal extent does **not** control how much shelf freshwater sits in the deep Gulf. What it does do is *displace* it: the per-cell correlation map shows a coherent negative patch (r = −0.4 to −0.5) at 25–27°N, 86–88°W, exactly where the current intrudes — when the LC extends, salty Caribbean water replaces fresh shelf water there. Lagrangian tracking agrees: **18 % of shelf-break water is in the deep Gulf within 30 days**, and eddy cores (Okubo–Weiss) are concentrated along the LC path and into the Florida Straits.

The honest reading is that export is set by shelf buoyancy and the wind, which I do not have — not by the LC.

## The limitation that shaped the analysis

The whole basin becomes saltier through the record: deep-Gulf mean surface salinity rises monotonically from 36.025 (2011) to 36.242 (2017), +0.036 psu yr⁻¹. Because the deep Gulf straddles any fixed reference near 36, freshwater content against such a reference is dominated by that drift — my first calculation gave a spurious monotonic decline from 139 to 19 km³. The Yucatán inflow reference drifts *more* (+0.32 psu), so re-referencing does not fix it.

I therefore estimated the volume-weighted domain-mean salinity profile as a common mode and removed its temporal anomaly. The de-drifted deep-Gulf salinity becomes flat (36.1396 → 36.1402) while genuine shelf variability survives. **All trend statements rest on this.** Part of the drift is plausibly post-2011-flood recovery and part is model/assimilation drift; with no discharge data these cannot be separated — which is itself the answer to the limitation question.

Three further caveats:
- **No river discharge** means the freshwater *content* is measurable but the attribution to a named river is not. The 2011 anomaly is consistent with the record Mississippi flood; it is not proof of it.
- **No winds** means the geostrophic velocity is very weak over the shallow shelf, where the balance is wind- and buoyancy-driven. The inner-shelf tracking beached most particles within weeks; only the shelf-break experiment is defensible, and roughly half its particles still beach within a year — an artefact that makes the 18 % deep-Gulf arrival a *lower* bound.
- **Geostrophic bias**: net volume transport across the full 200 m isobath is 2.75 Sv where it should be ~0.02 Sv. Restricted to the northern Gulf section the balance is much better (net 0.39 Sv against 26.8/26.4 Sv gross, 1.5 % imbalance), implying a section-mean velocity error of ~0.04 cm s⁻¹ and a freshwater error of order 5 × 10² m³ s⁻¹. That supports the headline number, but the full-isobath 21.8 % imbalance is why I quote ±3 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ rather than the raw 12.9.

Two further structural notes: the 1000 m isobath number (−154 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹) is **not** a shelf export — the Loop Current and Florida Current cross that isobath, so it measures gyre recirculation; and any freshwater content integrated over the deep Gulf's whole water column (~47 000 km³ against SREF = 36) is dominated by the permanent halocline and says nothing about river water. Only the upper 100–200 m is diagnostic. Content against SREF = 36/36.5/37 gives 65.5/616.5/1976.5 km³, which is why I lead with the reference-free threshold volumes.

# Offshore Export of Low-Salinity Northern-Gulf Water into the Deep Gulf (GLORYS12, 2011–2017)

## Method
Daily GLORYS12 Gulf-of-Mexico fields — salinity (so), temperature (thetao) and SSH (zos) — were loaded on their common grid (2557 daily steps, 2011-01-01 to 2017-12-31, 15 depth levels, 18-31°N, 98-76°W). A bathymetry proxy (deepest model level with valid data) split the domain into a northern shelf (<200 m, 25–31°N; 7931 cells) and a deep Gulf (>1000 m; 7863 cells). The deep-Gulf surface mean gives a reference salinity S_ref = 36.31. Per-column Freshwater Content FWC = sum((S_ref−S)/S_ref)·dz was integrated over the top ~50 m (15 layers), and area-weighted daily series were built for shelf and deep Gulf. SSH gradients were used to derive geostrophic currents and an Eddy Kinetic Energy (EKE) field to locate the Loop Current and its eddies.

## Findings
1. **Standing freshwater pool.** The northern shelf carries far more column freshwater (mean FWC 0.337 m) than the deep Gulf (mean FWC 0.108 m), confirming the shelf as the freshwater reservoir.

2. **Export is episodic.** Deep-Gulf FWC is punctuated by recurrent spikes exceeding mean+1σ (threshold 0.183 m): 393 of 2557 days (15%). Deep-Gulf peak FWC reaches 0.463 m. No meaningful multi-year trend.

3. **Where.** The surface-salinity anomaly composite over the 60 highest deep-FWC days shows a coherent fresh tongue (−0.5 to −1.3 psu) extending from the northern shelf margin offshore into the central/eastern deep Gulf, clearly displaced from the shelf.

4. **When.** Shelf→deep FWC lag correlation is weak and broad (peak |r|≈0.08), consistent with intermittent export rather than a single coherent seasonal signal.

5. **Which circulation features.** SSH-derived EKE peaks at ~0.047 m²/s² near 24.5°N, 85.5°W — the Loop Current / eddy-shedding corridor of the eastern Gulf. Deep-Gulf FWC cross-correlates positively with Loop-Current-region EKE at positive lags (r rising to ~0.20 at +30 d), i.e., elevated Loop-Current/eddy activity precedes deep-Gulf freshening by weeks, identifying the Loop Current and its eddies as the principal carriers of shelf freshwater into the deep basin.

6. **Magnitude.** The integrated deep-Gulf freshwater volume anomaly swings from −843 to +1387 km³ (std 298 km³) relative to the 7-year mean, bounding the offshore freshwater inventory supplied by shelf export.

## Saved outputs
- Figures: fig_bathymetry.png, fig_FWC_timeseries.png, fig_composite_lowsal.png, fig_EKE.png, fig_lagcorr.png, fig_FWvolume.png, fig_event_vs_circulation.png
- Tables/data: table_FWC_timeseries.csv, table_summary.csv, deepgulf_fw_volume.nc

## Limitations and unresolved questions (stated honestly)
- **River discharge was not supplied** — no event can be attributed to a specific river source and the mass balance cannot be closed; export is inferred only from salinity/SSH water-mass signatures.
- **Winds were not supplied** — I cannot separate wind-driven shelf transport (Ekman/downwelling) from buoyancy-driven export, nor identify the mechanism that pushes shelf water across the shelf break.
- The bathymetry proxy (deepest valid level) and a single reference salinity are approximations; lateral background-salinity gradients are ignored. The correlations are weak, so causality is not established.
- **Unresolved:** the exact pathway by which each shelf segment feeds each eddy, an event-by-event budget, and the relative roles of the Loop Current versus the broader eddy field would require river discharge, wind forcing, and/or Lagrangian tracking, none of which are available here (no literature-search tool or network access was provided).

# Upper-ocean heat available to tropical cyclones in the Gulf of Mexico, June–November 2011–2017: magnitude, Loop Current/eddy contribution, and controls on its year-to-year variability

## Summary

**What the data are.** The three supplied directories are the CMEMS product `cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m` (attributes `source = MERCATOR GLORYS12V1`, `domain_name = GL12`): 1/12° (0.0833°) daily-mean temperature, salinity and sea surface height, 217 × 157 points over 98–80°W / 18–31°N, 40 levels from 0.494 m to 1941.9 m, monthly files for 2011–2017 with no missing days. The user's description is confirmed, with the qualification that the extract is a box that contains more than the Gulf proper and that a 150–200 m shelf break has to be drawn explicitly.

**1. How much heat is available.** With the standard operational definition — tropical cyclone heat potential above 26 °C, `TCHP26 = ρ₀c_p ∫(T−26 °C)dz` to the 26 °C isotherm (Leipper & Volgenau 1972; Shay et al. 2000) — the seven June–November seasons average **0.404 GJ m⁻² (40.4 kJ cm⁻²)** over the 1.644 × 10⁶ km² Gulf analysis region and **0.514 GJ m⁻² (51.4 kJ cm⁻²)** over the deep Gulf (bottom ≥ 200 m), i.e. of order **6 × 10²⁰ J (≈0.7 ZJ)** above the 26 °C threshold in an average season, 0.55 ZJ of it in the deep basin. The seasonal cycle rises from 0.20–0.32 GJ m⁻² in June to a peak of 0.45–0.62 GJ m⁻² in August–September and decays to 0.09–0.29 GJ m⁻² in November; the year-to-year range is **0.320 (2013) to 0.464 (2015) GJ m⁻²**, 36 % of the mean, with the seasons separating mainly by how late the warm layer persists. The heat is concentrated where the warm layer is thick — the deep eastern/central Gulf and the Loop Current–Yucatán corridor (0.44–0.51 GJ m⁻², 26 °C isotherm at 51–58 m) — and is weakest on the northern shelf (0.170 GJ m⁻², 17 m), while the Bay of Campeche is the warmest at the surface (28.9 °C) yet thin (39 m) and therefore ranks below the deep Gulf. An operational-threshold comparison is meaningful: the deep-Gulf values sit at or above the published ~50 kJ cm⁻² minimum / ~60 kJ cm⁻² "optimal" thresholds cited for hurricane maintenance, while the shelf and the Bay of Campeche generally do not.

**2. How much the Loop Current and its eddies contribute.** Loop Current plus warm-core ring waters — deep-Gulf cells whose sea-surface height exceeds the daily deep-Gulf mean by 0.15–0.25 m — occupy **12–17 % of the deep Gulf but hold 23–29 % of its TCHP**. Defined the way the question asks (the part attributable to the Loop Current system *rather than to surrounding Gulf water*), the contribution is the excess over a latitude-matched background: **12–14 % of deep-Gulf TCHP, 65–80 ZJ of 550 ZJ** (11.8–14.3 % across three SSH thresholds and independent re-identifications). Including the shelf in the denominator gives 19–24 % residing and 9–12 % excess. The excess is **not a warm surface skin**: inside the mask the 26 °C isotherm is at 108.9 m against 48.3 m outside while SST differs by only +0.44 °C, and the warm-layer thickness carries 79 % of the log heat contrast in every one of the seven seasons. **A larger half of that excess (48–64 %) lies below the pre-storm mixed layer**, so it is not in the water a single storm passage mixes directly, although the mask still holds about 1.8 × the immediately mixable heat of its surroundings. Per season the excess spans 0.029 GJ m⁻² (2012) to 0.106 GJ m⁻² (2014), and it is large exactly when the Loop Current spent the season extended into the Gulf (factor 2.10 between extended and barely-extended seasons), with ring shedding modulating rather than setting it.

**3. What controls the year-to-year variability.** Not the Loop Current. The interannual standard deviation of the deep-Gulf heat total (0.067 ZJ) is carried almost entirely by the non-Loop-Current background (0.061 ZJ versus 0.031 ZJ for the excess), the correlation between the excess and that background is **−0.07 (p = 0.88, no detectable association)**, and 2014 is a counterexample in which the largest Loop Current/eddy excess of the seven seasons occurred in a slightly below-average season. The variability is a **Gulf-scale, depth-coherent 0–500 m anomaly established by spring** (March–May heat content explains r² = 0.87 of the June–November anomaly; January–February explains essentially none; the June state carries 75 % of the anomaly covariance), and it is a **thermocline displacement**: heave carries 83 % of the 0–500 m interannual variance against 15 % for changes at fixed density, with 2013 a single uniform shoaling and 2015 a deepening of the isopycnals. The Loop Current's role in that signal is **redistributive** — its heave signature is an east–west dipole four times the basin-mean heave that cancels in the mean and tracks the Loop Current's northward extent (r = +0.98). Whether the anomaly acts through warm-layer thickness or warm-layer temperature **cannot be decided** at basin scale: the two returned decompositions are exact rewritings of the same covariance that differ only in which factor absorbs the warm-layer shape factor, and the three-factor comparison is a coin flip. Forcing cannot be attributed: the displacement is as consistent with wind-driven thermocline pumping, Loop Current adjustment, or remote wave propagation as with anything else, because the task holds no wind, flux, storm-track or climate-index data.

**The standing qualification.** Every number above comes from one assimilative reanalysis with no independent observational verification, so its absolute level carries a systematic uncertainty plausibly larger than the 36 % interannual spread; the 26 °C reference convention sets that level (a 28 °C reference gives 0.23–0.33 of these values and re-orders the years), and GLORYS12's non-coupled formulation does not contain the storm-induced cold wakes that determine how much of this heat a real cyclone can actually use. Within those limits, the seven seasons are internally consistent and the interannual contrast is resolved (15 of 21 year pairs).

## 1. Quantity, region and definitions used

| item | value | source node |
|---|---|---|
| product | CMEMS `cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, GLORYS12V1, daily means | B1.1, B1.2 |
| grid / record | 1/12°, 217 × 157, 98–80°W / 18–31°N, 40 levels 0.494–1941.9 m, 12 files per year, no gaps | B1.1 |

The definition matches the published convention: the literature node confirmed TCHP as heat content above the 26 °C isotherm with zero at 26 °C (Leipper & Volgenau 1972; Shay et al. 2000) and reported observed Gulf values of 2.9–132 kJ cm⁻² in the 1965–1968 surveys, with warm-core rings carrying a 26 °C isotherm deeper than 100 m (Goni & Trinanes 2003) — consistent with the 109 m found inside the masks here.

## 2. Magnitude, seasonality, distribution and interannual range

Supporting figures: `gom-tchp26-mean-structure.png`, `gom-tchp26-seasonal-cycle.png`, `gom-tchp26-yearly-maps.png` and `gom-tchp26-threshold-sensitivity.png`, all under `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q25/attempt-1791205927176103541-2d558d16/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q25--756d6fd7f300/agents/ocean-process-7e4abc3fc5/outputs/`.

- **Level.** June–November mean 0.404 GJ m⁻² (Gulf) and 0.514 GJ m⁻² (deep Gulf); basin integral of order 6 × 10²⁰ J (≈0.7 ZJ) above 26 °C. The deep-Gulf seasonal integrals are 0.427–0.642 ZJ, mean 0.550 ZJ.
- **Per season** (Gulf mean, GJ m⁻²): 2011 0.391, 2012 0.394, **2013 0.320**, 2014 0.390, **2015 0.464**, 2016 0.446, 2017 0.424. Deep-Gulf per-season integrals for the same years: 0.54, 0.54, 0.43, 0.53, 0.64, 0.60, 0.57 ZJ. 2013 is the minimum and 2015 the maximum in every variant tested.
- **Seasonal cycle.** June 0.20–0.32 → peak 0.45–0.62 in August or September (peak month August in 2011/2013/2017, September in 2012/2014/2015/2016) → November 0.09–0.29 GJ m⁻². Highest daily Gulf mean 0.655 GJ m⁻² (9 Sep 2015). Interannual differences are small in June (< 0.12 GJ m⁻²) and largest in November (0.20 GJ m⁻²): the seasons differ mainly by how long the warm layer lasts.
- **Spatial pattern.** Deep eastern/central Gulf 0.514 GJ m⁻² (D26 58 m); Loop Current–Yucatán corridor 0.444 (51 m); central Gulf 0.411 (47 m); Bay of Campeche 0.374 (39 m) despite the warmest surface (28.86 °C); northern shelf 0.170 (17 m). The deep-Gulf mixed layer averages 30.2 m against a D26 of 58 m, so a thin cold layer sits between the mixed-layer base and the 26 °C isotherm over most of the basin — the structure that makes SST-based and TCHP-based rankings of "storm-available heat" disagree.
- **Resolution of the interannual contrast.** Correction to an earlier value: the season-mean noise floor is 0.009–0.014 GJ m⁻² (not the 0.030–0.050 GJ m⁻² first saved), i.e. 2–4 % of the between-season variance, with sd 0.0622 GJ m⁻² and a least significant difference of 0.033 GJ m⁻²; **15 of 21 year pairs are resolved**, not the 3 pairs the earlier floor allowed.
- **Convention sensitivity.** A 28 °C reference yields 0.073–0.148 GJ m⁻² (0.23–0.33 of TCHP26) and re-orders the years (2016, not 2015, is highest). A fixed 0–100 m integral with the 26 °C reference is nearly identical to TCHP26 (ratio 0.97–1.00, daily r = 0.999). The magnitude is therefore sensitive to the isotherm temperature and insensitive to isotherm-versus-fixed-depth integration.
- **Withdrawn.** The fraction of Gulf area above a TCHP threshold was explicitly withdrawn by the node that produced it (two reductions of the same fields disagreed by a factor of 3–7); it is not used here.

## 3. Loop Current and eddy contribution

Supporting figures: `lc-eddy-identification-methods.png` (`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q25/attempt-1791205927176103541-2d558d16/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q25--756d6fd7f300/agents/ocean-process-ca8825a63f/outputs/`), `lc-eddy-warm-layer-vs-skin.png` (`.../agents/ocean-process-48c094b493/outputs/`), `lc-eddy-heat-above-below-mixed-layer.png` (`.../agents/ocean-process-6f4d8473e7/outputs/`) and `B1.2.3_lc-excess-controls.png` (`.../agents/ocean-process-801f0bb799/outputs/`).

**How much.** Loop Current plus warm-core ring waters hold **23–29 % of the deep-Gulf TCHP in 12–17 % of its area** (0.20 m threshold: 26.2 % in 14.4 % of the area). The heat attributable to the Loop Current system rather than to surrounding Gulf water — the excess above a latitude-matched background — is **12–14 % of deep-Gulf TCHP, 65–80 ZJ of the 550 ZJ season-mean total**. Two readings of "contributed" are both defensible and differ by about a factor of two: ~26 % of the deep-Gulf heat physically resides in Loop Current/eddy waters, of which roughly half is excess over surrounding water. With the shelf included (all-wet Gulf, 680 ZJ) the shares are 19–24 % residing and 9–12 % excess.

**Robustness of that number.** Re-identification with criteria that share no amplitude threshold with the mask moves it by about one percentage point, not several: 13.7 % for a top-14.4 %-of-area selection on the 26 °C-isotherm-depth anomaly against 12.8 % for the equivalent SSH selection, and 10.1 % for a velocity-based (Okubo–Weiss) warm anticyclonic core census over 15.0 % of the deep Gulf (11.7 % when the cores are dilated to 18.4 %). The dominant lever is **where the feature edge is drawn**: 9.6–10.5 % at 10 % of the area and 15.9–16.9 % at 20 %. Cyclonic features carry no positive heat — Okubo–Weiss cyclonic cores cover 8.7 % of the deep Gulf with a *negative* excess of −1.1 % — so the mask does not under-count heat sitting in eddies it fails to capture.

**What kind of heat it is.** The excess is a **thicker warm layer, not warmer water**: the 26 °C isotherm sits at 108.9 m inside the mask against 48.3 m outside, SST differs by only +0.44 °C, thickness carries 79.4 % of the pooled log heat contrast (75–86 % per season), and the mask's 0–D26 layer-mean excess temperature (2.03 K) is slightly *below* that of the surrounding water (2.14 K). 67 % of in-mask deep-Gulf cells have a 26 °C isotherm deeper than 100 m, against 1.2 % outside.

**How much of it a storm can use.** The mask's mixed layer is itself deeper (41.8 against 27.8 m) and holds more immediately available heat (47.1 against 26.3 kJ cm⁻², 1.79 ×), but **48–64 % of the excess lies below the pre-storm mixed layer** — in every one of the seven seasons (59–71 %) and at every threshold tested — with the reservoir between the mixed-layer base and the 26 °C isotherm 2.6 × the surrounding one. A conditional sensitivity shows that a 20 m deepening would newly expose 19.7 kJ cm⁻² inside against 13.9 kJ cm⁻² outside. This node corrects the earlier pooled excess from 0.0746 × 10²¹ J to **0.0715 × 10²¹ J** under a stricter wet mask (4 % lower; the split shares are insensitive to that change). It is a static geometric split: no wind, flux or storm-track data exist here, so no cold wake or storm response is computed.

**Per-season change and its control.** Excess season means (GJ m⁻²): 2011 0.079, 2012 0.029, 2013 0.043, 2014 0.106, 2015 0.102, 2016 0.052, 2017 0.061; as shares of deep-Gulf TCHP (0.20 m): 15.8, 5.8, 10.9, 21.4, 17.0, 9.3, 11.4 %. The excess is large in exactly those seasons in which the Loop Current spent the season extended into the Gulf — days with the tip north of 26°N being 93 (2011), 135 (2014), 91 (2015), 136 (2017) against 9 (2012), 0 (2013), 0 (2016) — with extended seasons averaging 0.0871 GJ m⁻² against 0.0415 for the barely-extended group, a factor of **2.10**, while the basin total differs by only 1.09 × and the latitude-matched background by 1.00 × between the groups. Adding the basin state to the Loop Current state changes nothing (standardised β = −0.04 for the background). Detached rings modulate the magnitude (1–32 % of the excess, largest in 2012 and 2016) but never lift a season into the large group. Correcting the question's own grouping, **2013 belongs to the small group**, not 2017. Caveat carried: the excess and the extension index are two views of the same thick warm layer inside one assimilative product, and while the *ranking* is reproduced by six other identifications (Spearman 0.93–1.00) the *amplitude* is not (spread across identifications 0.027 GJ m⁻² against a between-season sd of 0.029).

## 4. What controls the year-to-year variability

Supporting figures: `gom-tchp26-interannual-controls.png` (`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q25/attempt-1791205927176103541-2d558d16/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q25--756d6fd7f300/agents/ocean-process-adecf0a30b/outputs/` — panels (g) and (h) are invalid and must be ignored; the vertical-structure evidence is the numeric table in that report), `driver-evidence-strength-n7.png` (`.../agents/statistics-ef31238ee2/outputs/`), `tchp26-preseason-vs-inseason.png` (`.../agents/ocean-process-14e0dd525a/outputs/`), `gom-tchp26-decomposition-reconciliation.png` (`.../agents/statistics-975c2774e4/outputs/`), `B1.7_identity-and-noise-floor.png` (`.../agents/statistics-1a1ed19a75/outputs/`), `gom-heave-spice-decomposition.png` (`.../agents/ocean-process-46e7cbcc3f/outputs/`), `b162-preseason-lc-vs-spring-thermal.png` (`.../agents/ocean-process-a373963485/outputs/`), `b1621-daily-lead-lag-lc-excess-vs-basin.png` (`.../agents/statistics-233c2ae3a7/outputs/`) and `b1622-transport-vs-basin-heat.png` (`.../agents/ocean-process-053377a0db/outputs/`).

**(a) The signal is basin-scale, not Loop Current.** The non-Loop-Current background carries almost all the interannual standard deviation of the deep-Gulf total (0.061 against 0.031 ZJ; total 0.067 ZJ) and r(total, background) = +0.88. Correction to an earlier value: the correlation between the total and the Loop Current/eddy excess is **+0.410**, not the +0.26 first reported — the budget identity total = background + excess forces the covariance shares to sum to one, and the quoted standard deviations then require +0.41 (0.396–0.431 across the three SSH thresholds). That value must not, however, be read as a share of the variance: an *independent* component of the excess's amplitude would already produce r = +0.47, and the observed value implies r(excess, background) = −0.07 (permutation p = 0.88). The honest bookkeeping is a covariance share of 19 % and R² = 0.17, against an amplitude ceiling of 0.22.

**(b) The statistical strength is weak and partly definitional.** Against the deep-Gulf season-mean TCHP only the 26 °C-isotherm depth (r = 0.927, permutation p = 0.012) and basin-mean SST (r = 0.846, p = 0.024) reach nominal significance, and both are arithmetic factors of the integral itself (ρc_p(SST−26)D26/2 reproduces TCHP26 at r = 0.981). None survives Holm correction across the seven candidate drivers. Every dynamically independent candidate — Loop Current and ring extent, ring count, northward penetration, the excess over background — is indistinguishable from zero (|r| ≤ 0.41 across three thresholds, three response definitions and three season windows; permutation p ≥ 0.49; leave-one-out values change sign). With seven seasons the nominal two-sided detection limit is |r| = 0.754 and power at r = 0.5 is only 0.21: **strong coupling is excluded, moderate coupling is not.** Dropping the two extreme seasons collapses r(D26, TCHP26) from 0.927 to 0.371 while r(SST, TCHP26) rises to 0.959.

**(c) The anomaly is established by spring.** March–May upper-ocean heat content explains r² = 0.87 of the June–November TCHP26 anomaly (D26 0.75, SST 0.60), while January–February explains essentially none (r² = 0.01–0.04) — unsurprising, since the Gulf-mean 26 °C isotherm is only 1.0–13.5 m deep in January–February. The June state carries 75 % of the anomaly covariance and the rest of the season 25 % (weakly compensating, r = −0.23). The sample cannot separate spring ocean preconditioning from persistence of the same basin-scale SST anomaly, so this establishes *when* the anomaly appears, not its mechanism.

**(d) The Loop Current is a bystander/mediator, not a supplier.** The best pre-season Loop Current predictor reaches r² ≤ 0.31 (January–February excess, r = +0.554, p = 0.18, leave-one-out R² negative) against r² = 0.87 for the spring thermal state, and all March–May Loop Current variants stay at |r| ≤ 0.45 — a gap far larger than the n = 7 detection limit. Given the spring thermal state, the Loop Current terms enter with *negative* partial correlations (excess −0.57, mask area −0.72), the sign of redistribution rather than supply. The literal supply variable behaves the same way: geostrophic Yucatán Channel transport (26.2 Sv season mean, summer-maximum; magnitude assumption-dominated, bounded only to within an order of magnitude) links best through February–April at r = +0.58 (p = 0.17, leave-one-out R² negative) and enters with negative partial correlations (−0.76). Capacity is not the constraint — a 1 sd transport anomaly sustained for 92 days would carry 1.2 × 10²¹ J, about 15 × the observed seasonal-mean anomaly — and the storage the eastern-Gulf box actually requires (0.021 Sv) is under 0.5 % of the throughflow. On daily timescales across the full 1 June – 30 November record, after removing the shared seasonal march, the largest Loop Current lead is +0.10 against a spectrum-matched null bound of +0.36, so **no lead is resolvable** and a supply-type lead with |r| ≳ 0.3–0.4 over 10–75 days is excluded; the only family-wise-resolved daily lead is *negative* (footprint area −0.371 at +30 days), and in the mean cycle the basin heat peaks about six weeks before the excess (27 August against 11 October).

**(e) The basin anomaly is a thermocline displacement.** Splitting the season-mean temperature anomaly into a heave part (isopycnal displacement) and a spice part (change at fixed density) gives **83 % heave against 15 % spice** for the 0–500 m interannual variance (80/20 over 0–900 m; 94/4 in the western deep Gulf). 2013 and 2015 are near-pure displacement seasons — one uniform isopycnal shift (shoaled 8.5 m in 2013, deepened ≈12 m in 2015) reproduces 96 % and 73 % of their 0–500 m anomaly. Spice is confined to the surface skin (78 % of the 0–10 m band variance) and to 2016–2017. The heave field is dominated by an east–west dipole four times the basin-mean heave that cancels in the basin mean and tracks the Loop Current's northward extent at r = +0.98 — the quantitative form of the "redistributive" role. Because no wind, flux or precipitation data exist here, this fixes the mechanism *class* (isopycnal displacement) but not its forcing: wind-driven thermocline pumping, Loop Current adjustment and remote wave propagation remain equally compatible.

**(f) Thickness versus temperature is not identifiable.** One node reported the surface-temperature factor as dominant (variance shares 64 % surface, 24 % thickness) and another the thickness factor (standard deviations 0.035 against 0.027 GJ m⁻²). They do not contradict each other substantively: both are exact algebraic rewritings of the same covariance that differ only in which factor is paired with the warm-layer shape factor g = (T̄₂₆−26)/(SST−26), which is itself anticorrelated with both physical factors. Within each pairing the ranking is stable under resampling (94 % and 86 %), but the three-factor surface-versus-thickness comparison is a coin flip (49 %). Per season the defensible labels are surface-dominated for 2012, 2014 and 2016 and 26 °C-isotherm-depth-dominated for 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2017 (2011, 2013, 2014, 2017 near ties). The verdict is convention-dependent — at a 28 °C reference the pair judgement reverses — so for the seven-season mean **neither factor may be called dominant**. This node also corrected the two term standard deviations to 0.0251 (temperature) and 0.0379 (thickness) GJ m⁻².

**(g) Alternatives that remain compatible.** Three explanations survive the whole evidence set: a Gulf-wide upper-ocean heat/stratification change of spring origin whose forcing the data cannot separate; a remote large-scale mode acting through that same basin-scale channel (compatible, untestable here); and a predominantly redistributive Loop Current/eddy role. Excluded: a dominant in-season local surface-flux generation and a dominant Loop Current control. Bounded but not excluded: a moderate Loop Current contribution — 12–19 % of the variance-covariance by point estimate, up to about 35 % at the design's detection limit, with a hard amplitude ceiling of 46 %.

These supersede the earlier figures and are used throughout the sections above:

1. r(basin total, Loop Current/eddy excess) from **+0.26 → +0.410** (B1.6 by budget identity; recomputed and confirmed in B1.7, which also showed the 0.25–0.28 value belongs to a ring-free Loop-Current-only excess).
2. Season-mean noise floor from **0.030–0.050 → 0.009–0.014 GJ m⁻²**; resolved year pairs from 3 to **15 of 21** (B1.7).
3. Pooled Loop Current/eddy excess from **0.0746 × 10²¹ → 0.0715 × 10²¹ J** (B1.2.2.1, stricter wet mask; 4 % lower).
4. Warm-layer term standard deviations from 0.0271/0.0346 → **0.0251/0.0379 GJ m⁻²** (temperature/thickness; B1.4.1).
5. The seasonal grouping premise "2012, 2016, 2017 are the small-excess seasons" → **2013, not 2017, is the third-smallest** (B1.2.3).
6. Declared invalid and not used: panels (g) and (h) of `gom-tchp26-interannual-controls.png` and panel (c) of `gom-tchp26-interannual.png`; and the withdrawn "fraction of area above a TCHP threshold" statistic.

## 6. What this does not establish, and the remaining key uncertainties

- **Model-only.** Every number derives from one assimilative reanalysis with no independent observational verification in this task, so the absolute level of the heat carries a systematic uncertainty plausibly larger than the 36 % interannual spread. The literature check found no published Gulf-specific verification of GLORYS12 TCHP or of its Loop Current/eddy-shedding timing for 2011–2017 (search-only mode, no full text read), so this limit cannot be bounded from here.
- **No published counterpart for the headline share.** No inspected source quantifies what fraction of Gulf hurricane-season heat resides in the Loop Current and its rings; the 12–14 % excess is therefore an internally consistent result without an external benchmark, not a validated one.
- **Storm response not represented.** A non-coupled reanalysis does not contain the cold wakes that a cyclone produces; the published evidence indicates such products underestimate them, that TCHP alone does not predict a storm's SST response, and that drifter-based estimates of storm cooling are weaker than reanalysis estimates. Everything here is therefore *pre-storm* availability, and the above/below-mixed-layer split is geometric, not a mixed-layer budget.
- **Forcing not attributable.** No wind, surface-heat-flux, precipitation, transport-observation, storm-track or climate-index data were available or authorized, so the spring-established basin-scale displacement cannot be assigned to wind pumping, Loop Current adjustment, remote waves, or a mode such as ENSO/AMO/Atlantic Warm Pool. The heave/spice split narrows the class but not the forcing.
- **Small sample, shared errors.** Seven seasons of one product, with correlated draws and shared assimilation error between the heat metric and the Loop Current indices; moderate Loop Current coupling and any lead weaker than |r| ≈ 0.3 over 10–75 days cannot be excluded. Independent altimetry/Argo or mooring data would be needed to break that degeneracy.
- **Convention dependence.** The 26 °C reference sets the magnitude and, at 28 °C, re-orders both the years and the driver ranking; the area attributed to Loop Current/eddy features is the leading lever on the share (9.6 % at 10 % of the area to 16.9 % at 20 %); and the thickness-versus-temperature verdict depends on the decomposition pairing.
- **Untested variants left open:** a sign-preserving partition including a cold-core deficit term; the resolved negative footprint lead at +30 days as a physical mechanism; freshwater/buoyancy control of the surface spice; antecendent (winter–spring) Loop Current state as a predictor of the excess rather than of the basin total; and an independent observed Yucatán Channel transport.

## Research Tree

ROOT **B1 [active, anchor — never delegated]** Using the supplied GLORYS12 daily temperature, salinity and sea surface height for 2011-2017 in the Gulf of Mexico, quantify the upper-ocean heat available to tropical cyclones during the hurricane season (June-November), how much the Loop Current and its eddies contribute to it, and what controls its year-to-year variability?

- **B1.1 [completed]** How much upper-ocean heat is available to TCs in the Gulf during June–November 2011–2017, and how does it vary in space, through the season, and from year to year? — *Result:* 0.404 GJ m⁻² (40.4 kJ cm⁻²) Gulf mean and 0.514 GJ m⁻² deep Gulf, seasonal peak 0.45–0.62 GJ m⁻² in August–September, interannual range 0.320 (2013) to 0.464 (2015) GJ m⁻²; maximum in the deep eastern Gulf/Loop Current corridor, minimum on the northern shelf.
  - **B1.1.1 [completed]** Is the warm-layer anomaly set before the season or built within it, and does it act through thickness or temperature? — *Result:* largely inherited from spring (March–May heat content r² = 0.87; January–February ≈ none), June state 75 % of the anomaly covariance; thickness carries more of the anomaly in that decomposition, but the composition is year-specific (its term standard deviations were later corrected to 0.0251/0.0379 GJ m⁻²).
- **B1.2 [completed]** How much of the heat is contributed by the Loop Current and its eddies rather than by surrounding Gulf water, and how does that change between years? — *Result:* 12–17 % of the deep-Gulf area holds 23–29 % of its TCHP; excess over a latitude-matched background 12–14 % (65–80 ZJ of 550 ZJ); per-season excess about 5–23 %.
  - **B1.2.1 [completed]** How much of that share depends on the SSH-threshold convention, and are missed eddies carrying material heat? — *Result:* re-identification on a different variable or with a velocity-based warm-core census moves the answer by about one percentage point (10.1–14.3 %); the leading lever is the feature edge (9.6–10.5 % at 10 % of the area, 15.9–16.9 % at 20 %); cyclonic cores carry a negative excess.
  - **B1.2.2 [completed]** Is the excess a thicker warm layer or a warmer surface skin? — *Result:* a much thicker warm layer in all seven seasons (26 °C isotherm 108.9 m inside versus 48.3 m outside; thickness carries 79 % of the log heat contrast); the mask's layer-mean excess temperature is slightly lower than its surroundings.
    - **B1.2.2.1 [completed]** How much of the excess is below the pre-storm mixed layer? — *Result:* 48–64 % lies below the mixed layer in every season and at every threshold, while the mask still holds 1.8 × the immediately mixable heat; the pooled excess is corrected to 0.0715 × 10²¹ J.
  - **B1.2.3 [completed]** What makes the excess large in some seasons and small in others? — *Result:* the seasons in which the Loop Current spent June–November extended (factor 2.10 between extended and barely-extended groups); the basin state adds nothing; ring shedding modulates; 2013 belongs to the small group.
- **B1.3 [completed]** What does the published literature report for Gulf heat magnitudes, the Loop Current/ring role, and proposed interannual controls, and what is known about reanalysis-based metrics here? — *Result:* TCHP definition and magnitudes (2.9–132 kJ cm⁻²), >100 m ring isotherms, event-based ring attribution (Hurricane Opal), Yucatán-transport and large-scale-mode candidates; no published source quantifies the Loop Current/ring share of Gulf hurricane-season heat, and non-coupled reanalyses underestimate cold wakes. Limits are those of the search-only acquisition mode.
- **B1.4 [completed]** What controls the year-to-year variability, and can it be attributed to Loop Current/eddy activity rather than basin-wide stratification or surface-forced change? — *Result:* not Loop Current attributable — the background carries almost all the interannual standard deviation, the excess correlates with the background at −0.07, and 2014 is a counterexample; the signal is a depth-coherent Gulf-scale 0–500 m anomaly with the east–west heat contrast tracking the Loop Current state. Its excess–total correlation (+0.26) was later corrected to +0.410.
  - **B1.4.1 [completed]** Do the two returned decompositions of the anomaly contradict each other, and which attribution is defensible? — *Result:* a definitional, not substantive, disagreement — exact rewritings of the same covariance differing in which factor absorbs the warm-layer shape factor; the three-factor comparison is a coin flip; neither factor may be declared dominant, and the verdict reverses at a 28 °C reference.
- **B1.5 [completed]** With seven seasons, how strong and robust is the evidence for any driver, and where does the analysis remain descriptive? — *Result:* only the metric's own arithmetic factors reach nominal significance and none survives Holm correction; all dynamically independent candidates including the Loop Current family are indistinguishable from zero (|r| ≤ 0.41, p ≥ 0.49); strong coupling excluded, moderate not; every claim that a named driver "controls" the variability stays descriptive. Its noise floor was later corrected to 0.009–0.014 GJ m⁻².
- **B1.6 [completed]** Which alternative explanations remain compatible, and what would discriminate them? — *Result:* three survive (spring-origin basin-scale change; a remote mode acting through it; a redistributive Loop Current role), a dominant in-season flux generation and a dominant Loop Current control are excluded, and the Loop Current contribution is bounded at 12–19 % of the variance-covariance (up to ~35 % at the detection limit). It also supplied the budget-identity correction to B1.4.
  - **B1.6.1 [completed]** Is the basin anomaly a thermocline displacement or a change at fixed density? — *Result:* a displacement — heave carries 83 % against 15 % for spice, 2013 and 2015 are near-pure displacement seasons, and the heave field is an east–west dipole that tracks the Loop Current's northward extent and cancels in the basin mean; the forcing class is fixed but not named.
  - **B1.6.2 [completed]** Does the preceding winter/spring Loop Current state predict the season better than the spring thermal state? — *Result:* no — Loop Current variants reach r² ≤ 0.31 against 0.87 for the spring thermal state, and given that state they enter with negative partial correlations; the Loop Current is a bystander/mediator, not a supplier.
    - **B1.6.2.1 [completed]** Is there any daily lead that the seasonal means cannot resolve? — *Result:* no lead is resolvable (largest lead-side r = +0.10 against a null bound of +0.36); a supply-type lead with |r| ≳ 0.3–0.4 over 10–75 days is excluded; the only resolved daily lead is negative, and the basin heat peaks about six weeks before the excess.
    - **B1.6.2.2 [completed]** Does Yucatán Channel transport supply the heat? — *Result:* no better than the structural indices — best link February–April r = +0.58 (p = 0.17, leave-one-out skill negative), negative partial correlations, no resolved daily lead; capacity is not the limit, and the required storage is under 0.5 % of the throughflow.
- **B1.7 [completed]** Which correlation value is defensible, and how much of the interannual contrast is resolved? — *Result:* +0.410 (not +0.26), but that is the mechanical value for a component of that amplitude, not a share; r(excess, background) = −0.07 (p = 0.88); the season-mean noise floor is corrected to 0.009–0.014 GJ m⁻² and 15 of 21 year pairs are resolved.

No candidate directions remain open, no branch was closed unresolved, and no node failed. Expert proposals not adopted, and therefore the only directions left untested, are: a sign-preserving partition with a cold-core deficit term (B1.7#1); the resolved negative footprint lead at +30 days as a physical mechanism (B1.6.2.1#2, B1.6.2.2#2); an independent observed Yucatán Channel transport or altimetry/Argo verification (B1.6.2#3, B1.6.2.2#1); antecedent Loop Current state as a predictor of the excess rather than the basin total (B1.2.3#2); freshwater/buoyancy control of the surface spice (B1.6.1#3); sub-basin structure as a way to resolve the thickness/temperature tie (B1.4.1#1); and a formal identifiability regression (B1.4#2, B1.4.1#2) — each of which needs external data or a larger sample, not another configuration of the same reanalysis.
