# Onshore intrusion of Kuroshio water onto the East China Sea shelf northeast of Taiwan

**Data:** GLORYS12V1 daily reanalysis (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, v202311), 1/12°, 50 z-levels, May–Nov of 1993–2011 and 2023, 119–129°E / 24–35°N. Only `thetao`, `uo`, `vo` supplied — **no winds, no salinity**, so no density, geostrophy, PV or wind-forcing diagnosis. 140 monthly realisations.
**Deliverables:** `analysis.ipynb` (30 cells, all executing), `code/` (33 scripts), `outputs/` (derived data), `figures/` (9 final figures).

## 1. Transport

| | mean ± s.d. (Sv, positive = onshore) | 2023 |
|---|---|---|
| **Sector A** (25.22–26.30°N, NE of Taiwan) | **+2.57 ± 0.75** | +3.21 |
| **Sector B** (26.30–28.40°N, southern ECS) | −1.14 ± 0.64 | −1.47 |
| Net across the whole 614 km gate | +1.42 ± 0.48 | +1.74 |
| gross onshore / gross offshore | +4.09 / −1.52 | +4.91 / −1.70 |

The gate is the 200 m isobath of a land-aware smoothed bathymetry, 614 km from (25.22°N, 122.01°E) to (28.40°N, 126.65°E), median water depth 143 m. The intrusion is a **localised onshore branch confined to the NE-Taiwan sector**; north of 26.3°N the shelf break exports water instead. The two sectors are strongly anti-correlated (r = −0.85): the flow largely *sloshes* between them rather than varying in unison, which is why the net exchange (~1.4 Sv) is much smaller than the onshore branch.

**Robustness.** Replacing the contour gate by the straight chord joining its endpoints changes Sector A from 2.60 to 2.75 Sv (r = 0.979) and Sector B from −1.16 to −1.10 Sv (r = 1.000) — as required for non-divergent flow, the depth-integrated transport is insensitive to the gate's detailed path. Sector A is **8.9 % of the upstream East Taiwan Channel transport** (28.9 ± 4.5 Sv at 24.2°N over 0–1000 m; literature 20.6 ± 3.1 Sv — the model is biased high, so treat the fraction, not the absolute, as the robust quantity).

## 2. Depth

45 % of the Sector A transport lies above 47 m and 86 % above 92 m; the 0–50 m layer alone carries 1.21 Sv, ~47 % of the branch. That is essentially the whole water column over the gate (median depth 143 m) — the intrusion is not a thin surface film, but it is also not bottom-intensified. There is **no seasonal deepening**: the vertical structure is near-identical from May to November.

## 3. Timing

Maximum in **autumn**. Seasonal Sector A (May→Nov): 2.32, 2.32, 2.47, 2.58, 2.39, 2.97, 3.13 Sv; gross onshore transport also peaks in Sep–Oct. Year-to-year spread exceeds the seasonal amplitude (1993–2011 range 2.0–3.4 Sv). **2023 was the strongest of the 20 supplied years** (3.21 Sv, +0.9σ), with the excess concentrated in Sep–Nov (3.18, 4.58, 4.63 Sv) — an amplification of the normal autumn maximum, not a different seasonal shape. Being one year 11 years after the rest of the record, it is an outlier to report, not a trend.

## 4. Pathway and residence time (Lagrangian)

~340,000 isobaric particles released in the East Taiwan Channel (24.1–24.6°N, 122.0–123.3°E) at 8 depths on days 1/11/21, advected 90 days with a midpoint scheme on 12-h sub-steps.

- **Fast.** Median transfer takes **3.5 days** (IQR 3–5 d, p90 8 d) — a topographically steered jet, not cross-shelf diffusion.
- **Concentrated.** 92.3 % of crossings occur between 25.5 and 26.3°N (median crossing longitude 123.05°E) — the same sector that carries the Eulerian onshore transport. Crossing fractions by release depth: 35 % (10 m), 28 % (30 m), 30 % (50 m), 24 % (75 m), 27 % (100 m), then a collapse to 0.8 % at 150 m and ~0 below — a cutoff set largely by the shelf-break water depth.
- **Mostly transient.** 82.9 % of particles never reach the shelf; 13.6 % cross and return offshore; only **3.5 % are still over shelf water at day 90** (~20 % of crossers). Retained water drifts north-east along the shelf to a median end point of (29.0°N, 125.0°E).

## 5. What controls the variability

Two-way balanced variance decomposition of the monthly signal: **residual (synoptic/eddy) 59 %, year-to-year 26 %, seasonal cycle only 15 %** for Sector A. The seasonal cycle explains even less of Sector B (3 %) and the Kuroshio index (3 %).

Against the de-seasonalised Sector A anomaly (n = 140; |r| < 0.17 not significant):

| predictor | r (deseason.) | reading |
|---|---|---|
| Upstream Kuroshio transport (24.2°N) | **−0.38** | a *stronger* Kuroshio gives *less* intrusion — barrier, not source |
| Upper-ocean ΔT(0–100 m) | **−0.38** (−0.53 for KI) | weakly stratified column intrudes more readily |
| Eddy kinetic energy, eddy corridor S of gate | −0.21 | eddy stirring opposes the mean branch (weak) |

Lead-lag correlations peak at lag 0 (contemporaneous). A best 3-predictor regression reaches only **R² = 0.29**. So: **the intrusion is an eddy/synoptic phenomenon**, weakly modulated by the large-scale state — not a monsoon- or seasonally-driven one. On the seasonal cycle it is the weakly-stratified, weak-Kuroshio autumn that favours it, consistent with the observed autumn onshore migration of the Kuroshio axis.

## 6. Blockers and honest limitations

1. **No winds, no salinity** (as stated in the task). Density, geostrophic shear, PV, wind-stress curl, and any salinity water-mass census are impossible. Dec–Apr is not supplied, so the season of maximum winter-monsoon forcing is absent — "seasonal cycle" here means May–November only. The classical monsoon control of the intrusion therefore **cannot be tested with the supplied data**, and I do not claim it.
2. **Model bathymetry.** GLORYS12's shelf break NE of Taiwan sits ~0.5–1° east of some published charts; transports are attached to the model's own shelf break (self-consistent for a model budget) but geographical labels shift accordingly.
3. **Isobaric tracking.** Depth is fixed, so particles cannot ride a sloping thermocline and no vertical excursion onto the shelf is represented; this biases the retention estimate *low*.
4. **Fate diagnostic ambiguity.** "Retained" uses end-point depth < 200 m (3.5 %); the stricter shelf-side-of-gate test gives 2.1 %. Both are small and the conclusion is unchanged.
5. **Lagrangian vs Eulerian disagreement on ranking years.** The crossing fraction correlates with Sector A seasonally (r = 0.60) but only weakly year-to-year (r = 0.31); with 3 release dates per month, 2023 is the strongest Eulerian year yet the weakest Lagrangian one. The Lagrangian experiment is reliable for *pathway, depth, timescale* — **not** for ranking individual years.
6. **Reanalysis, not observations**, and a small sample (140 months; one year 11 years detached). Results are this model's answer at this resolution.

No literature full texts were downloaded (search_only); the literature anchors used (KI index box, ETC transport 20.6 ± 3.1 Sv, autumn ECS shelf-break onshore flux ~3 Sv maximum) come from public snippets only.

# Kuroshio onshore intrusion onto the East China Sea shelf NE of Taiwan — GLORYS12V1 analysis

**Data:** `thetao`, `uo`, `vo` (daily-mean, 50 depth levels, ~1/12°), domain 24–35°N, 119–129°E, May–Nov of 1993–2011 and 2023 (20 years × 7 months × 3 variables = 140 monthly-mean fields/variable; **no missing files**). Salinity and winds were NOT supplied → water-mass fraction and direct wind-forcing tests are impossible; intrusion is diagnosed from temperature structure plus velocity. All figures/tables are saved in `/workspace/outputs/`.

## 1. Transport
- **Onshore intrusion transport** (westward u<0, upper 0–200 m, shelf-break band 121.3–122.7°E, mean over 25–27°N): **0.59 ± 0.14 Sv** (range 0.26–0.97 Sv).
- Independent check, onshore flow through the east face of a shelf box (25–28°N, 120.5–122.5°E): **1.19 ± 0.37 Sv**.
- Both give a median onshore Kuroshio transport onto the shelf of **O(0.5–1) Sv**.

## 2. Depth
- The intrusion is a **subsurface** feature. Strong-minus-weak composite temperature profile grows downward to a **maximum of +3.0 °C at ~66 m**, decaying to +0.25 °C by 110 m; weak months carry a strong **cold** subsurface anomaly (−1.1 to −1.5 °C at 56–66 m). Depth scale ≈ 40–65 m (halved by ~78 m), signal to ~110–130 m — the Kuroshio Subsurface Water range (~50–150 m).

## 3. Timing
- Upper-200 m intrusion transport peaks **Jul–Aug (~0.6–0.7 Sv)**, weakest in autumn (~0.35–0.45 Sv).
- Upstream Kuroshio transport is largest in late spring/early summer (May–Jun ~44 Sv), least in Oct–Nov (~38 Sv).

## 4. Pathway
- Cross-shelf section at 25.5°N shows a coherent **onshore (westward) jet at ~50–150 m over the shelf break**, peaking ~−35 cm/s at 122.3°E, **bounded east by the offshore Kuroshio core** (+60 cm/s at 123.5–124°E). Strong-intrusion composites show warm subsurface anomalies with onshore flow; weak months show strong cold (upwelled) anomalies.

## 5. Controls on variability
- Q_intr is best predicted by the **shelf-box east-face onshore transport Q_ef** (r = +0.55; de-seasonalized +0.51, ρ = +0.57); partial corr(Q_intr, Q_ef | stratification) = +0.49 → robust. It also rises with stratification (r = +0.35) and shelf surface T (r = +0.38).
- The **upstream Kuroshio transport does NOT control the intrusion** (r = +0.10, p = 0.24; partial r = +0.09, p = 0.27). Kuroshio core speed is weakly anti-correlated with the intrusion (de-seasonalized r = −0.18) and with the shelf-break 110-m anomaly (r = −0.34).
- The 110-m shelf-break anomaly is essentially the **local shelf subsurface temperature** (r = +0.81 with T150; +0.88 de-seasonalized) and is negatively correlated with Q_ef (r = −0.48): stronger onshore flow advects cooler subsurface water onto the break. So the index reflects the **local shelf–slope advective-thermal balance**, not large-scale Kuroshio strength.
- Wind- and eddy-driven controls (winter monsoon, typhoons, eddy shedding) **could not be tested** (no wind data) — the main unresolved control.

## 6. 2023 anomaly
- 2023 has the **warmest May–Nov mean shelf-break anomaly of the record** (II_break +0.57 °C; T150 +18.05 °C), with a very warm early season (Jun +1.4 °C), **yet contains the three weakest months in the entire 21-year record** (Sep −1.24, Oct −1.73, Nov −1.84 °C). This is a late-season collapse of the *subsurface* warm anomaly while the *surface* stayed warm (Tsurf +0.7 to +1.2 °C) — consistent with late-season upwelling/mixing or reduced onshore transport of warm subsurface water, but the driver cannot be confirmed without winds.

## Limitations / unresolved
- **No salinity** → no true Kuroshio-water fraction; a temperature-only index may conflate air–sea heat flux with water-mass origin.
- **No winds** → interannual variability cannot be attributed to monsoon/typhoon forcing.
- Single reanalysis (GLORYS12V1), no independent validation; effective resolution ~1/12°.

## Saved artefacts (`/workspace/outputs/`)
- Figures: fig_bathymetry_regions.png, fig_mean_circulation.png, fig_section_25N.png, fig_section_velocity.png, fig_intrusion_depth.png, fig_pathway_composites.png, fig_monthly_pathway.png, fig_seasonal_cycle.png, fig_interannual.png, fig_controls_scatter.png, fig_controls_scatter_index.png, fig_synthesis_timeseries.png
- Tables: table_diagnostics.csv (140 months × 16 columns), table_summary.csv
- Report: final_report.md

# Summer coastal upwelling off Zhejiang–Fujian: strength, location, timing, and which proposed driver the supplied GLORYS12 fields support

## Summary

**Quantification.** In the supplied GLORYS12 daily fields (thetao, uo, vo), every May–November of 1993–2011 and of 2023 contains a Zhejiang–Fujian coastal cold band. Measured as the coastal band (20–80 km offshore, 26–31.5°N) minus a reference band (150–300 km), the June–September mean contrast is **0.91 ± 0.17 °C** for 1993–2011 (July–August mean **1.15 °C**), ranging from **0.61 °C (2002) to 1.21 °C (1998)** — a factor of two between the weakest and strongest summer. The coldest water lies **25–50 km from the coast in all 20 years** (not at the shoreline; the 0–25 km strip is *warmer*), centred at **28.9 ± 1.0°N**, with the −0.5 °C anomaly reaching 50–75 km offshore in 13 of 20 years. The signature is not surface-confined: the band's bottom water is 4.3–5.6 °C colder than its own surface every June–September. Timing under the primary definition averages onset **10 Jul** and peak **9 Aug**, but the timing is definition-dominated (see below), so the calendar dates are one defensible definition rather than an observed property.

**Drivers.** The fields **demonstrate neither proposed driver** — and, importantly, they do not exclude either. The southwesterly-monsoon (Ekman) branch cannot be measured at all, because no wind stress, sea level or vertical velocity was supplied; what can be tested — the structure the mechanism would imprint — is absent (the cooling is bottom-intensified rather than surface-intensified, the seasonal onset is bottom-first, and no velocity-derived quantity explains more than 4.3 % of the cold-band variance). The Kuroshio-subsurface/Taiwan-Warm-Current branch is best read as **compound**: its along-shore Taiwan Warm Current leg is clearly present (a persistent, seasonally flat poleward throughflow at the shelf break, poleward on 100 % of days in every bin deeper than 20 m) but is not shown to drive the cold band, while its cross-shelf leg — onshore subsurface supply guided by topography — is **not supported**: no onshore flow at the 50–100 m isobath survives a choice of cross-shore frame, no canyon- or shelf-break-localised onshore jet exists, the deep shelf-break onshore flow peaks in **September**, one to two months *after* the coastal cold-band peak, and the shelf bottom water is coldest at the start of the available window and **warms monotonically** through every season, so no colder water arrives during the upwelling season. The cold anomaly looks **inherited and re-exposed** by the seasonal thermocline rather than created by summer ventilation (bounded, not excluded — December–April fields are not supplied).

**What the data do support:** an annually recurrent, spatially fixed, summer-peaking but bottom-anchored coastal cold band, superimposed on a persistent Taiwan-Warm-Current-like poleward shelf-break throughflow, in a model whose cross-shore velocity cannot be used as an upwelling diagnostic.

---

## 1. Data and metric actually used

CMEMS GLORYS12V1 reanalysis (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`), daily `thetao`, `uo`, `vo` only, domain 119–129°E / 24–35°N, 1/12°, 50 z-levels (0.49–5728 m), 20 seasons × 214 days (1 May–30 Nov) for 1993–2011 and 2023. Every year contains exactly seven monthly files, so **no December–April data exist in the supplied files**; there is **no wind stress, no salinity, no sea level and no vertical velocity** variable. The box truncates the southern Fujian coast.

Primary metric (node B1.1): **CUI** = SST(150–300 km band) − SST(20–80 km band), area-mean over 26–31.5°N, **positive when the coastal band is colder**. It is a *thermal expression* of upwelling and cannot by itself attribute a mechanism. The raw index also contains the shallow shelf's seasonal heat budget (it peaks at 2–3 °C in October–November, above the summer band), so seasonal-cycle-removed anomalies were used for event-scale and interannual work.

## 2. Strength, location and timing, year by year

**Strength.** July–August 1993–2011 mean CUI 1.15 °C (the value defining the seasonal threshold 0.575 °C); June–September 0.91 ± 0.17 °C. Largest 5-day contrast of a season: 2.34 °C (2007) to 3.56 °C (2023), mean 2.92 ± 0.35 °C. Excess coastal cooling relative to the seasonal cycle (`cum_excess`) 7.5 °C·day (2004) to 60.6 °C·day (1995), mean 33.4 ± 12.9 °C·day — the metric with the largest relative interannual spread (±39 %).

**Location.** 25–50 km from the coast in **all 20 years**; latitude of the strongest June–September anomaly 28.9 ± 1.0°N, with 17 of 20 years between 29.08 and 29.42°N (the exceptions, around 26.7°N, are 1993, 1999, 2010); offshore extent of the −0.5 °C anomaly 50–75 km in 13 years, 75–100 km in 2 (1995, 1998) and ≤ 50 km in 5 (1999, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2023). Depth: the band's bottom is 4.3–5.6 °C below its surface in every June–September (mean 4.8 °C) — a bottom-anchored, not surface-confined, signature (see the cross-shore structure and bottom-field views in
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-50129ff0f2/outputs/cross-shore-structure.png` and `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-50129ff0f2/outputs/bottom-fields-jjas.png`).

**Timing.** Onset mean 10 Jul (doy 191 ± 26; earliest 16 Jun 1994, latest 22 Sep 1993); peak mean 9 Aug (doy 221 ± 28; 16 of 20 years between 11 Jul and 26 Aug); decay in August–September, but censored at the 15 Oct window edge in 10 of 20 years because the autumn shelf cooling exceeds the summer band. Onset and strength covary: the two latest onsets (1999, 2002) are the two weakest summers. Season recurrences and driver tests are shown in
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-50129ff0f2/outputs/timing-and-driver-tests.png`.

**How robust is this?** (node B1.1.1, which also corrected the wording of B1.1's mean-flow statement) Per-year **strength rankings** are stable across defensible surface-SST contrast definitions (pairwise Spearman 0.84–1.00, Kendall W = 0.95), degrade but do not collapse when depth/bottom-temperature definitions are added (W = 0.72), and are **not reproduced by any kinematic metric** (best Spearman 0.47). **Timing is the least robust quantity**: across 112 index/threshold/smoothing combinations the median per-year onset standard deviation is 42.5 d, larger than the 26 d interannual spread, and is driven almost entirely by the index definition (41.7 d) rather than by threshold (4.4 d) or smoothing (0.7 d). Definition sensitivity is visualised in
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/statistics-ada5caa4c3/outputs/upwelling-index-robustness.png`.

**Per-year values** (from the saved table `B1.1_yearly_upwelling_metrics.csv`; CUI = June–September mean, °C; the timing columns are the primary definition and carry the ±42 d definitional spread):

**2023.** 2023 was the **warmest summer in the record** (band SST +0.95 °C above the 1993–2011 mean, z = +3.2) — but the offshore reference band was also warm (+0.78 °C, z = +2.7), so this is a **shelf-wide thermal anomaly, not a demonstrated upwelling anomaly**: every upwelling-contrast and timing metric lies inside the 1993–2011 prediction interval, and the nominal "earliest onset and peak" is definition-dependent (2023's peak rank moves from 1st to 19th earliest across index definitions). The 1993–2011 versus 2023 comparison also mixes any upwelling change with twelve unsupplied intervening years (2012–2022).

## 3. The southwesterly-monsoon (wind-driven Ekman) mechanism

**What can be tested.** No wind stress was supplied, so the forcing cannot be measured; only the structural and seasonal signature the mechanism would imprint can be examined. Published work (node B1.4) treats the monsoon as setting the summer seasonal envelope of the Zhe–Min upwelling and predicts surface-led cooling with offshore surface transport; the literature channel was partly blocked (HTTP 429) and Chinese-language work is under-sampled, so that node is signposting, not consensus.

**What the fields show.** The signature is **not** present:

- The cooling is **bottom-intensified**, not surface-intensified (band bottom 4.3–5.6 °C below band surface every June–September); in August the inner shelf is 27.7 °C at 0.5 m over 22.8 °C at 25 m.
- The seasonal onset is **bottom-first** by about 18 days on average (16 of 20 years with fixed thresholds; 12–16 of 20 across definitions), and there is no vertical ordering within synoptic events (near-bed and surface anomalies correlate r = +0.61 at lag 0). Ordering evidence:
  `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-205a53e729/outputs/bfj-bottom-vs-surface-ordering.png`.
- **No velocity-derived quantity is usable as an upwelling diagnostic here.** With the seasonal cycle removed, no velocity quantity explains more than **4.3 %** of the cold-band anomaly variance (best single predictor 3.72 % over all days, 4.27 % in June–September; a post-hoc seven-predictor combination reaches 7.01 % with 5.53 % leave-one-year-out, against a 0.9 % chance level) — an order of magnitude below what a driver verdict needs. Continuity in a coast-following frame gives **downwelling** (−1 to −9 m/day) in the coastal band. See
  `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-1195346bf7/outputs/B1.8.1.2-coldband-vs-crossshore-daily.png`.

**Important qualifications (accepted from the discussion node B1.9 and from the frame tests).** The cross-shore component of the summer flow **cannot be given a reliable sign**: its sign flips within ±5.6° of the assumed coast-normal azimuth while the data constrain the azimuth only to 15–30°, and at the 50–100 m isobath two defensible frames differ by a median 36.6°, giving **+5.5 mm s⁻¹ (onshore) versus −60.0 mm s⁻¹ (offshore)** for the same quantity and the same days (see
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-7996b8b201/outputs/B1.8.1.1-frame-level-sign-controls.png`). Consequently "there is no Ekman cell" is **not** demonstrated either. Under the data's own per-cell isobath normals the June–August mean does carry the **classical two-layer sign** — offshore above ~20 m and onshore below ~35 m in the 0–20 km inner band (+20.0 mm s⁻¹ at 0.5 m, −19.6 mm s⁻¹ at 21.6 m, −34.0 mm s⁻¹ at 34.4 m; onshore on 89–96 % of days) — but the flow is ~90 % along-shore, that residual is only a few mm s⁻¹ of a 110–145 mm s⁻¹ along-shore jet, the curvilinear cross-shore field is less along-shore-coherent than the fixed-azimuth projection (0.806 vs 0.907), and the structure is **not connected** to the cold-band variability (no significant annual correlation; on the 428 coldest days it corresponds to ≈0.01–0.03 °C). It is a descriptive summer-mean structure, not an explanation of the cooling. Figure:
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-d8e1e72b17/outputs/B1.8.1-curvilinear-cross-shelf.png`.

**The one monsoon-calendar-locked dynamical signal.** The shallow (0–20 m) coastal along-shore current is poleward, peaks in July (1.09 m² s⁻¹ per unit width) and **reverses to equatorward in September–November** (78 % of days), while the shelf-break branch is **seasonally flat** (18.3–19.6 m² s⁻¹ in every month, 0 % of September–November days equatorward) — the signature of a seasonally reversing coastal branch on top of a persistent throughflow. A reversal of this kind is what the monsoon calendar predicts, but without wind stress it is not diagnostic. Structure:
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-c9a5e70af4/outputs/B1.7-alongshore-jet-structure.png`.

**Verdict on this branch:** not demonstrated; not excluded; and the fields do not show the classic surface signature the mechanism implies. The single most consequential missing measurement is **wind stress** (e.g. ERA5 along-shore component) — the user supplied only thetao/uo/vo, so this branch is untestable as posed.

## 4. The Kuroshio-subsurface / Taiwan Warm Current / topographic-guidance mechanism

**What is present (consistent with the mechanism).** A real, bottom-trapped cold layer: in every one of the 20 seasons the 20–50 m bin at 27.5–30.5°N is 6.6–8.2 °C colder than Kuroshio-box water at the same depth (cold on 92–100 % of June–September days), the 50–100 m bin is 4.7–6.3 °C colder, the anomaly is bottom-trapped (18.8 °C in the lowest 10 m at the 50–100 m bin, 20.7 at 10–20 m, 22.8 at 20–30 m, 25.6 at 30–50 m), the coastal anomaly relative to same-depth offshore water peaks at −8.2 °C in July–August, and the bottom water temperature (≈18.8 °C at 50–100 m) equals the offshore temperature found near 200 m depth. A persistent, depth-persistent poleward shelf-break throughflow is unambiguously present (poleward on 100 % of days in every bin deeper than 20 m; 11.8 m² s⁻¹ per unit width in the 50–100 m bin; continuous from the Taiwan Strait at 24–25°N to 32°N; near-bottom 10 m poleward at 0.09–0.15 m s⁻¹). Jet–cold-band relations:
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-c9a5e70af4/outputs/B1.7-jet-vs-cold-band.png`.

**What is not supported.**

1. **No summer ventilation of the bottom layer.** In all 20 seasons the 50–100 m bottom water is coldest at the very start of the available window and then warms monotonically (dTb/dt +0.002 to +0.017, mean +0.010 K day⁻¹; 15 of 18 tested seasons have their minimum within six days of 1 May). The cross-isobath (onshore-Kuroshio-pathway) advective term is ≈0 in the 50–100 m bin (−0.007 K day⁻¹) and a net *warming* in the 20–50 m (+0.19) and 100–200 m (+0.21) bins; the candidate offshore source is not colder than the resident shelf bottom water. So **no colder water arrives during the upwelling season**, and the summer cold anomaly is inherited and re-exposed by the seasonal thermocline. This is a bound (residual closure ±0.03 K day⁻¹) rather than an exclusion, and it rests on May–November only.
2. **The onshore near-bottom supply has no frame-independent sign.** At the 50–100 m isobath the disputed cross-shore flow is a few mm s⁻¹ residual of a 110–145 mm s⁻¹ along-shore jet on a nearly flat shelf (isobath-normal slopes 0.02–0.08 %); the isobath frame gives +5.5 mm s⁻¹ onshore, the coastline frame −60.0 mm s⁻¹ offshore, the frames differ by a median 36.6°, and switching the vertical level definition flips the sign inside one frame. **No onshore-supply statement can be carried from these fields.**
3. **No topographic guidance.** No canyon- or shelf-break-localised onshore jet exists; the onshore near-bottom branch, where present, is localised by **bottom depth** (h < 40 m inner shelf: 583 of 4033 shelf cells, mean −15.5 mm s⁻¹) while the 40–150 m mid-shelf carries near-bottom offshore flow, and the 150–600 m shelf break is essentially zero. The user's phrasing — onshore intrusion "guided by topography" — is therefore not reproduced.
4. **Wrong phase for driving the summer peak.** At the 50–100 m isobath the depth-integrated cross-isobath transport is **offshore in every month of May–November** (0.2–2.7 Sv), most offshore in June–July and least in September–October. The deeper 125–175 m shelf-break ribbon does show onshore flow peaking in **September** (+2.5 cm s⁻¹; September–November peak in 12 of 20 years, and onshore under a fixed 310° coast-normal in September–November), which matches a published shelf-break budget giving the Kuroshio onshore flux a summer minimum (<0.5 Sv) and an autumn maximum (~3 Sv) — but that autumn maximum is **one to two months after the coastal cold-band peak (9 Aug)**, so it cannot be the driver of the summer upwelling. (Only the *phases* survive all five cross-shelf definitions tested; amplitudes, and at some latitudes the sign, do not.) Figure:
   `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q29/attempt-1791228294381909006-458b65c8/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q29--aca6640d9bac/agents/ocean-process-d1aa5a5e4d/outputs/cross-isobath-transport-phase-zhejiang-fujian.png`.
5. **The Taiwan Warm Current is present but not shown to drive.** The poleward jet correlates with the cold band only weakly at daily scale (r = +0.26 for the inner-shelf jet, p ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁶ with AR(1)-effective n ≈ 290), not at all for the shelf-break jet (r = +0.04), with the *wrong* sign for the near-bed cold anomaly (r = −0.21), and not significantly between years (r = +0.31, p = 0.19, n = 20). Both are strongest in the south (r = +0.75 across latitude bands), but that is a shared northward decay of two coastal quantities, not evidence of a link.
6. **Water-mass identity is unresolved.** Salinity — the classical tracer for Kuroshio subsurface water — was not supplied, so the cold bottom water cannot be identified as Kuroshio subsurface water rather than locally formed water; the source-temperature ambiguity is not removable by further temperature-only analysis.

**Verdict on this branch:** the compound reading is best supported — the along-shore Taiwan Warm Current leg is weakly supported (a genuine throughflow, not shown to drive the upwelling), and the cross-shelf Kuroshio-subsurface leg with topographic guidance is **not supported by these fields and cannot be tested further without salinity**.

## 5. Overall conclusion

- The **upwelling signature itself is robust**: annually recurrent, spatially fixed (25–50 km offshore, centred 28.9 ± 1.0°N), summer-peaking, bottom-anchored, with per-year June–September strength 0.61–1.21 °C.
- **Neither proposed driver is demonstrated, and neither is excluded.** The monsoon branch is untestable without wind stress and lacks its expected surface signature; the Kuroshio-subsurface branch has a present Taiwan Warm Current but no demonstrable onshore supply, no topographic guidance, the wrong seasonal phase at depth, and a bottom layer that is inherited rather than ventilated in summer.
- Any attribution resting on the model's cross-shore velocity cannot be made with these fields: the cross-shore component is ≤ 4 % of the relevant velocity scale, its sign is frame- and level-dependent, and it explains ≤ 4.3 % of the cold-band variance. The temperature field, not the velocity field, is the evidence base here.

**Key uncertainties, all needing data not supplied** (so they are limits, not refutations): (1) **along-shore wind stress** — the decisive measurement for the monsoon branch; (2) **salinity or another tracer** — water-mass identity for the intrusion branch; (3) **December–April** of the same product — converts "inherited cold pool" from inference to observation and could reveal or exclude a spring intrusion; (4) **2012–2022** — separates the 2023 warmth from a trend or step; (5) **higher resolution with a realistic coastline and bathymetry** — the model is 1/12° and tide-free, resolves only water deeper than ~6–16 m, and its internal deformation radius is 0.5–1.7 grid cells, which is why the cross-shore sign is not obtainable.

**Correction trail carried in this answer.** B1.2.1 superseded B1.2's "robust August-to-September reversal" (it is an along-shore reversal only, and the cross-shore sign is unresolvable) and withdrew B1.2's internal conflict (which came from a mislabelled zonal component). B1.1.1 corrected B1.1's mean-flow wording and showed the timing to be definition-dominated. B1.5 and B1.3.1 each corrected a draft of their own. B1.8.1.1 superseded the sign of the 50–100 m near-bottom flow in both B1.6 and B1.8.1, and B1.8.1.2 corrected B1.8's sign attribution of the near-bottom covariance (the physically expected sign, at ~2 % magnitude).

**ROOT — B1 [active]** *Which proposed driver — the southwesterly monsoon or onshore intrusion of Kuroshio subsurface water guided by topography and the Taiwan Warm Current — do GLORYS12 daily temperature and velocity (May–Nov 1993–2011 and 2023) support for the summer coastal upwelling off Zhejiang–Fujian, and how strong, where and when is that upwelling in each year?*

- **B1.1 [completed]** Where, when and how strong is the coastal upwelling in each May–November of 1993–2011 and 2023, and how does it vary from year to year? → all 20 seasons contain the cold band; Jun–Sep contrast 0.91 ± 0.17 °C (Jul–Aug 1.15), per-year 0.61–1.21; coldest water 25–50 km offshore, centred 28.9 ± 1.0°N; nominal onset 10 Jul, peak 9 Aug; 2023 warmest summer on record.
  - **B1.1.1 [completed]** How dependent is the per-year quantification on index and baseline — do independent metrics rank the 20 seasons consistently, and is 2023 distinguishable from the 1993–2011 spread? → strength rankings robust for surface-SST definitions (Spearman 0.84–1.00) but not reproduced by kinematic metrics (0.47); timing definition-dominated (onset SD 42.5 d > 26 d interannual); 2023 distinguishable in absolute warmth only, no upwelling metric outside the prediction interval. *Corrected B1.1's mean-flow wording.*
- **B1.2 [completed]** Do the thermal and cross-shore velocity structures show the signature expected of locally wind-driven Ekman upwelling tied to the southwesterly monsoon? → only in its weakest form; no wind-driven Ekman upwelling demonstrated; cooling bottom-intensified; the only azimuth-robust summer flow signal is the poleward along-shore jet. *(Its "Aug→Sep reversal" statement superseded by B1.2.1.)*
  - **B1.2.1 [completed]** Does the Jun–Aug inner-shelf cross-shore flow carry the upwelling-favourable sign, or is its sign unresolvable? → unresolvable: sign flips within ±5.6° of azimuth against 15–30° of geometric uncertainty; best estimate +0.01 ± 0.03 m s⁻¹; the earlier daily-band conflict came from a mislabelled zonal component.
- **B1.3 [completed]** Do the bottom-layer thermal structure and velocity field show onshore advection of Kuroshio subsurface water along the bottom, guided by topography and the Taiwan Warm Current? → bottom-intensified cold layer and weak onshore bottom flow, but no demonstrated intrusion and no separation from local processes; no topographic onshore jet; northward bottom flow peaking in July.
  - **B1.3.1 [completed]** Is the cold bottom water ventilated in summer or a retained remnant re-exposed each summer? → remnant reading supported: bottom water coldest at the start of the window, warming monotonically in 20/20 seasons, cross-isobath advection ≈0; no colder water arrives during the upwelling season. *(Own draft unit error corrected; December–April absent.)*
- **B1.4 [completed]** What signatures, timing and amplitudes does the literature attribute to each mechanism, and what could the supplied fields discriminate? → monsoon sets the summer envelope; Kuroshio subsurface/Taiwan Warm Current supplies a bottom cold high-salinity source reaching the inner shelf near the 50 m isobath; discriminators are vertical ordering, seasonal phase and cross-shore structure; search channel partly blocked, Chinese-language work under-sampled.
- **B1.5 [completed]** Does the cold anomaly appear first at the bottom or the surface, how do cross-shore velocities lead it, and does this differ between strong and weak years? → bottom-first seasonal onset by ~18 d (16/20 years; 12–16/20 across definitions), no ordering within synoptic events (r = +0.61 at lag 0), no velocity series leads temperature (|r| ≤ 0.08); bottom amplitude grows 25 % versus 63 % for the surface between weakest and strongest summers; velocity separates neither driver. *(Own draft window error corrected.)*
- **B1.6 [completed]** What is the seasonal phase of cross-shelf onshore transport at the 50–100 m isobath — summer or autumn? → near-bottom onshore layer peaks Jun–Aug in 20/20 seasons; depth-integrated transport offshore in every month (Jun–Jul most offshore, Sep–Oct least); the deeper 125–175 m shelf-break onshore flow peaks in September, matching the published Kuroshio phase but 1–2 months after the coastal peak.
- **B1.7 [completed]** Is the summer poleward along-shore jet a coherent, depth-persistent, shelf-break-connected Taiwan Warm Current, and does it track the cold band? → a real, continuous, depth-persistent, surface-intensified shelf-wide current, seasonally flat at the shelf break and seasonally reversing only in the shallowest bin; weak daily relation to the cold band (r = +0.26 inner shelf, +0.04 shelf break, −0.21 near-bed), not significant between years.

# Summer coastal upwelling off Zhejiang–Fujian: strength, location, timing and drivers from GLORYS12 (1993–2011, 2023)

## 1. What was analysed

GLORYS12V1 daily reanalysis (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, v202311), 1 May–30 Nov (214 days) for 1993–2011 and 2023 — 4,280 daily fields on the 0.0833° grid, 119–129°E / 24–35°N, 50 z-levels. The supplied variables are **thetao, uo, vo only**.

Everything below rests on two families of diagnostics:

- **State** — `ΔT(cell,z) = T_shelf(cell,z) − T_open(same latitude row, z)`. The obvious index ("coastal SST minus shelf-mean SST") turned out to be **useless**: shallow water heats and cools faster than deep water, so it peaks in *November*. Comparing at the same depth and latitude removes both that artifact and the meridional gradient. `CBI = −ΔT_bottom` over the shelf (h ≤ 200 m, 25–30°N) is the primary index; it is 5.1 °C in JJA.
- **Kinematics** — layer-integrated **cross-isobath** volume transports (Sv) across the 50/100/200 m isobaths in three layers (surface 0–20 m, middle, bottom 20 m above the bed), with partial bottom-cell weights, plus the kinematic bottom vertical velocity `w_b = −u_b·∇h`.

Bathymetry was recovered from the deepest wet level of the mask (no bathymetry file is supplied); `∇h` is computed from a 5×5-smoothed masked field to define the cross-isobath normal.

## 2. Headline answer

**The data support the monsoon as the *variable* driver and demote bottom intrusion to a steady background condition.**

The only cross-isobath transport that varies with the upwelling is the **surface-layer offshore flow across the inner shelf**, and the only place a textbook two-layer upwelling cell exists is the **inner shelf (h = 20–50 m)**. The onshore flow across the 100 m isobath is indistinguishable from zero and explains **R² = 0.00** of the interannual variance; the onshore flow across the 200 m isobath is a nearly constant **0.19–0.26 Sv in every month, including November**, when the upwelling has already ended — a background supply of cold water, not a driver. The Taiwan Warm Current tracks the upwelling interannually but is collinear with the surface transport and cannot be separated with 19 years and no wind field.

## 3. Strength

| index (JJA, 1993–2011) | value |
|---|---|
| CBI, whole shelf h ≤ 200 m | **5.12 °C** |
| CBI, inner shelf 20–50 m | 5.35 °C (Aug peak **6.09**) |
| CBI, mid shelf 50–100 m | 5.48 °C (Aug peak 6.05) |
| CBI, outer shelf 100–200 m | 5.15 °C |
| cold area with ΔT < −7 °C | **69 × 10³ km²** (Aug 98 × 10³) |

Monthly climatology of the shelf-bottom anomaly: 4.17 (May) → 4.51 → 5.29 → **5.53 (Aug)** → 5.24 → 4.92 → 4.72 (Nov).

Interannual range is 4.45 °C (1994) to 5.78 °C (1998); the 1993–2011 trend is +0.0090 °C/yr (r = +0.15, p = 0.54) — **no significant trend**. 2023 ranks 13th of 20 at 5.00 °C.

## 4. Location

The cold anomaly is concentrated on the Zhejiang coast between 28 and 29.5°N:

| threshold | centroid | mean depth | area |
|---|---|---|---|
| ΔT_bottom < −4 °C | 28.39°N, 123.91°E | 81 m | 282 × 10³ km² |
| ΔT_bottom < −5 °C | 28.27°N, 123.70°E | 82 m | 205 × 10³ km² |
| ΔT_bottom < −6 °C | 28.07°N, 123.00°E | 77 m | 97 × 10³ km² |

The area-weighted latitude profile of the shelf bottom anomaly jumps from −0.9 °C at 25°N to −4.5 °C at 26°N, peaks at **−5.9 °C at 29.0°N**, and weakens north of 30°N. So the upwelling signature is a mid-inner-shelf (≈80 m mean depth, i.e. onshore of the 100 m isobath), Zhejiang-centred feature — not a narrow coastal ribbon, and not a Fujian feature in this reanalysis.

Cross-check: [Lou et al. (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1117/12.898140), from MODIS SST, put the Zhejiang upwelling core at 29.5–31°N in water shallower than 50 m, with mean area ≈ 11,000 km² and a 2007 maximum of ≈ 25,000 km². My footprint is several times larger, but the criteria are not comparable (they threshold absolute surface SST over a shallow core; I threshold a bottom anomaly against the open ocean over the whole shelf). What *is* comparable is the year ranking: they found 2007 strongest and 2009 weakest of 2007–2009; in my CBI, 2007 is 3rd strongest (5.51) and 2009 is 15th of 20 (4.90). **That independent agreement on relative year strength is the strongest external validation in this study.**

## 5. Timing

Onset/peak/demise = first/last day at CBI ≥ 5.0 °C (5-day smoothed, runs ≥ 5 days). An absolute threshold is required: the shelf is colder than the open ocean at the same depth on essentially every day of the record, so any threshold relative to the seasonal mean returns the entire season.

- **Climatological onset DOY 181 (30 Jun), peak DOY 226 (14 Aug), demise DOY 299 (26 Oct)**; mean duration 120 days.
- Interannual spread is the real story: onset DOY **134–208**, peak DOY **192–268**, demise DOY **212–335**, duration **12–201 days**. "The upwelling season" is a two-month-wide window, not a date.
- Extreme years: 1994 (12-day season — see caveat in §10), 2006 (201 days, earliest onset 14 May), 1998 (onset 20 May, strongest CBI).
- Lou et al. (2011) report appearance in June, peak July–August, weakening by late September from SST — consistent with my June onset/July–August peak, though my demise is later because a bottom anomaly persists after the surface signature fades.

## 6. Kinematics — where the two-layer cell lives

Layer-mean cross-isobath velocity, JJA, 1993–2011 (cm/s, + offshore):

| band | surface 0–20 m | middle | bottom 20 m | surf − bot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **inner h 20–50 m** | **+1.48** | +0.10 | **−0.76** | **+2.24** |
| mid h 50–100 m | +2.10 | +1.12 | +0.43 | +1.67 |
| outer h 100–200 m | +2.37 | +1.15 | +0.68 | +1.69 |

Only the inner shelf has surface-offshore **and** bottom-onshore at the same isobath. Mid and outer shelf flow offshore at every level. On the inner shelf the bottom limb peaks in July (−1.13 cm/s) and **reverses** to offshore by September (+1.07), while the surface limb peaks in July too (+1.70).

This is the classical upwelling cell, and it is *shallow*: the compensating return flow is confined to h < 50 m.

## 7. Attribution

Three independent tests on `CBI`.

**(a) Daily, deseasonalised, pooled JJA** (standard Bartlett effective DOF, N_eff ≈ 450 for the surface transport):

| driver | r | p |
|---|---|---|
| **surface 0–20 m across h = 50 m (offshore)** | **+0.113** | **0.017** |
| bottom 20 m across h = 200 m (onshore) | +0.057 | 0.23 |
| bottom w, inner shelf | +0.107 | 0.11 |
| bottom 20 m across h = 100 m (onshore) | −0.060 | 0.085 |
| TWC northward at 24.5°N | +0.170 | 0.34 (N_eff ≈ 34) |

The surface transport is the **only** driver significant at zero lag, and the lag structure supports causation in the right direction: r rises to ≈ 0.17 at lags −3 to −10 days (driver leading) and decays to 0 by lag +10. Wind-driven surface divergence precedes the bottom cold anomaly by roughly 5–10 days.

**(b) Interannual JJA means (n = 19, 1993–2011):** Q50_surf r = +0.46 (p = 0.052), TWC_24.5N r = +0.43 (p = 0.068), TWC_27N r = −0.37 (p = 0.10, unexplained sign), Q200_bot r = +0.21, Q100_bot r = +0.05.

**(c) Multiple regression:** R² = 0.30, of which the surface transport alone supplies R² = 0.21, TWC 0.17, Q200_bot 0.04, Q100_bot 0.00. The bottom-intrusion terms add nothing.

## 8. Heat budget (inner shelf 20–50 m, mean 0–50 m, JJA, °C/day)

```
dT/dt = +0.0408    cross-isobath adv = −0.0269    along-isobath adv = +0.0152
       vertical adv = +0.0460 (see caveat)         residual = +0.0019
```

Cross-isobath advection is **the only negative (cooling) term** and removes about two-thirds of the 0.041 °C/day warming of the inner-shelf column. Decomposed by layer, the sign works out as it should: the onshore bottom limb imports cold water (cooling), the offshore surface limb exports warm water (also cooling), and the bottom contribution wins.

## 9. 2023

- Onset DOY 189 (8 Jul), peak DOY 210 (29 Jul) — **1–2 weeks early** — but the season then persisted to DOY 334.
- CBI = 5.00 °C, **13th of 20**: a normal-to-slightly-weak upwelling year. Surface offshore transport 0.62 Sv vs the 0.64 Sv climatology.
- Yet the shelf-mean SST anomaly (vs the 1993–2011 daily climatology) climbs to **+1.0 to +1.9 °C from August through October**, entirely outside the 10–90% envelope. The all-shelf cold-bottom anomaly stays elevated late (Sep–Nov: 5.58/5.46/5.49 vs 5.24/4.92/4.72).
- Reading: the upwelling *contrast* in 2023 was unremarkable, but it happened on a much warmer background — the bottom water was warm in absolute terms. This matches [Oh et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-024-00846-4), who document an East China Sea marine heatwave from **12 Aug to 13 Oct 2023** with an unusually delayed onset, over exactly this region (25–34°N, 120–128°E) and using GLORYS12 profiles.

## 10. Honest limits and caveats

1. **No wind field is supplied.** The Ekman transport that the monsoon hypothesis actually invokes *cannot be computed*. I test the monsoon only through its kinematic signature — the surface cross-isobath divergence — which is consistent with, but not proof of, wind forcing. This is the single largest limitation.
2. **No salinity.** No density, no geostrophy, no thermal-wind shear, no stratification. The transports are layer means of the total velocity, not an Ekman/geostrophic decomposition.
3. **The continuity-derived vertical velocity is unreliable** (level-by-level closure error 6.5–9 × 10⁻⁵ m/s against a mean |w| ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s). The `advv` budget term is reported but no conclusion rests on it. Only the kinematic `w_b = −u_b·∇h` is used quantitatively.
4. **The interannual attribution is fragile.** 1994 is a severe outlier — a 12-day season and a 24.5°N section transport of **5.6 Sv against 26–52 Sv in every other year**, which looks like a data problem in the Taiwan Strait rather than a physical result. Removing 1994 drops Q50_surf from r = 0.46 to **r = 0.29**, TWC_24.5N from 0.43 to 0.17, and the daily zero-lag result from p = 0.017 to p = 0.056. **The interannual results are therefore suggestive, not established**; the pooled daily result is the more trustworthy of the two, and it is weak (r ≈ 0.11).
5. The Taiwanese Warm Current's own reported behaviour (stronger near-bottom intrusion between the 50 and 100 m isobaths, 10–17 day pulsation — see the [Acta Oceanologica Sinica 2011 analysis](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13131-011-0149-9) and [Jing et al.](https://doi.org/10.2112/JCR-SI50-106.1)) is *along*-isobath, and I measured only *across*-isobath fluxes. My near-zero cross-isobath flux at 100 m is consistent with the TWC carrying subsurface water along the shelf rather than across it, but I cannot verify the intrusion pathway directly.
6. Single reanalysis, single realization, no observational validation.
7. One documentation bug: the `kuro_north` index written in `step2_yearly.py` has dimensionally wrong units (m⁴/s, not m³/s). It was not used; the analysis uses `sec245_north`/`twc_north`/`sec305_north`. Similarly `sst_anom`/`bt_anom` in `upw_indices.npz` are identically zero because the anomaly reference and the averaging zone are the same — also unused.

## 11. Deliverables

```
analysis.ipynb               single notebook; executes end-to-end in ~a minute, 0 errors,
                             reproduces every number and figure above
code/lib_common.py           grid metrics, gradients, smoothing, distance-to-coast

```

All original data under `/import/home3/share/mafzhang/CMEMS_ECS/` were read only; nothing was copied or modified. Figures use a colour-vision-validated categorical palette; no chart uses two y-scales.

原始最终答案（英文）
## Final Research Report — Summer Coastal Upwelling off Zhejiang–Fujian (GLORYS12, 1993–2011 & 2023)

### Data actually analysed
GLORYS12V1 daily-mean potential temperature (thetao) and zonal/meridional velocity (uo, vo) on the native 0.083° grid, domain 119–129°E / 24–35°N, top ~300 m, May–Nov of 1993–2011 and 2023. **No wind and no sea-surface-height fields are supplied**, which bounds which drivers can be tested.

### 1. Strength
A cold coastal band exists every month of every year. Index UI = (offshore SST, 126–129°E) − (coldest near-shore SST, 120.5–123.5°E, 26–31°N):
- Climatological cycle ≈ +5.7 (May), +4.5 (Jun), +4.7 (Jul), +3.3 (Aug), +3.2 (Sep), +5.3 (Oct), +7.7 °C (Nov).
- JJA-mean UI = 3.0–5.4 °C. Strongest summers: 2001 (5.4), 1995 (5.0), 1996 (4.8), 2010 (4.7), 1993 (4.5). Weakest: 2002 (3.0), 1999 (3.1), 1997 (3.2). 2023 (3.7) is slightly weaker than the 1993–2011 mean.
- A year-round bottom cold pool exists: coastal 40–90 m water is only ~20.4–22.3 °C in Jul–Aug while SST reaches 27–28 °C (90–140 m water ~16–17 °C).
Figures/tables: `fig1_seasonal_cycle.png`, `table_coldband.csv`, `table_summer_by_year.csv`.

### 2. Location
Coldest coastal water sits at ~29–31°N, 121.3–123°E (Zhejiang, northern ZF shelf) adjacent to the coast, shifting to ~29.5°N in mid-summer and poleward in autumn. The 28°N section shows a coastal cold wedge (SST ≤26 °C at 121.5°E vs 28–29 °C at 126–129°E) extending down the shelf water column. Figures: `fig2_hovmoller_upwelling.png`, `fig3_section_28N.png`.

### 3. Timing
The cold coastal band is continuous May–Nov (never disappears). Stratification (SST − 110 m T) peaks in Jul–Aug (~11 °C), the classic upwelling-season structure.

### 4. Drivers
- **Southwesterly monsoon (D1): cannot be tested.** No wind data are supplied. The only indirect evidence is the JJA coastal cross-shore velocity, which is offshore (u>0) at essentially all depths, monotonically decreasing from +0.15 m/s at the surface to +0.05 m/s at 90 m and −0.04 m/s at 130 m: a weak surface-intensified offshore flow with weak bottom return — the sense of Ekman upwelling, but weak and overprinted by the background northeastward flow (u up to +0.6 m/s offshore). Not diagnostic.
- **Bottom intrusion / Taiwan Warm Current (D2): strongly supported as the setting, only consistent as mechanism.** A vigorous, year-round northward alongshore flow (vo ≈ +0.13 to +0.22 m/s through the whole water column) confirms the Taiwan Warm Current / Taiwan Strait throughflow. Cold (~16–17 °C) subsurface water lies immediately offshore of the shelf break and the coastal bottom cold pool is its obvious source — consistent with a topography-guided bottom intrusion. However, the monthly-mean box velocities show no resolved mean onshore bottom jet; cross-shore convergence at 55 m is ~1×10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ (noise level).
Tables: `table_velocity_shear.csv`, `table_master_index.csv`.

### 5. Verdict
- The data **strongly support** persistent ZF coastal upwelling (strong coastal SST minimum + year-round shelf-bottom cold pool) and a vigorous northward Taiwan Warm Current throughout the water column.
- The data are **consistent with, but do not uniquely prove**, topography-guided bottom intrusion of cold Kuroshio subsurface water (D2).
- The data **cannot test** the southwesterly-monsoon (D1) hypothesis because no wind is supplied.

### Missing evidence / unresolved questions
(i) Wind forcing needed to test D1; (ii) whether the mean bottom onshore flow is genuinely absent or simply under-resolved at 0.083° and monthly means; (iii) the relative quantitative contributions of D1 vs D2; (iv) no sea-surface height / geostrophic diagnostics for the TWC.

原始最终答案（英文）
# East China Sea SST fronts in OISST (1982-2023): mapping the fronts, how they changed, and why

## Summary

The supplied archive is NOAA OISST v2.1 daily 0.25° sea surface temperature restricted to a
120-128°E / 25-34°N box (1982-2023, 15,340 days, 864 ocean cells) — the middle and lower East
China Sea plus the northern Taiwan Strait, not the whole East China Sea. Inside that box two
coherent thermal fronts emerge: a dominant, all-season, NE-trending outer-shelf/shelf-break front
complex, and a subordinate inner-shelf coastal front present only in the cold half-year. They are
winter-strong and summer-weak, with a spring peak in frontal occurrence and an August-September
minimum.

- **Mapping (delivered figure):** `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q30/attempt-1791232367930798502-30d5182d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q30--eeaf3865a5d0/agents/ocean-process-ca172dcd60/outputs/ecs-sst-fronts-map-1982-2023.png`
  (climatological front axes, seasonal presence, plus the seasonality/trend panels in
  `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q30/attempt-1791232367930798502-30d5182d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q30--eeaf3865a5d0/agents/ocean-process-ca172dcd60/outputs/ecs-sst-front-seasonality-trends.png`).
- **Strength:** domain-mean front strength has **no established trend** over 1982-2023. The one
  front-strength change that survives scrutiny is a **modest winter intensification of the coastal
  band**, robust in shape (a weakening-to-strengthening reversal near 2001) but bounded in
  amplitude: +12 to +26 % raw between 1982-1991 and 2012-2023 depending on smoothing scale, with a
  **scale-independent physical part of about +10 % (defensible range 0 to +15 %)**.
- **Position:** **no front displacement is established** at this resolution; the coastal axis shows
  only a weak westward tendency in the direction expected from the warming pattern.
- **Seasonality:** the shape of the seasonal cycle did not change (spring occurrence peak, deep
  summer minimum, no change in the month of maximum). The reportable seasonality change is
  **winter-side**: a stronger winter-versus-summer contrast of the northern front.
- **Explanation:** the dominant, robust change in the record is a nearly season-independent
  **regional warming of +0.28 °C/dec**. The winter warming is spatially structured (largest
  122.5-123.5°E, and 84-165 km offshore of the Subei/Jiangsu coast), and that structure — not a
  change in frontal dynamics — **is consistent with** the coastal-band front intensification. No
  mechanism can be **demonstrated** here: the supplied data contain only SST, so buoyancy/plume,
  coastal-current, wind-mixing and air-sea flux explanations can be bounded or excluded but not
  separated.

Several statements made during the analysis were corrected by later, more focused analyses; those
corrections are flagged in the text and listed in Sections 4-7.

---

## 1. Data, scope and the leading caveat

- Source: `/import/home3/share/mafzhang/OISST/sst`, variable `sst`, daily, 1982-2023, 36 × 32 grid
  (0.25°), 864 valid ocean cells (B1.1). A companion `/import/home3/share/mafzhang/OISST/ice`
  directory covers the identical box and was **closed as irrelevant**: sea ice does not occur at
  25-34°N in this region in any year of the record.
- "Front" here means an axis of locally maximum |∇SST| (ridge of a 1-σ smoothed field), i.e. a
  strong-gradient axis, not a frontal jet; strength is a thermal-gradient proxy, not a transport.
- **The dominant uncertainty for every change claim** is that front strength is a spatial
  derivative of fields whose small-scale variance is not stationary. The within-month gradient
  variance of the coastal/northern bands is about 1.8× larger after 2007 than before (ratio 1.81,
  CI 1.47-2.28; best step year 2007) while daily SST variance is unchanged — the signature of the
  documented ~46 % pre-2007 OISST small-scale variance deficit (Pathfinder → operational AVHRR).
  Gradient amplitude is therefore inflated in the recent era, and no gradient-based series can be
  fully freed of this confound.

## 2. Where the fronts are (the map)

| axis | cells | extent (centres) | seasons present |
|---|---|---|---|
| outer-shelf / shelf-break complex (dominant, NE-trending) | 137 | 25.4-33.6°N, 120.4-127.6°E | all four |
| inner-shelf coastal front | 21 | 27.1-31.1°N, 121.9-123.4°E | DJF + SON only |
| minor summer axis (truncated by the 128°E boundary) | 4 | ~26.9-27.6°N, ~127.6°E | JJA only |

The union of seasonal axes is 164 cells, 19 % of the ocean cells. The dominant complex corresponds
to the published Kuroshio/shelf-break front; the coastal axis corresponds to the published
Zhejiang-Fujian (Zhe-Min) coastal front. The published Yellow Sea-Bohai front group and the
Changjiang-diluted-water front lie partly or wholly outside this box; the literature node notes
that the summer diluted-water front is principally a salinity/barrier-layer front rather than a
temperature front (B1.2).

**Thermal contrast** (two non-interchangeable measures): the instantaneous cross-front proxy at the
axis is DJF 1.9 °C, MAM 1.8 °C, JJA 0.9 °C, SON 1.0 °C over ~50 km; ridge-zone seasonal mean
|∇SST| is 3.77 / 3.57 / 1.82 / 2.06 °C per 100 km; the 50-km difference of the smoothed mean field
is a median 0.51-0.55 °C. At basin scale the expression is a DJF R2−R1 = +3.24 °C cross-shelf SST
difference and a JJA R3−R2 = −3.12 °C difference.

## 3. Seasonality (climatology)

Single-peaked: annual mean daily |∇SST| is 2.03 (coastal), 1.47 (outer), 1.54 (northern) °C/100 km;
monthly maxima are 3.48 °C/100 km (February, coastal), 2.45 (March, outer), 2.29 (February,
northern); minima are 0.57-0.94 °C/100 km in August everywhere; DJF/JJA ratios are 3.20 / 2.18 /
1.94. Front *occurrence* (P|∇SST| ≥ 2 °C/100 km) is 41-58 % in DJF against 1-6 % in JJA, with an
occurrence peak in March for the outer front (MAM 50.2 % vs DJF 41.7 %) and a February-April
plateau for the coastal front. The mean-magnitude maximum (February) and the occurrence maximum
(March) differ by about a month because the occurrence statistic saturates; this is a definitional
offset, not a contradiction (B1.1.1).

The published spring-peak/no-summer-maximum pattern is thus **reproduced**; the published absolute
occurrence values (7.01 % Kuroshio, 4.04 % Zhe-Min) are **not comparable** to a gradient-threshold
definition and remain unverified, because they come from per-pixel Cayula-Cornillon detection
(B1.1.1, B1.1.1.3).

## 4. How strength changed

**No established trend in overall front strength.** The subset-mean annual |∇SST| trend is
+0.017 ± 0.022 °C/100 km per decade (OLS p = 0.13), and every trend that B1.1 reported at OLS
significance loses it under dependence-aware inference: series have AR(1) up to 0.87 and effective
degrees of freedom as low as 4-6 (B1.1.1). A single linear trend is also the wrong model.

**The robust front-strength result is a two-stage coastal winter change** (B1.1.1, B1.1.1.1):

- Break at ≈2001 (95 % likelihood set 1992-2003), in winter-mean |∇SST| at every smoothing scale
  and in occurrence probability; slopes 1982-2001 = −0.55 → 2002-2023 = +0.78 °C/100 km per decade
  at σ = 1 (AR(1) p = 0.004 post-2002).
- The break is **not** aligned with the documented OISST input-stream transitions: trend-plus-step
  models at 2002/2007/2012 fit far worse than a free-break two-segment fit; the January-February-only
  series (whose first AMSR-E-affected winter is 2003) still breaks at 2003; and the change is
  winter-concentrated and coastal-confined, whereas an instrument or resolution change must be
  season-independent.
- A reversal of this kind and date matches the published Zhe-Min front intensity change (down to
  ~2002, up afterwards), so the published turning point is reproduced.
- **Amplitude, corrected twice:** B1.1.1.1 bounded the era increase to +12 to +26 % (best +12 to
  +20 %, lower bound 0 under full amplitude standardisation); B1.1.1.1.1 then **replaced** the
  "point" reading: standardising each cell by its own same-year roughness gives +20.9 % raw at
  σ = 1 but only ~+10 % for the scale-independent part, and the two defensible identifications
  disagree (+8.6 to +15.4 % temporal vs ≈+21 % cross-cell), with the functional form of the
  contamination unidentified. Defensible wording: **"+12 to +26 % depending on smoothing scale; the
  scale-independent physical part is ≈+10 % (0 to +15 %)"**
  (`.../statistics-75e3f133d4/outputs/ecs-coastal-winter-front-roughness-standardisation.png`).

**The strongest single front signal is in the north.** The northern coastal strip (121.4-122.6°E,
>30.5°N, 53 cells) shows DJF |∇SST| +0.323 °C/100 km per decade (AR(1)-residual p = 0.002;
  5-year block-bootstrap CI +0.246 to +0.592), era 1982-1991 2.16 → 2012-2023 3.13 (+45 %), while
  the rest of the northern shelf rises only +0.048 (CI −0.004 to +0.149); threshold-occurrence
  versions of the northern DJF change are also significant (bootstrap p = 0.021-0.034) (B1.1.1,
  B1.3.2). Note that B1.3.2 used a 381-cell northern mask versus B1.1's 317 cells, giving +0.083 vs
  +0.090 °C/100 km per decade — same sign and significance, slightly different magnitude. This
  strip lies partly (north of 32.6°N, 84-165 km offshore) in the **southern Yellow Sea off the
  Subei/Jiangsu coast**, i.e. the strongest relative winter increase is not in the East China Sea
  proper (B1.3.2.2).

**The outer/shelf-break front has no established full-record change.** Its only significant signal
is a first-half decline (1982-2001: −0.089 °C/100 km per decade, AR(1) p = 0.017) that vanishes
after 2002 (+0.015, p = 0.75). Consequently the published **opposite-sign pair (Kuroshio front
decreasing, Zhe-Min increasing) is not reproduced as a robust contrast**: the coastal-minus-outer
difference is +0.090 (bootstrap CI −0.043 to +0.231, p = 0.151), and the two fronts are better
described as the same two-stage shape with different amplitudes (B1.1.1, B1.1.1.3). A per-cell
occurrence analysis shows the outer front's change is spatially incoherent (149 of 276
AR(1)-significant cells negative, 127 positive), so "the Kuroshio front is weakening" is a
regional/definition-specific statement, not a domain-wide coherent decline
(`.../statistics-697c7cc12e/outputs/ecs-front-probability-change-map.png`).

## 5. How position changed

**Not established.** The chain of corrections matters here:

- B1.1 (OLS): winter axes drift 3-10 km/dec, coastal and northern axes west, shelf-break east.
- B1.1.1: only the coastal front's annual-mean longitude survives AR(1) adjustment
  (−0.022°/dec, p = 0.023); winter drifts are marginal (p = 0.059, 0.098) and non-monotonic.
- B1.1.1.2: the **sign pattern** of a winter front-pair divergence (coastal west ≈1.4-3.2 km/dec,
  shelf-break east ≈2.4-6.7 km/dec) survived dependence-aware tests and an equal-weight band
  metric, but amplitudes were metric-dependent by a factor 2-3
  (`.../statistics-34d340bec2/outputs/ecs-front-position-drift.png`).
- **B1.1.1.2.1 (latest, supersedes the shelf-break claim): no eastward shelf-break displacement can
  be reported.** Amplitude-free locators give +3.0 km/dec (95 % CI −0.4 to +13.1, p = 0.078), and
  per-row measures are non-significant at every smoothing scale (p = 0.41-0.80); only
  amplitude-weighted gradient centroids are significant, i.e. the signal lives in *where the
  gradient is strongest*, not in a front locator. A surrogate test confirms the pre-2007 variance
  deficit cannot manufacture a position drift.

Two limits make this a negative result rather than a proof of absence: the per-row metric has
28-35 km interannual scatter (minimum detectable drift ±20-26 km/dec at 80 % power) and the 0.25°
grid quantises position at ≈22-24 km, so a few km/dec is below resolution. What remains is a
**weak westward tendency of the coastal axis**, in the direction expected from the warming pattern
(uniform shelf warming predicts westward isotherm motion of 6-18 km/dec; the coastal axis moves
about one third of that, the other fronts less).

## 6. How seasonality changed

The **shape did not change**: no change in the month of maximum, single-peaked cycle, spring
occurrence peak and August-September minimum in both halves of the record; the domain's seasonal
SST-cycle amplitude changes by −1.5 % with unchanged phase (B1.1, B1.1.1, B1.3).

What is reportable is a **winter-side seasonality change in the north**: the DJF/JJA ratio of
northern front strength rises +0.122 per decade (AR(1) p = 0.001, moving-block bootstrap p = 0.002,
Mann-Kendall p = 0.0002) — the most robust front seasonality change in the record. B1.3.2 first
reported that 30 % of this came from a summer-side term requiring a second mechanism; B1.3.2.1
**corrected** this: on the northern mask the winter numerator alone still gives a significant ratio
rise in 5 of 7 front definitions (6 of 7 in the coastal strip), and the box-edge explanation is
rejected (removing the 128°E-truncated summer axis makes the offshore summer decline larger, not
smaller). A summer-season signal is real but **two-signed** (coastal summer strengthening, offshore
123.5-126.5°E summer relaxation) and only significant for smoothed amplitude metrics, so "the
northern summer front weakened" is not valid for the north as a whole
(`.../statistics-f96a652265/outputs/ecs-northern-summer-side-ratio-robustness.png`). The coastal
DJF/JJA ratio (+0.274/dec) and the coastal seasonal amplitude (+0.142) are **not** established
(AR(1) p = 0.026/0.19; bootstrap p = 0.14/0.12) — they are borderline at best.

## 7. Why the fronts changed

**The background change is unambiguous and large.** The box warms at +0.275 ± 0.073 °C/dec
(AR(1)-adjusted p = 0.028; block-bootstrap CI +0.045 to +0.373) — the only full-record trend that
survives every test — almost season-independently (DJF +0.258, MAM +0.330, JJA +0.248, SON +0.263).
Its spatial structure is a single coherent mode: EOF1 of DJF anomalies explains 55 % of the
variance with one sign everywhere and PC1 warms at +0.272 °C/dec (B1.3,
`.../ocean-process-773459403c/outputs/ecs-warming-pattern-front-change-mechanisms.png`).

**The front changes are consistent with the spatial structure of that warming, not with a change in
frontal dynamics.** Superimposed on the uniform mode, DJF warming is cross-shore structured
(+0.12 °C/dec in the innermost band below 121.5°E, +0.28 at 121.5-122.5°E, **+0.43 at
122.5-123.5°E**, +0.24-0.29 offshore), while JJA warming is flat across the shelf. The winter
coast-to-offshore warming contrast change peaks **140-165 km offshore (+1.26 °C)** against +0.22 °C
in the land-adjacent cell, and the winter coast-minus-mid-shelf SST difference fell by 0.48 °C
(CI −0.69 to −0.09) between the 1982-1991 and 2012-2023 eras (B1.3, B1.3.1). Three quantitative
consistency tests support this reading:

1. **Closure on the warming gradient.** The first-order prediction from the winter warming pattern
   reproduces the northern winter front change almost exactly (area mean +0.187 predicted vs +0.220
   observed °C/100 km; cell-by-cell in the strip 121.4-122.6°E: +1.00 vs +1.01 at 32-33°N, +0.89 vs
   +0.93 at 33-34°N), and the same closure holds for the coastal front (B1.3.2,
   `.../ocean-process-cbd3619322/outputs/ecs-northern-front-winter-warming-differential.png`).
2. **It is a gradient/contrast change, not a sharpening.** The front-axis-to-background gradient
   ratio is unchanged (1.89 → 1.98 at grid scale), and the increase is present in smoothed
   era-mean fields (+14.8 % for the coastal band), i.e. it is a coastal-band-wide change in the
   mean cross-shore structure (B1.1.1.1, B1.3).
3. **The land-adjacency alternative is bounded, not eliminated.** The land-adjacent strip — the
   only cells whose footprint can include land — carries 12-14 % of the southern coastal front
   increase and about 5 % of the northern strip increase; the ring profile of the winter front
   change peaks 28-84 km from land rather than at the coast; the isolated islands (Jeju, northern
   Taiwan) do not reproduce the mainland winter-deficit/summer-surplus fingerprint; and per-cell
   the front change anti-correlates with land-neighbour count (r = −0.11) (B1.3.1, B1.3.2.2,
   `.../ocean-process-bc42d2528b/outputs/ecs-northern-strip-land-adjacency-vs-physics.png`). The
   artifact and buoyancy hypotheses predict the *same* coastal fingerprint, so the ~5-16 % bound is
   geometric, not amplitude-based.

**What the data cannot do.** This is association, not attribution: the front metric and the SST
trend are computed from the same fields, and the record contains no wind, current, river discharge,
mixed-layer or air-sea flux data. Ranked by how well SST alone constrains them (B1.3):
spatial structure of the warming — constrained and sufficient; air-sea heat flux — partially
bounded (the seasonal uniformity excludes a change in seasonal monsoon heat exchange as the main
term, but a year-round flux change cannot be separated from advective import); Kuroshio/Taiwan Warm
Current — order-of-magnitude only (uniform-warming advection explains −40 to −97 km of the observed
29-209 km winter westward isotherm migration, allowing at most a modest extra onshore expansion);
river discharge/buoyancy — pattern-consistent but unverifiable, and B1.3.1's sector ranking
(Changjiang/Hangzhou Bay largest) was **corrected** by B1.3.2.2, which finds the Changjiang mouth
to be the *weakest* mainland sector, so a plume driver is not favoured; wind-driven mixing — not
separatable, and the sign expected from a uniform winter-monsoon weakening is opposite to the
observed cross-shore structure. The published mechanisms (tidal mixing with topographic slope,
monsoon wind and winter air-sea heat loss, river discharge, seasonal Kuroshio onshore migration;
B1.2) remain candidates that this dataset cannot test.

**Residual product-side caveats that remain open:** (i) the largest five-year step in the northern
strip increase is 2007, one of the OISST input-stream transitions, though the step is
winter-specific, ring-uniform in relative terms and not accompanied by a regional-mean SST step;
(ii) the ~46 % pre-2007 small-scale variance deficit inflates gradient amplitudes, so the front
amplitude carries a factor-of-two bracket; (iii) the pre-2007 variance deficit and the 2002
AMSR-E onset cannot be excluded as contributors to the exact date within the 1992-2003 break
window; (iv) the April-2023 ship-bias change is not a material driver (dropping 2023 changes the
main trends by < 0.05).

## 8. Key uncertainties that would need data not available here

1. **Cross-product replication** (CCI/C3S, MODIS/Himawari 1-2 km, in-situ Zhe-Min buoys): the only
   route to convert the amplitude bracket (≈+10 %, 0 to +15 %) and the 5-16 % land-influence bound
   into measured numbers.
2. **Non-SST drivers** (ERA5 wind and turbulent fluxes, Changjiang discharge, coastal-current or
   Taiwan Warm Current indices, mixed-layer depth): required to turn the pattern-match between the
   warming structure and the front change into a demonstrated mechanism.
3. **Higher-resolution coastal product**: needed to quantify how much of the coastal front's
   gradient OISST cannot resolve at 0.25°.
4. **Published attribution of the regional warming** was not separately reviewed in this run (the
   literature node covered fronts and front mechanisms, in search-only mode), so the +0.28 °C/dec
   background trend is reported as measured here, not certified against published rates.
5. **Domain truncation**: 120-128°E / 25-34°N excludes the Yellow Sea north of 34°N, the Korea
   Strait and the Bohai; the strongest relative winter front increase found here already lies
   partly in the southern Yellow Sea, and the supplied ice record is unusable in this latitude
   band.

## Research Tree

ROOT **B1 [active]** — Using the supplied OISST daily SST for 1982-2023 over the East China Sea,
map the main sea surface temperature fronts, determine how their strength, position and seasonality
have changed over the record, and explain the changes.

- **B1.1 [completed]** Where are the main fronts, their climatological thermal contrast and seasonal
  cycle? → Two coherent fronts mapped inside the 120-128°E/25-34°N box: a dominant all-season
  NE-trending outer-shelf/shelf-break complex (137 cells) and a cold-half-year inner-shelf coastal
  front (21 cells), plus a minor summer axis truncated by the 128°E boundary; winter-strong,
  summer-weak, spring occurrence peak; requested map and seasonality figures delivered.
  - **B1.1.1 [completed]** Have strength, position and seasonality changed, and do the changes
    survive dependence and record-inhomogeneity testing? → Corrects B1.1: only the warming
    (+0.277 ± 0.077 °C/dec) survives every test; the coastal winter change is real in shape
    (break ≈2001) but not as a linear trend; the published opposite-sign front pair is not a
    statistically established contrast; the spring-peak seasonality is reproduced; the northern
    DJF/JJA ratio is the most robust seasonality change.
    - **B1.1.1.1 [completed]** Is the post-2002 coastal intensification geophysical or a
      data-stream/variance artifact? → The ≈2002 break and the reversal are geophysical in timing
      (not aligned with stream transitions, winter-concentrated, coastal-confined); the amplitude
      is inflated by the pre-2007 variance deficit; the change is a coastal-band increase, not
      front sharpening.
      - **B1.1.1.1.1 [completed]** Can the amplitude bracket be narrowed to a point estimate? →
        Corrects B1.1.1.1: standardisation does not give a point estimate; +12 to +26 % depending
        on scale, with a scale-independent part of ≈+10 % (0 to +15 %) and the contamination
        functional form unidentified.
    - **B1.1.1.2 [completed]** Are the front-position drifts established? → Corrects B1.1 to
      metric-dependent 1.4-6.7 km/dec; the divergence sign pattern (coastal west, shelf-break east)
      was reported as established, amplitudes not; the divergence does not scale with the SST-trend
      pattern.
      - **B1.1.1.2.1 [completed]** Is the eastward shelf-break drift physical? → Corrects
        B1.1.1.2: no eastward shelf-break displacement can be reported — amplitude-free locators are
        non-significant (+3.0 km/dec, CI −0.4 to +13.1) and the surrogate test shows the variance
        deficit cannot fabricate a drift. Position change remains unestablished.
    - **B1.1.1.3 [completed]** Does the verdict change under the published probability-style front
      definition? → Definition-dependent in magnitude: the outer front shows no coherent domain-wide
      decline (149 negative vs 127 positive significant cells); the sign-stable features are the
      coastal-band winter strengthening, a widening coastal-minus-outer contrast and the ≈2002
      reversal; the published "decreasing Kuroshio front" is a first-half-of-record statement.
  - **B1.1.2 [closed]** Does the sea-ice record add anything to the winter front climatology? →
    Closed: the ice variable covers the same 120-128°E/25-34°N box where sea ice never occurs.
  - **B1.1.3 [closed]** How large is the OISST coastal-gradient deficit relative to a 1-2 km
    product? → Closed: requires a high-resolution product that is not supplied and is outside
    search-only literature mode.
- **B1.2 [completed]** What does the published literature establish? → Named ECS fronts (Zhe-Min
  coastal front along the ~50 m isobath, Kuroshio/shelf-break front, Yellow Sea-Bohai group), the
  summer diluted-water front being salinity/barrier-layer rather than thermal; published
  spring-peak seasonality; a published two-stage Zhe-Min intensity change (down to ≈2002, up
  afterwards) and a published opposite-sign Kuroshio/Zhe-Min pair; OISST limits: ~46 % pre-2007
  mesoscale variance underestimate, input-stream changes in 2002/2005-2007/2023, warming trend
